Cleaner, faster reading online with fewer adverts

Access to exclusive newsletters only for subscribers

These will include unique insight from our writers alongside thought-provoking opinion

Exclusive in-depth features and unmissable columnists for Mirror+ members

Click here to subscribe to Mirror+ now

Ed Miliband's first trip to Washington could have gone worse.

Ed Miliband, the newly minted Foreign Secretary, sensibly ignored shouted questions from reporters on whether he still thought Donald Trump was a "an idiot, a racist and a misogynist" on his way to meet Secretary of State Marco Rubio. He wouldn't want have to lie on camera in front of his host, that simply wouldn't do.

‌



Afterward, the readouts of the meeting from the two sides were different in exactly the ways you'd expect. The 90-minute meeting was productive and warm, our side said. They talked about the special relationship and NATO, Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz, just as you'd expect.

The US State Department's note of their chat was a little more curt, and had different highlights - particularly urging us to spend more on defence, a frequent bugbear of the President and a thorny subject for Andy Burnham. Spokesperson Tommy Pigot said: "The two discussed the importance of Europe taking on a greater role in its own security."

We understand Ed also met with top members of the Senate Foreign Relations committee while he was in town. I deeply hope he also had time to try a half-smoke from Ben's Chilli Bowl and had a cocktail in Off The Record, as all visitors to DC should.

‌



Tone Deaf in Vegas

Trump gave a speech in Las Vegas the other night. And that location alone tells you a lot.

It's the third time he's been back to Vegas since his second inauguration - and the second since April. So is he secretly slipping out and hitting the slots? Nah, it's just the only place his economic message is landing. Well, one bit of it. Maybe.

It's kind of understandable that people in Las Vegas like his "no tax on tips" policy. Vegas has such a big hospitality industry that there's a third rush hour at about midnight, because that's when casino shift changes tend to be. The other thing Vegas has a lot of, which Trump doesn't seem so keen to talk about is undocumented workers. If Trump carried out his promise of mass deportations in Sin City, it would most likely sink into the desert.

Article continues below

Anyway, if Trump's going to Vegas for the second time in four months, it means someone in his team has decided to try and get him on message again. Their third shot at a reboot as the Republican Party stares down a severe drubbing in November's midterm elections. All he needs to do is get up on that stage, say "NO TAX ON TIPS" and then shut up.

Of course he didn't. He said "NO TAX ON TIPS" a few times, then it was all "the communists are coming" and "I want to fire the Supreme Court", and "the radical left want to ban gasoline". And that's why he has a 38% approval rating.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe murder probe cops reopen investigation into attempted burglary
News.content:
Ann Widdecombe murder probe cops reopen investigation into attempted burglary

Terror cops investigating Ann Widdecombe's death have re-opened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year

View 3 Images Police investigating the death of Ann Widdecombe have issued an update (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Terror police investigating the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe have reopened a probe into reports of an attempted burglary at an address in London last year.

The Met Police received a report of the incident in April. Enquiries were carried out by the force working with Counter Terrorism cops. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed, "pending any new lines of enquiry".

The attempted burglary investigation has now been re-opened with counter-terror cops in London identifying a new line of enquiry which was not pursued at the time "which may have been relevant", senior national co-ordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said.

Meanwhile, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) say they are investigating the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member amid allegations they "failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry" related to the attempted burglary. This was a "mandatory conduct referral" the IOPC said.

View 3 Images Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home on July 9 (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/Shutterstock)

Ann Widdecombe, who was 78, died after she was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times, a court was told last month as a 28-year-old man appeared in court charged with her murder.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham, South Yorkshire, appeared in Westminster Magistrates Court accused of attacking the ex-Tory MP turned Reform spokesperson at her home in Devon.

Kerry was also arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism – but he has not been charged with this offence.

View 3 Images A sketch of Kerry when he appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court (Image: Julia Quenzler / SWNS)

Article continues below

An IOPC statement on the latest developments said: "We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today,” a spokesperson for the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

"The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.

"Counter Terrorism Policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage."

News.title: 'Gunman' bursts into US hospital sparking lockdown and huge police response
News.content:
'Gunman' bursts into US hospital sparking lockdown and huge police response

The lone male suspect remains contained inside the emergency department at Bonney Lake Hospital, near Seattle, authorities have said

View 2 Images Armed police officers rushed to the scene at Bonney Lake Hospital (Image: Komo News)

A man has walked into the emergency department at a US hospital then claimed to be armed and issued threats, triggering a hospital lockdown and a massive police response.

‌



The incident at MultiCare Bonney Lake Hospital began to unfold at around 9:20 am local time (5.20pm UK time) when the man entered the emergency room and made the threats, Bonney Lake Police Chief Mark Berry said.

‌



The hospital was immediately placed on lockdown with Bonney Lake police officers and Pierce County Sheriff's Office deputies rushing to the scene. Patients were evacuated from the building, Berry said.

‌



The lone male suspect remains contained within the emergency department, authorities have said. SWAT officers and crisis negotiators are at the scene and are actively in talks with the man. Berry said there is no threat to the public outside the immediate vicinity and that authorities are hopeful for a peaceful resolution.

View 2 Images SWAT negotiators are at the scene (Image: Komo News)

‌



Man fights for life after plunging from Majorca flats onto pair drinking at bar READ MORE :

In an official statement, MultiCare confirmed that all staff and patients are safe and that no injuries have been reported.

It said: "We are currently responding to a security incident in the MultiCare Bonney Lake Emergency Department. All staff and patients are safe, and there are no reported injuries," the statement read. "Bonney Lake Police are on site and working with a negotiator. The safety and well-being of our patients, staff, and community remain our highest priorities. We are closely coordinating with law enforcement and will share additional information when available."

The hospital confirmed that the Bonney Lake Emergency Department has been closed and is not accepting patients.

Article continues below

Authorities have yet to release further details regarding the suspect or a possible motive. Negotiations were still ongoing on Friday.

News.title: Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
News.content:
Levy, from Tottenham, north London, was found guilty at the Old Bailey on Friday of two counts of murder, two counts of rape, grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation.

He was remanded into custody ahead of sentencing on 12 August.

The IOPC later confirmed its investigation began in January following a voluntary conduct referral from the Metropolitan Police and remains ongoing.

It added that issuing misconduct or gross misconduct notices does not necessarily mean disciplinary proceedings will follow.

The watchdog is examining the management of Levy over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 on sexual assault charges up to his arrest in September 2025.

Levy had been released from prison on licence in February 2023 and was briefly returned to prison in May 2024 after being accused of rape and breaching his licence conditions but was not charged.

On Friday, he was convicted at the Old Bailey of two murders, rape and other charges including grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation against the surviving woman.

The jury, which was given a majority direction in the trial, found him guilty on all counts.

During his trial jurors heard Levy had a string of convictions for attacking women dating back to July 2018, including one carried out against a prison officer in 2022.

An IOPC spokesperson said: "We are examining whether action could or should have been taken to prevent his reoffending, and if all officers involved in his management followed policies, procedures, and training.

"We are also assessing whether any learning, whether individual, force-wide, or nationally, or other changes should be implemented in light of the events under investigation."

News.title: Counter-terror police reopen attempted burglary probe as part of Widdecombe inquiry
News.content:
Counter-terrorism police investigating the death of ex-MP Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into a report of an attempted burglary at a London address in April last year.

The BBC understands the reported incident occurred at a property used by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. No arrests were made and the investigation was closed.

On Friday Counter Terrorism Policing said a line of inquiry had been identified that was not "pursued by them at the time".

Counter Terrorism Policing London has made a mandatory referral over its handling of the initial investigation to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The Metropolitan Police had received a report of an attempted burglary in the Greater London area, the statement said, with the initial investigation carried out by the Metropolitan Police and Counter Terrorism Policing London.

The BBC understands that the incident being referred to as an "attempted burglary" in the statement from Counter Terrorism Policing was one at Nigel Farage's home in south London.

Farage has previously referred to it as a "lit incendiary device" being pushed through his letterbox.

Police had said "damage was caused to a door but nothing was stolen".

The police watchdog has said it is investigating allegations that a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member "failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry" related to the attempted burglary.

"We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a Counter Terrorism Policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of enquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025.

"Counter Terrorism Policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage."

Ann Widdecombe, the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman, was found dead at her home in Devon last month with serious injuries.

Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was later charged with her murder.

Kerry was initially arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July, before being additionally arrested on 13 July on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism.

Widdecombe had served as Tory MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.

News.title: Infantino denies claims Uefa paid off alleged 'lover'
News.content:
Gianni Infantino's alleged lover was given a severance payment over the affair by Uefa while he was its general secretary, according to a Daily Telegraph investigation, external.

A spokesman for the now Fifa president was reported to have told the paper Infantino "strongly denies these categorically untrue allegations".

Uefa, for whom Infantino was general secretary from 2009 to 2016, issued a statement confirming "a departure payment was made to the individual in question".

The allegations come as Infantino fights for his future as Fifa president following his aborted plans to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

BBC Sport has contacted Fifa and Infantino for comment.

The Telegraph reported that Uefa paid a six-figure sum to the woman, who had an alleged relationship with Infantino, who is married, during his time at European football's governing body.

"Fifa president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory," a Fifa spokesman told the Telegraph.

"No employee at Uefa and Fifa has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved."

Uefa confirmed a payment was made to the woman in question and that it covered the fees for her to complete an MBA course at a local business school.

It said all payments were in line with regulations at the time, but those regulations have since been tightened and "reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation".

News.title: Watch: BBC asks Infantino if he will resign as Fifa president
News.content:
The BBC has asked Fifa president Gianni Infantino if he has the support of football's South American governing body, Conmebol.

The Fifa head has faced multiple calls to resign after his highly controversial attempt to sell private stakes in the World Cup, which he later abandoned.

Infantino, who did not answer the BBC's questions, was in Colombia for the inauguration of the country's new President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The BBC's South America correspondent Ione Wells later asked the Fifa president if he would step down.

News.title: Obesity rates have doubled in England since 1993 - what's going on?
News.content:
If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.

There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.

It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?

And can anything be done about it?

According to new analysis by the King's Fund, 15% of England's adult population - those aged 16 and over - in 1993 was obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.

Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.

Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.

Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.

"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.

News.title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
News.content:
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.

It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.

By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.

With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.

It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.

July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.

There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.

For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.

It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.

News.title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
News.content:
AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves.

"I don't want anyone who has the ambition and talent to join our armed forces to be deterred, so it's contingent on us to make sure that we've got our act together," he added.

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

News.title: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
News.content:
A book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London.

Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s.

The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member.

Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia.

News.title: Police failings revealed as sex offender left free to murder and attack women
News.content:
His first victim was attacked was on a busy Tube in central London.

Levy boarded and positioned himself directly in front of the woman, before leaning his elbow on her. She moved away.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her, over her clothes, on her vagina. Such was the force Levy used, that she felt like it was an attempt to push his fingers inside her through clothing.

She grabbed Levy's hand and asked what he was doing, but he did not respond.

When other passengers asked if she was all right, Levy protested his innocence.

"What are you talking about - look my hand is covered," he said, pointing to the jumper draped over his arm.

Levy then called her "crazy" and "stupid" and got off the tube at Westminster station.

The woman got off at the next stop, upset and crying.

She went on to report the assault to BTP. There was CCTV available of Levy, but police did not identify him. He would only be linked to the case two years later, after more women had been attacked.

A year after his first Tube assault, he assaulted three more women in quick succession and was arrested.

After being assaulted herself, the first of those three victims then filmed Levy sexually assaulting a second, unidentified woman, travelling in the same carriage.

The first woman immediately reported what had happened to BTP and provided the footage. Levy assaulted a third woman a week later.

After he had been questioned and had denied the three offences, BTP officers said they did not have enough evidence to charge, and he was released on bail.

The subsequent BTP investigation was full of delays. It was weeks before identity parades were arranged, and BTP did not approach the CPS for six months.

When it did, in May 2025, a CPS team had to scramble to make an emergency charging decision overnight, because BTP had again arrested Levy and wanted him in court the next day. This was highly unusual - BTP had known about the initial offences for six months.

In a statement, BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

The University of Glasgow, where Arday worked for just over a year before moving to Cambridge, has commissioned its own review of his appointment.

"Jason Arday was employed as Professor of Sociology of Education at the University of Glasgow, from January 2022 to March 2023," a statement said.

"The Principal has commissioned a review of the appointment with the aim of understanding all the facts and learning lessons for the future."

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and Pink, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: Police make further arrests as Thetford disorder continues
News.content:
More arrests have been made over disorder linked to anti-immigration protests that saw crowds attempt to storm the homes of suspected asylum seekers and a police officer "seriously bitten".

Asylum seekers were removed from properties in Thetford on Thursday for their own safety, Norfolk Police said.

Two men in their 40s were arrested as protests in the market town continued for a third night, and a woman was arrested on Friday in relation to an assault on a police officer, bringing the total number detained to six.

Protesters attempted to enter homes where they believed asylum seekers were living on Tuesday and Wednesday night, when officers were also "subjected to significant aggression".

News.title: Brothers jailed for killing man and injuring his son while racing cars home
News.content:
Following sentencing, Rhys' wife Caroline Jenkins, also known as Carrie, said in a statement she often wondered what difference it would have made to her family's future "if we'd hugged a little tighter and a little longer" when she waved them off that day.

She said, for her son, life "without a dad who was involved in everything you did is a hard adjustment" and it "carried an element of PTSD".

Carrie said Ioan was emotionally and physically scarred by the crash.

"It's impossible to convey the full impact Rhys' death had on us," she said, and there remains a "massive hole left in our lives by his unnecessary death".

Ioan, who broke both arms, and suffered a fractured rib and perforated bowel, said he wished his dad was still here to "watch me grow up and be my dad".

Rhys' youngest son, Gruff, was six when the crash happened.

In his own victim impact statement, he said he was in bed when police arrived to tell his mum what had happened.

After being told his dad had died, he said: "I ran out of the house. I didn't know where I was going. It was the worst feeling of my life."

The court was told Umar Ben Yusaf's car was not directly involved in the crash, but the "competitive" nature of his driving with Abubakr Ben Yusaf contributed significantly.

Judge Timothy Petts said the trauma the Jenkins family had been through in the last 21 months was "difficult for me to summarise".

"You have all been suffering with your own devastating grief but also trying to deal with the practical consequences of Rhys's death and Ioan's injuries.

"It has been an horrendous time for all of you," he told them.

Petts said to Umar and Abubakr Ben Yusaf that he was satisfied they were racing each other.

"Both of you were constantly riding your luck at high speed, completely unnecessarily, and eventually it ran out with appalling consequences.

"Rhys Jenkins never stood a chance because you were so close to him when you lost control. He was driving perfectly properly and did nothing wrong. He had no time to avoid the collision."

Sgt Sara John, from Dyfed-Powys Police's serious collision investigation unit, said: "The sentences passed today cannot undo the tragic loss suffered by Rhys's family."

She added she hoped the outcome "provides them with some closure as they begin to move forward with their lives, which have been changed forever".

"The actions of Abubakr and Umar Yusaf on that day were catastrophic. Their choice to drive in the manner they did shows their utter disregard towards other road users."

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after search at Midlothian beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search was launched over reports of concern for the girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

The force said the girl's family was aware.

News.title: England footballer Toney charged with assault in Soho
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: Gen Z want their parents to pay for family holidays – the Bank of Mum and Dad has to close
News.content:

The other day I came across research that showed one-third of British families believe that mum and dad should never stop paying for the family trip. Generation Z are even holding firm that the parent should contribute 52 per cent of the family holiday funds. And it’s already happening: multi-generational holidays are booming with more than double the number of British people going on holiday compared to four years ago.

In many ways, I was completely shocked. How on earth can anyone afford to take their family on holiday, especially when their children are in their 20s and early 30s? Why would anyone expect that? Why on earth should parents foot the bill for holidaying when everyone is now becoming cash-strapped?

Surely the Bank of Mum and Dad has to shut down at some point? For most, it’s not even possible for parents to keep paying for their children, especially when they’re not really children anymore.

open image in gallery Parent trap: it is a time of cost of living struggles, sure – but young people expecting the all-inclusive treatment is unacceptable ( HBO )

But then I realised that I’m guilty of this too. I am 60 at the end of this year and I wanted to organise a special family holiday to celebrate. I have four children and my second son is in a very serious relationship, so there was going to be six of us on holiday. I currently don’t have a partner, so we weren’t factoring that in. But we were thinking of taking my 92-year-old mother.

When it came to deciding where to go, I thought about previous holidays I enjoyed: Scotland, the Isle of Wight, North Devon. Unfortunately, my birthday is in December so we decided we would go after Christmas to get a cheaper holiday – and, at my children’s request, to go somewhere warm.

So we were looking at Thailand or Kenya, where I used to work as a volunteer teacher when I was 18 – or Tanzania or Zanzibar. I have various friends who go to South Africa in the winter. I also know that people go to the Caribbean.

We sat down and tried to work out the cost of a week's holiday for six people. Once you had factored in flights, seats, accommodation and food, I don’t think we were going to get much change out of £20,000. And while my children want to contribute, they don’t have spare income. So most of that was going to fall to me. Imagine doing that every year?

I love my children and I do understand that they are working and the cost of living has gone up, but I’m constantly shelling out £200 here and £200 there because there’s a shortfall in their rent or the car needs fixing, or they’ve run out of petrol. It's not that my children – 19, 22, 23 and 29 – don't work. They do work. However, their salaries do not keep up with the cost of living. Also they are saving for their rent, or they are putting aside money to potentially – and hopefully – buy a flat at some point.

open image in gallery ‘I couldn’t believe parents were paying for their grown-up children – then I realised I’m guilty of doing just that’ ( Lucy Cavendish )

I imagine that going on a holiday where everything is pretty much provided for must feel like manna from heaven for them. Yet it is financially horrifying.

When is this going to stop? When are children going to realise that at some point they’re no longer children and that they need to stand on their own two feet financially speaking?

When I was younger, this didn’t happen, mainly because you didn’t go on holiday with your parents; once I hit 18, that was the end of it. A family holiday when I was in my twenties would have been unthinkable.

However, that has totally changed. Lots of families holidaying together. And it all looks as if it is costing a pretty penny.

Not only is my social media feed full of pictures of friends of mine, various influencers and celebrities all somehow managing to holiday together with their adult children, I know countless people who are going on holiday with not just their adult kids but their children’s partners and sometimes even grandchildren.

I asked them how any of them can afford it – given the fact that I know young people don’t earn much money these days and the cost of living is crucifying, they basically tell me that they are funding the holiday.

Some of them even tell me they’ve paid for the entire holiday.

They’ve rented villas in Greece. They’ve booked onto activity holidays in the Dordogne. They are swimming around islands in Croatia. If they’re doing a staycation, they’ve rented very expensive holiday homes in Cornwall or Norfolk.

When is this going to stop? When are children going to realise that at some point they’re no longer children and that they need to stand on their own two feet financially speaking?

And it’s not just the cost of the accommodation. Everyone's got to get to wherever it is.

The last time I tried to book flights for myself and my 19-year-old daughter to Greece, the return fare including hold luggage (of course she needs to take every lotion and potion going plus many changes of outfits) and the designated seat so we could sit together came to over £1,000 – and that's just for two people.

How on Earth can anyone afford to do this regularly?

open image in gallery Holidays can be stressful as it is – adding your adult children into the mix is only going to complicate matters ( Various Artists Limited/BBC )

For many people of my generation it feels like an impossible situation. Not only are our children coming on holiday and ordering the most expensive thing off the menu - steak anyone? They are also piling on the drinks, renting jet skis, going shopping, asking if friends can come along.

Yet many people of my generation are still sandwiched between looking after elderly parents (and helping out financially) while also paying off student loans. And it is not only young people that the cost of living has affected. Whenever I look at my grocery bills, I almost faint with the shock. Despite using less electricity and gas, my direct debit has gone up. Nothing is going to get any cheaper in the future. Also, our work is precarious. Many of us are either out of work or freelance or being replaced by AI. In the press recently, there have been many articles by women in their 50s saying that they can no longer find a job despite the fact they are highly qualified.

The Bank of Mum and Dad is shuddering under the pressure. And, as a single parent, I am just the Bank of Mum. So when I realised how much my birthday trip would cost, the plan was shelved.

Unfortunately, this bank is shutting its doors.

Instead, we’ll have dinner at a local pub – not glamorous, and we won't be posting pictures all over social media – but I think it’s about time that we all got realistic about what we can afford and what we can’t afford.

News.title: Labrinth was ready to walk away from music. But then he realised he had more to say
News.content:

Labrinth was the quiet man – the mastermind producer and songwriter behind an endless stream of hit records, films and critically acclaimed TV scores. He was the golden boy, a go-to for pop stars like The Weeknd, Beyoncé, Madonna, and Rihanna. He was not someone known for making trouble. So it was a shock, earlier this year, when he posted an expletive-laden, all-caps message to Instagram announcing he was walking away from the US teen drama series Euphoria, his record label, and the entire music industry. “F*** COLUMBIA,” he wrote. “DOUBLE F*** EUPHORIA. IM OUT [sic]. THANK YOU AND GOOD NIGHT.”

That since-deleted post landed just a month before the much-delayed third and final season of Euphoria. The musician, real name Timothy McKenzie, had been enlisted by show creator Sam Levinson to score the first two seasons, then the third – only now Labrinth was to be joined by Oscar-winning composer Hans Zimmer. In early interviews, he seemed excited at the prospect, telling one journalist: “A lot of the compositions I’ve fallen in love with have been his, so it’s weird that I get to even just be in the presence of this scoring god.” But by April, he’d pulled his music from the show, and Zimmer received sole credit for the season three score.

If you’d been paying attention to Labrinth’s solo album Cosmic Opera Act I, released at the beginning of this year, you might have noticed allusions to his discontent long before the Instagram post. On the dark, dramatic “Implosion”, he observes in a menacing mutter: “And they mark us out of 10/ In a game we’ll never win/ Chasing all this fame/ Till we meet our bitter end.” What could he be talking about?

Labrinth laughs when I bring up those intriguing lyrics. “I was definitely in a transition period,” the 37-year-old says. “I think every artist has been in that place where they’re like, what the hell is all this? As I’m getting older, too, I feel like everything you were conditioned to find important is actually kind of stupid.” We’re meeting at a smart cocktail bar in King’s Cross. For a while, it seemed unlikely that this interview would happen – I was initially told that Labrinth was “done” talking about Euphoria, about all of it. But then he released another album, Cosmic Opera Act II, in May – four months after its predecessor – and it felt like he did, in fact, have more to say.

open image in gallery ‘As I’m getting older, I feel like everything you were conditioned to find important is actually kind of stupid’ ( Press )

I would have understood if he were cagey from the beginning, given recent events. Instead I find him to be relaxed, upbeat, and very funny. Labrinth was raised by gospel-loving parents in Hackney with his eight siblings; he’s maintained his London cool despite flitting between here and the home he shares in LA with his wife and three children. Cool being the operative word: it’s a heatwave day, but the fashion-forward Labrinth looks effortless in an all-black ensemble and tinted shades, like a chic scientist. He’s excited at what he feels is a new era for the music industry, with fewer gatekeepers: “They were like, ‘Play ball, bitch, follow these rules…’ I think that doesn’t exist in the same way.” Now, he thinks, it’s more of an even playing field, at least in the sense that artists are freer to release music how and when they want.

open image in gallery Cosmic guy: Labrinth at the Met Gala in 2023 ( AFP/Getty )

This was where Cosmic Opera Act I – his first solo album in three years – came in. He began writing it years ago, inspired by his love of Star Wars and composer John Barry, famed for his James Bond soundtracks: “I was always messing around with scoring, and I wanted to make a record solely on my laptop, by myself.” Clearly, he had a lot to get off his chest. His disillusionment with the industry creeps into Cosmic Opera’s jittery, ominous sound, but it is also glaringly evident in the lyrics, which call back to when he first started, and where he finds himself now. His career took off in 2010 with Tinie Tempah’s Brit Award-winning debut single “Pass Out” – which he co-wrote and produced – he was then signed to Syco, the record label owned by reality TV svengali Simon Cowell. A string of chart hits followed, from his debut solo single “Let the Sun Shine” to further Tinie collaborations, “Frisky” and “Earthquake”.

“I’ve got mad respect for the guy,” Labrinth says of Cowell. “The way he shows up [for artists] is very different to what people saw on TV. He’s got foresight – he sees potential, even if it’s something far from what he knows.”

Cowell’s gut instinct proved correct. Labrinth quickly became one of the most in-demand figures in the industry, writing songs on The Weeknd’s Grammy-nominated breakthrough Beauty Behind the Madness, and an Oscar-nominated entry on the 2019 Lion King soundtrack. Early fans likely associate him with a throbbing, synth-heavy sound – the same one he brought to the Euphoria score – but he also excels in a fragile, piano-based vulnerability. His 2014 single “Jealous” was so moving that Adele used it to make her cry while shooting her “Hello” music video. “Snot going everywhere,” she told one interviewer. “I can’t cope with that song. You could play it at my kid’s birthday and I’d burst into tears.”

open image in gallery Labrinth performing with Zendaya at Coachella festival in 2023 ( Getty )

Levinson clearly recognised his talents too, inviting him to score what would become a cultural phenomenon that made Labrinth an international star along with the show’s cast – Zendaya, Sydney Sweeney, Hunter Schafer, Jacob Elordi. The show generated plenty of controversy for its depictions of drug use, nudity and violence, but it was praised for its acting and, of course, the music. Labrinth won an Emmy for “All of Us”, featuring vocals from Zendaya, and brought her out to great fanfare at Coachella festival in 2023.

So where did it all go wrong? He knew the question was coming, but suddenly Labrinth falters, unsure of how much to say. “I think I got tired of everything – that industry stuff we were talking about, the way people approach doing business,” he says slowly. Working on season two was also a very different experience to season one: more money, more people, more pressure. “It’s just the way everything was handled wasn’t great for me, and I got frustrated with that because I’ve seen that in music and film,” he says. “Let’s be clear, when I work for someone, I work for them, so how they want to use the music doesn’t matter.” It’s everything outside the creative process that he dislikes: “Going to an awards ceremony and everyone’s either high or s***-faced, in their suit and tie, and they’re all drained.”

open image in gallery Labrinth performing at Coachella earlier this year ( Getty )

At the time, he meant it when he said he was quitting: “For real like, I’m finished with this s***, I’m gonna go sell coconuts in the Caribbean and never talk of being an artist again,” he says. “But I think I was very angry [about the Euphoria situation], and my wife was like, ‘Babe, just take a minute’.” He praises her for reminding him about what really matters, asking him, “‘Why do you want to be bigger?’ Like, I don’t know, because loads of people told me I should want to be bigger?!”

He’s still with his record label, but he’s not spoken with Levinson since. Interviewed by Rolling Stone, the director said he “didn’t know” what had happened and praised Labrinth as “an incredible collaborator… who really built the foundation of the sound of Euphoria.” But he added that he’d decided to take a different approach to the film’s soundtrack in season three.

open image in gallery Labrinth: ‘I’m not looking for anyone to validate what I’ve said’ ( Press )

Labrinth shrugs when I quote this back to him. “Everyone does their press run how they do it,” he says. “I’m not looking for anyone to validate what I’ve said. I’m not trying to cover anything up or save myself. I said what I said.”

There’s a song on Cosmic Opera Act II that I adore, “Bouncy Castles & Trampolines”, that expresses a yearning to get back to a more innocent time: “Whatever happened to being young and careless?/ Super Soakers and figurines/ Keep me young, please keep me dreaming.” On the same album there’s “Prostitute”, containing the lyrics: “Money on the dresser/ I’m a prostitute/ No Vaseline/ This is how they do.” He giggles when I tell him that lyric made me shudder. His wife had the same reaction: “That’s how visceral it is, though, right?” he asks. “We’re literally being pimped out by the same people supposed to [help] us.”

We’re literally being pimped out by the same people supposed to [help] us

He planned on taking a break, but there’s no way he can sit still for long. He keeps a Korg synthesiser next to his bed. “I keep creating projects that I’m excited about, and there’s the same old big s*** – collaborations, whatever,” he says. “I feel very focused on making something that feels meaningful to me.” He still wants to see change in the industry, a world where artists make things and collaborate for the fun of it, not because they’re trying to further their own careers. “We need to rewire the way artists even think about all of this,” he says. “Everyone’s thinking about how to turn themselves into a franchise or a legacy, turning their passion into a business. If you made no money off this, would you still want to do it? You need to ask every artist that question.” But I don’t need to ask Labrinth that. I already know the answer.

‘Cosmic Opera Act II’ is out now

President Donald Trump’s Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Dan Caine, is seeking an “off-ramp “ from the ongoing war in Iran, according to a new report.

Caine has privately told other top administration officials that the country needs to find a way to exit the war, according to CNN, which cited three sources familiar with the matter.

Despite Trump claiming throughout the war that a peace deal, which would include his demand that Iran never obtain a nuclear weapon, was within reach, fighting has continued for more than five months.

“Caine is looking for an off ramp,” one of CNN’s sources said.

The general’s meetings with Trump officials, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, are just to make clear the limitations and pitfalls of different military options, according to the sources.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s Chairman of the Joint Chiefs, General Dan Caine, is seeking an 'off-ramp' from the ongoing war in Iran, according to a new report ( Getty Images )

Joseph Holstead, a spokesperson for Caine, told CNN, “We do not discuss the Chairman’s confidential conversations with the President, the Secretary, or other senior leaders, nor do we comment on anonymous, agenda-driven characterizations of those conversations by sources who were not privy to them”.

A White House official praised Caine’s know-how, calling him an “incredible asset to President Trump’s national security team.”

“The General always provides accurate, unbiased information and a host of options to the Commander-in-Chief, who ultimately makes decisions based on what he feels is best for US national security”, the official said.

The Independent has reached out to the White House, the Office of the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Department of State for comment.

Trump’s war has primarily been an air campaign, relying on fighters to launch strikes against Iran instead of deploying ground troops. Caine and other Trump officials privately think it's unlikely that an air campaign alone can put enough pressure on the Iranians to agree to a deal that’s favorable to the president, according to multiple people familiar with recent discussions who spoke with CNN.

open image in gallery The Iran war, which is both costly and unpopular with Americans, has dragged on for more than five months ( AFP via Getty Images )

Meanwhile, Trump has denied recent reports that the US military’s weapons stockpile is dwindling.

“The U.S. has massive amounts of ‘munitions,’ especially of certain types. Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed. Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history.

“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!” Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday.

Trump’s threats came after Reuters reported Tuesday, citing two unnamed sources, that the Army has used “virtually all” of its long-range Army Tactical Missile Systems and Precision Strike Missiles.

A recent report has also found that the Pentagon is running low on missile interceptors.

The US military had 2,330 Patriot systems and 452 Terminal High Altitude Area Defense systems before the war, according to the report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies. As of July 27, an estimated 759 to 827 Patriot systems and 234 to 278 THAAD systems remain, the report said.

open image in gallery Despite Trump claiming throughout the war that a peace deal was within reach, fighting has dragged on ( Getty Images )

During a Senate Appropriations Committee hearing last month, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said US military operations in Iran have cost an estimated $37.5 billion. He also asked Congress for an additional $67 billion to, in part, replenish weapons stockpiles, blaming the Biden administration for not properly funding the Pentagon.

The price of gas has also surged during the war, sitting above $4 a gallon Friday, according to motor club AAA. The price of a gallon of gas was just below $3 at the start of the war, according to the Associated Press.

Just 28 percent of Americans said they approved of Trump’s handling of Iran in a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

President Donald Trump derided a federal appeals court ruling halting construction of his White House ballroom and demanding he seek congressional approval, insisting it would “severely jeopardize the lives and welfare” of White House staff.

In a lengthy Truth Social post Friday afternoon, the president said two judges on the D.C. Court of Appeals had made a “politically motivated” and “totally wrong” decision and characterized his White House ballroom project as crucial for national security.

“The Circuit Court’s decision, which is totally wrong on the vital subject of STANDING, of which the plaintiff has none, severely jeopardizes the lives and welfare of the people who work, and will be working, at the White House — including all future Presidents of the United States, and their families, as well as the lives of all those visiting…” Trump wrote.

In a 2-1 decision, the appellate judges said the president was only a “temporary tenant” of the White House and had unprecedentedly knocked down the East Wing, paid for with American tax dollars, to build a 90,000-square-foot space without consulting Congress.

But Trump disagreed and further characterized his project as a national security matter because the administration is building an underground bunker, complete with a military facility, emergency operation center and more.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has rushed the construction of his White House ballroom, claiming its necessary for national security purposes ( AFP/Getty )

“It is all tied together as one big, expensive, and very complex unit, which is vital for National Security and Military Operations of the United States of America!” Trump wrote.

Though the president is insisting the project should continue, the judge’s ruling allows necessary national security construction to continue as legal challenges play out. It only halts above-ground, non-national security-related construction.

The court’s ruling will take effect for two weeks to give the Trump administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court, which the president said he would do.

Trump continued to rage about the ruling on Friday night and their view a president is a “temporary tenant” of the White House.

“We are not tenants, who pay rent and do all other things that a tenant must do, we are PRESIDENTS, elected by the people of the United States of America, and have many rights, including the right to fix, renovate, secure, protect, and beautify the White House grounds, which has been built and rebuilt, renovated and rerenovated, repaired and, simply, MADE BETTER, many times since 1792, and never needing the permission of Congress, or anyone else, to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“This decision, made after much of the work has been done and paid for, is a National Security Threat at the highest level. It is also a National Disgrace.”

Judge Patricia Millet, an Obama appointee, and Judge Brad Garcia, a Biden appointee, ruled in favor of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the group suing the administration to stop construction of the ballroom.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now,” they wrote.

open image in gallery Last year, the president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make room for his new ballroom – sparking outrage from Democrats and members of the public ( Getty )

In doing so, they agreed with a lower court ruling, issued in April, that found Trump overstepped his authority when he demolished the East Wing to make room for the new ballroom.

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy. This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom. What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require,” the judges added.

Meanwhile, Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, said she would have sided with the administration.

The Independent has asked the White House for comment.

Last year, Trump announced he would build the new glamorous ballroom, without using American taxpayer dollars, to serve as an entertaining space for state dinners and events.

open image in gallery Progress on the White House ballroom construction, pictured July 11, shows the administration moved forward with above-ground work while legal challenges played out ( Reuters )

But much like Trump’s other D.C. beautification projects, the cost, scale and public understanding of the project have changed over time.

The cost of the ballroom has surged from its original $200 million estimate to $400 million – with some believing it could cost upwards of $600 million. While Trump has said private donations will pay for the ballroom itself, in June the administration transferred more than $300 million from the Secret Service budget to cover security upgrades to the White House.

The administration has continued building the ballroom as legal challenges play out, arguing the ballroom is essential for national security because they are building an underground bunker containing a military complex, a hospital and an emergency operations center.

As judges have increasingly ruled against the construction of the White House ballroom, the administration has increasingly characterized the project as a pivotal national security or military project.

In Friday’s Truth Social post, the president referred to the project as “the desperately needed Military Center” even though the dispute is over the ballroom.

Former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton, a prominent Democrat who lost the presidency to Donald Trump in 2016, has warned of one Republican attack on progressive members of her party that will be “very effective” in the midterms.

After progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over centrist congresswoman Haley Stevens in Tuesday’s Democratic primary for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, Clinton suggested that Republicans will baselessly label him as a “communist,” and it will work to dissuade voters.

“The real fight will be how do we make sure that people who voted for Haley feel comfortable voting for Abdul El-Sayed, and how do we get Independents to feel comfortable?

“And you can see that it’s not just about Michigan, but the Republican messaging is communist, socialist. It’s going to be a very effective attack,” Clinton told Kara Swisher during the journalist’s Pivot podcast with author Scott Galloway.

open image in gallery Former Secretary of State Hilary Clinton, a prominent Democrat who lost the presidency to Donald Trump in 2016, has warned of one Republican attack on progressive members of her party that will be 'very effective' in the midterms ( AFP via Getty Images )

Trump was quick to celebrate El-Sayed’s election win, calling it “Great news for the Republican Party.”

“El-Sayed, a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the Socialist…Now, the Dumocrats crazy policies will only get worse!” he wrote on Truth Social Wednesday.

Despite the pro-Israel group AIPAC spending tens of millions on Stevens’ campaign, El-Sayed — a former public health official who has accused Israel of genocide in its war against Hamas in Gaza — narrowly beat her in Tuesday’s race. Israel has vehemently denied allegations of genocide.

open image in gallery The prominent Democrat suggested the GOP will baselessly accuse members of her party, including progressive Abdul El-Sayed, of being communists, and it will work to dissuade voters ( Getty Images )

When Swisher probed further on whether labeling a politician a communist is an effective attack, Clinton said, “That's the attack that Trump is leading with and I assume they've tested it and I assume that they have reason to believe that it's effective or they wouldn't be beating the drum on it.”

“It's not just him. [Vice President JD] Vance has done it. Others are doing it. They are trying to bring back scare tactics about our candidates, and it didn't work in New York. [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani was elected, and there was a lot of money spent against him,” Clinton said.

Mamdani, a democratic socialist who has been commonly misstated as a communist, won his election in November against a member of the Democratic establishment, former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo.

Two democratic socialists whom Mamdani backed in the June primaries in New York, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, also won their races.

Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the U.S. that supplies drinking water to more than 20 million people, has hit a record low.

The reservoir, located behind Hoover Dam on the Arizona-Nevada border, fell to 1,040.5 feet above sea level at 1 a.m. MST on Friday, marking its lowest level since it was first filled in the 1930s, according to data from the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation, CNN reported. The drop surpasses the previous record low of 1,040 feet, set in July 2022.

While water levels climbed slightly above 1,040.50 feet before sunrise Friday, officials say the drop is a sign of the challenges ahead.

"It's grim, and we obviously need to do something – and fast," Brad Udall, a senior climate scientist at Colorado State University's Colorado Water Center, told USA Today.

Lake Mead is a critical water source for the Southwest, providing drinking water for between 20 and 25 million people. It is part of the larger Colorado River Basin system, which supplies water to around 40 million people across seven states, tribal communities and parts of Mexico.

open image in gallery Lake Mead dropped to a new record-low elevation of 1,040.5 feet Friday morning, breaking the previous low set in July 2022 ( Reuters )

open image in gallery As water levels drop, the receding water exposes hidden shorelines, old rocks, land and objects that stayed underwater for decades ( Reuters )

The Colorado River also plays a major role in American agriculture, providing irrigation for about 5 million acres of farmland. That includes farms in California’s agricultural regions that produce a significant portion of the country’s fruits and vegetables.

Because of below-average snowmelt runoff from the Rocky Mountains this year, officials announced a plan in April to keep more water in Lake Powell rather than releasing it downstream to Lake Mead. The move was designed to protect Lake Powell’s water levels during a dry year, but it also means less water is flowing into Lake Mead, contributing to its continued decline.

The Bureau of Reclamation warned at the time that keeping more water in Lake Powell would speed up Lake Mead’s decline and could reduce Hoover Dam’s hydropower capacity by up to 40 percent as early as the fall.

Before the adjustment, Lake Mead was projected to fall to about 1,055.99 feet by the end of September. With less water released from Lake Powell, projections showed it could drop closer to 1,035 feet.

The reservoir’s dramatic decline has reshaped the landscape around Lake Mead. As the water recedes, it has exposed previously submerged shorelines, rocky terrain and areas that have been underwater for decades. The July 2022 record low drew national attention when it exposed a body found inside a barrel, several sunken boats and other remains.

Earlier this week, Colorado officials announced a program aimed at easing the Colorado River water crisis would pay people in Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico to use less water. While it could save enough water to supply hundreds of thousands of homes for a year, officials say much larger cuts are needed.

A separate federal plan, announced July 31, could require Arizona, California and Nevada to reduce Colorado River use by up to 3 million acre-feet annually, which is enough water to supply about 6 million households for a year.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.title: The best luxury hotels in the Cotswolds
News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. Whether near picturesque Broadway in the north of the region or close to Bath in the south, location is a key attribute to them all: some offer serene escapes in acres of their own rolling parkland; others sit amid superb gardens; and several take over classic honey-stone villages that look as if they have been beamed in from a halcyon era of the past.

They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs. Facilities are top-notch too, ranging from beautiful bars and quiet terraces to blissful spas with inviting pools and even an opportunity for equine adventures.
