Sports.title: Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
Some of the elites criticising Gianni Infantino are sheer hypocrites. How can the money-obsessed leeches behind the Super League expect us to listen to their confected moral outrage as they bleed our beloved game dry, writes IAN HERBERT

Unlock more of the best of our football coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

The most preposterous man in football is staggering on, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself, so perhaps that’s why the biggest hypocrites of another dark week for football appear to have got away with it.

On Sunday, Real Madrid decided to weigh in on the Gianni Infantino scandal, instructing their media people to put out a sanctimonious statement welcoming the scrapping of the egghead’s plans to sell off a slice of the World Cup, and thanking UEFA for fulfilling their ‘duty’ to ‘protect football’.

You really could not make some of this stuff up. Yes, that moralising really did come from the same Real Madrid whose avarice stank football out when they led the contemptible group of 12 clubs who attempted the European Super League breakaway coup, a few years back.

Infantino’s intellectual and moral decrepitude may have been there for us all to see in his email offering nations a small cash consideration if they back his plans to raise $20billion, but have we forgotten the European club men with whiteboards and coloured marker pens, explaining their own despicable little earner in 2021?

Real’s executives back then were just as atrocious as Infantino is now – worse, in fact, given that the FIFA scheme was not actually a breakaway proposal designed to leave the have-nots behind – while the money men they indirectly inveighed against on Sunday are the one and the same suits from JPMorgan Chase, hired by them to advise on the Super League.

Given that the US finance house were forced to apologise for their part in that episode, you might have fancied they’d learned their lesson about how ferocious the backlash to a sell-out like this would be. No. They just couldn’t resist getting their snouts in the football trough again.

Gianni Infantino is somehow staggering on as FIFA President, drowning in such vanity and ego that he cannot see how he embarrasses himself

But many of his critics do not have a leg to stand on. These are clubs that tried to form the breakaway European Super League - and only buckled after immense fan pressure (pictured)

So, please let’s get this right. The new flank in football's civil war is not between the idealists and the profiteers, but between competing profiteers fighting over who gets to cash in on the game.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin, are currently casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions, protectors of the meritocracy, guardians of the fans against billionaire opportunists. Yet this is the self-same organisation which expanded the Champions League into a sprawling competition with 64 extra fixtures in 2024, to create greater TV income and more sponsorship revenue.

The self-same organisation which has been engaged in a pitched battle for territory with FIFA. That fight has spawned the Nations League and the expanded Club World Cup, with each governing body viewing the other’s new tournament with deep suspicion. UEFA’s objection is not to football becoming more commercial but to someone else collecting the commercial rewards.

Our own Premier League claim a moral high ground for themselves, too, proclaiming to be the world's greatest and most unpredictable domestic competition, while generating more money than any such league in history. Yet it is driven by the same monopolistic greed, behaving as though sharing a fraction of the wealth with the rest of the football pyramid would be an act of unconscionable sacrifice.

Don’t let it be forgotten that its biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020. Or that the Premier League held talks with CVC Capital Partners, one of the world's largest private equity firms, about selling a stake in future broadcasting and commercial revenues, at the same time.

That came to nothing, either, but here was an elite equally willing to explore new ways of extracting financial value from our game. The people’s game.

Whenever the redistribution of Premier League wealth is discussed, we witness the language and narrative suddenly change and those overseeing the competition which has negotiated television contracts worth billions begin to fret about the pennies.

It was clear when a White Paper on football governance was published a few years back that a greater flow of money down from the Premier League would be egregiously hard to extract.

UEFA, under Aleksander Ceferin (right), are casting themselves as the defenders of football's traditions. Yet they expanded and distorted the Champions League to generate more revenue

It shouldn't be forgotten that the Premier League's biggest clubs, led by Liverpool and Manchester United, made their own power grab through Project Big Picture in 2020

The gilded elite division continued to maintain the fallacy that they were helping the rest, when 70 per cent of the money they sent down below was Championship parachute money. An insurance policy for the division’s own members laughably dressed up as ‘solidarity payments’.

It has taken Government intervention to force a more equitable share of the Premier League’s wealth throughout the game, in the shape of the Independent Football Regulator, with its ‘backstop’ power to force a settlement if none is agreed.

Faced with such a prospect, the Premier League have finally just voted for an additional £1.5billion from those in the gilded cage, to be shared with the EFL’s clubs, though even that is not allocated yet. The cash, to be funded by a two per cent lift in the transfer levy on all top-flight deals, will clearly need to be crowbarred from clubs swimming in wealth, given the opposition led by Manchester City’s petro-dollar billionaire owners – another of the merry little European Super League band.

We understand other members of the so-called ‘Big Six’ are also unhappy that they may now find themselves coughing up more than less elevated Premier League clubs. It’s been left to the more moderately wealthy members of the division, who faced down the big clubs over the Super League, to challenge them again.

If there was one positive to come out of the Super League scandal, it was the way it cut the grasping, spiritually remote 'Big Six' down to size. 'It's like emerging from a slightly abusive relationship,' the owner of one of the smaller Premier League clubs told me at the time.

This weekend, the FA Cup begins its beautiful seasonal arc once more, carrying the customary thrill and sense of pride among all who will compete in its extra preliminary round. North Ferriby, at home to St Helens, Northwich Victoria, playing away to Beverley Town, and Nelson, entertaining Stockport Georgians, are just three of those taking part who know what a precarious financial reality and existential threat look and feel like.

For all the weekend’s 438 competing clubs, reaching the first round proper – six ties away, in November – would be monumental, with £47,750 prize money for those who win at that stage.

But any who progress that far will also experience the chill of strictures forced down from the top of the game. This will be the second season with no replays from the first round proper onwards – a diminishment the FA said was necessary because of increasing pressure on the calendar, particularly following UEFA's expansion of their club competitions.

The early rounds of the FA Cup still bring with them a sense of thrill and pride - though replays with England's top clubs are now sadly a thing of the past

Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go

Critics, especially in the EFL and non-League, have argued that a vital source of income is being removed from smaller clubs, who can no longer earn lucrative replay gates against bigger opponents.

But those little people are shouting in the dark. The abolition of replays, fourth-round matches spread over five days and the scheduling of the 2027 final before the Premier League campaign finishes, rather than as the climax to the season, belong to the story of the competition’s devaluation and diminishment. The Cup has been crushed into virtual irrelevance by football's high and mighty.

As of last night, Infantino’s brazen conceit and vanity were keeping him in a job which any intelligent and self-respecting industry would by now have forced him from. He is no doubt banking on the relentless news cycle moving on and UEFA’s threat to boycott FIFA’s competition receding into the distance.

Qualification games for the 2030 World Cup are just a year away and Infantino can safely calculate that national associations will not want to take the financial hit that a boycott would carry. It seems significant, and concerning, that a mere 11 national associations, including England and Wales, have voiced opposition to him remaining in post.

Yet for all the sound and fury, there is something deeply unsettling and incomplete about some of this moralising. Infantino is taking the logic of those presiding over the elite game to its natural conclusion, not dragging them somewhere they do not wish to go. He is the most despicable emblem of a game which is slowly devouring itself, but by no means the only one.

Sports.title: Inside Sir Ben Ainslie's mission to finally end Britain's wait for America's Cup glory: How history - and a secret weapon - are inspiring Olympic legend's team in Naples
Sports.content:
Inside Sir Ben Ainslie's mission to finally end Britain's wait for America's Cup glory: How history - and a secret weapon - are inspiring Olympic legend's team in Naples

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

A couple of notable letters crop up on the wall. They are correspondence from Lord Nelson and nestle among the high-value art in the Royal Yacht Squadron ‘Castle’, in Cowes, Isle of Wight.

The handwriting looked fine to me, a nice round hand.

Said James, steward of the place, where he has worked, other than for a brief spell elsewhere, since he was 16, with a degree of understatement: ‘There is a reason it is not quite as legible as it might have been.

‘By this stage, the Admiral was no longer able to write with his stronger arm.’

So, we are at the very citadel of sailing, a place built with eight-feet deeper walls on the land side than on the waterfront. ‘The French would have known better than to have approached us by sea,’ was the thrust of James’s non-negotiable reasoning.

He was wearing a black tie. All staff and some 540 members of the Royal Yacht Squadron wear the same neckwear along with their dark blazers. They are in mourning.

Sir Ben Ainslie is looking to help end Britain's long wait for America's Cup glory

For it is merely 200 years since Admiral Nelson left us, aged 47, aboard Britain’s flagship HMS Victory, shot by a French sniper during the Battle of Trafalgar off the coast of Spain. Dead but victorious.

Which sort of brings us to today, and Sir Ben Ainslie’s attempt, now as team boss rather than helmsman, to win the technology-led, F1-on-water America’s Cup, the oldest international sports competition in the world dating back to 1851, when it is next held in Naples next year. We have famously never won it.

Ainslie was made an honorary member of the Squadron (you can’t apply, chaps or chapesses), under whose banner the British attempt fights, soon after winning his fourth Olympic Gold medal at London 2012, before being elevated to full membership three years ago.

There is a major departure in his latest attempt, however, in the male-dominated Royal Yacht Squadron. Jemima Lines, 29, a kitefoiler and adventurer, is enlisted to become a participating member of the on-board team of five, and thus the first woman to participate in the Cup since aviation pioneer Sir Thomas Sopwith’s wife Phyllis in 1934 and 1937.

Lines was given the role for her exceptional background, one entirely in keeping with the traditions of the event. For one thing, she is the fourth daughter of a special forces soldier, born in Kent and educated at Bristol University as an engineer. Her father was Ralph Crathorne, who died earlier this year, aged 67, in a mountaineering accident in Scotland.

‘I owe so much to him and how I see everything in life,’ she said during Cowes Week, only a few weeks after getting married. ‘Everything I have achieved is down to his influence. He wanted us to explore everything in the world, and I am pleased to be doing this as a result.

‘We’d often be late for school because my father had taken us all to the beach and we’d be kiting, that was from the age of eight, and he always wanted us to do bigger adventures. This is the biggest change I have ever made, to be involved in the America’s Cup.’

Ainslie, as ever, had a busy week in Cowes, being his sport’s most celebrated figure. A day earlier he had welcomed Anne, Princess Royal, as the new Admiral of the Yacht Squadron, in succession to her father, the late Duke of Edinburgh. She is a loyal supporter of the old cause.

Ainslie's wife Georgie (left) is his stalwart supporter in his ambition, now as team boss

Ainslie is now sipping a restorative drink and eating sandwiches on the Royal Yacht Squadron terrace after sailing competitively for the first time since the last America’s Cup in Barcelona a couple of years ago. He is doing his best to pretend it is not the case, but his 49-year-old body has been given a decent examination out on the water.

He is off next to the annual Squadron Ball later, along with wife Georgie (née Thompson), previously of Sky Sports News, his stalwart supporter.

Sitting close to where the America’s Cup began under the gaze of Queen Victoria, Ainslie said: ‘I’m confident we can win the Cup in the end. You know how it is with our maritime history. We have to do it.’

Handwriting, good, bad or indifferent, it is a story that would earn its place on the Castle wall.

Sports.title: UEFA ‘paid off’ Gianni Infantino’s alleged lover as pressure grows on FIFA president
Sports.content:
UEFA ‘paid off’ Gianni Infantino’s alleged lover as pressure grows on FIFA president

Gianni Infantino's position as FIFA president could come under fresh scrutiny following allegations of an affair with a junior member of staff while he was general secretary of UEFA

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino is facing allegations about his time at UEFA (Image: Abdelmajid BZIOUAT / AFP via Getty Images)

Gianni Infantino allegedly arranged for his lover to be paid off by UEFA while he was in a position of power at European football’s governing body.

‌



Infantino is now desperately trying to hold onto his position as president of FIFA, but allegations about the 56-year-old’s behaviour at his previous employer, which he denies, have now surfaced.

‌



The Telegraph reports that a female employee of UEFA, who was allegedly in a relationship with Infantino, allegedly received a six-figure pay-off and funds to study an MBA after he was challenged over the situation.

‌



Infantino, who is married with four children, was UEFA’s general secretary at the time of the alleged affair with a junior employee, who was promoted to a management position during the relationship.

Gianni Infantino state of play as 211 nations decide desperate FIFA president's fate READ MORE :

UEFA could boycott 5 tournaments in next 11 months after new Gianni Infantino statement READ MORE :

He is said to have been challenged by Michel Platini, UEFA’s then president, over the alleged relationship, prompting her to leave the organisation with a substantial payment.

A UEFA spokesperson told the newspaper: “We are aware of the allegations and can confirm a departure payment was made to the individual in question, coupled with the payment of fees for an MBA course at a local business school. The payment was in line with the regulations that existed for departing staff at the time.

‌



“Such UEFA have been tightened since 2016 and the current staff regulations – which apply to all UEFA employees at whatever level – reflect those found in a modern, high-profile organisation.” Mirror Football has contacted UEFA.

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino has been married to Leena Al Ashqar for 15 years (Image: Roberto SCHMIDT / AFP via Getty Images)

The allegations come at a time of increased scrutiny on Infantino, who is fighting to hold onto power at the top of FIFA following a backlash over his secretive plans to sell stakes in tournaments like the World Cup. His former employer, UEFA, are now the organisation leading the attempts to remove him from power.

‌



“FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory,” a FIFA spokesperson told the Telegraph.

“No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino’s behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved. All company actions related to employees, including any departure and severance packages, have always been approved by the appropriate directors in accordance with all applicable regulations.”

Infantino spent 16 years working for UEFA until leaving to become FIFA president in February 2016, a position he has held ever since.

Article continues below

He married Leena Al Ashqar in 2001 after they met through her work for the Lebanese Football Federation.

Sports.title: Andrew Flintoff releases statement after shock England departure and confirms next job
Sports.content:
Andrew Flintoff releases statement after shock England departure and confirms next job

England cricket legend Andrew Flintoff has confirmed he has left his job with England Lions ahead of moving to a role in Australia later in the year

View 2 Images Andrew Flintoff has stepped down from England Lions (Image: Gareth Copley/Getty Images)

Ashes icon Andrew Flintoff has announced his decision to step away from his coaching role with the England Lions. The England cricket legend is set to join Sydney Thunder later this year in Australia's Big Bash League.

‌



Flintoff, who started his role with the Lions in September 2024, leaves after less than two years in the position. The 48-year-old earned the job after first working with England's one-day team in an informal consultant role as he recovered from significant injuries he suffered in a car crash filming for the television show Top Gear.

‌



The ECB had permitted Flintoff to leave an upcoming tour to South Africa early to coach in the Big Bash, but Flintoff has made the decision to end his time with the international set-up.

‌



He has joked that his replacement has 'big pants to fill'. Mike Yardy will step in as head coach for the four-day Professional County Club Select XI match against Pakistan Men next week.

Posting on Instagram, Flintoff said; "Unfortunately, I’ve made the decision to step away from my role with the Lions. Not only have I enjoyed my time having the opportunity to work with the best young cricketers in the country, but have taken great pride in seeing them develop.

FA announce changes after tragic death of ex-Arsenal footballer aged 21 READ MORE :

UEFA could boycott 5 tournaments in next 11 months after new Gianni Infantino statement READ MORE :

"I’d like to thank the coaches and staff for all their passion, tireless work and support they give everyday.

‌



"In particular Ed Barney who I’ve loved working with and was so lucky to have as a performance director, and obviously Rob for trusting me with one of the most Important roles in English cricket.

"I can’t wait to get started with the Thunder later in the year and see where coaching takes me. Good luck to whoever takes over you have some big pants to fill."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Ed Barney, ECB men's performance director, said: "Fred has helped to transform the Lions environment into a programme that has had a major impact on young players. By creating an environment that both supports and pushes excellence at all times he has helped bring forward a new generation of young players.

"Coaches have also flourished alongside him, whether early in their coaching journey or with decades of experience, and he has consistently maximised the expertise around the group. We wish him the best in the next stage of his coaching career and look forward to a time he returns to the English game."

Flintoff had come under severe scrutiny for his decision to take on the Sydney job while in charge of England's Lions. Managing Director of England Men's Cricket, Rob Key, defended Flintoff, suggesting that his passion should not be doubted, as he could have earned more money doing something different with his career.

‌



"I saw something I thought was unfair, actually, on Andrew Flintoff, where it said he shouldn't have been doing that Lions job because he's not doing this job now, the England head coach's job," Key said.

"I think that's done a complete disservice to one of our greatest cricketers who, for the last three [sic] years, has done that Lions job when he could have done a hell of a lot of other things, earning a lot more money. But his passion [is] to actually try and bring the next generation through, and people like Sonny Baker, Mitch Stanley… so many of these players have come under his wing."

View 2 Images Freddie was involved in a serious crash while filming an unaired series of Top Gear back in 2022 (Image: PA)

‌



Flintoff's return to cricket came after a difficult time recovering from his brutal Top Gear crash. The former all-rounder suffered serious facial and rib injuries after the open-topped three-wheeled vehicle he was driving rolled over.

Speaking on Freddie Flintoff’s Field Of Dreams: Ultimate Test, he said: "It was, what – 18 months ago? And you know, I’ve suffered with things like depression in the past before, but this time was different. I didn’t know if I had it in me to carry on, not that I wanted to die or anything like that, I just didn’t know if I had it in me, and that took a while.

“The one thing, I think, getting quite deep here, but the one thing you just want to be is happy in yourself, and try and be accepting of yourself of what you are. It took me a long time to be like that, and then the crash put me back again, and now it’s like finding myself or finding the person I want to be.”

Sports.title: Five Brits ready to shine at European Athletics Championships in Birmingham
Sports.content:
Five Brits ready to shine at European Athletics Championships in Birmingham

The likes of Keely Hodgkinson and Zharnel Hughes may hog the headlines but this quintet will hope to show what they can do on the big stage.

View Image Zharnel Hughes (centre). (Image: David Davies/PA Wire)

The likes of Keely Hodgkinson and Zharnel Hughes will grab the headlines, but the European Athletics Championships also offer up-and-coming athletes the chance to shine.

‌



After all, it was on the European stage that Hodgkinson claimed her first senior outdoor gold medal – the 800m crown in Munich four years ago – while Dina Asher-Smith did the same back in 2016 in Amsterdam.

‌



So, for the packed-out crowds expected at Birmingham’s Alexander Stadium, this summer’s championship represents the chance to revel not only in the best of British athletics but also get a sneak peek at the sport’s future in this country. And to ensure that you are clued up on that next generation, we have picked out five emerging talents ready to spread their wings.

‌



Five to watch

Emily Newnham (400m hurdles and 400m)

Emily Newnham insists that her priority is the 400m hurdles, although given her form over 400m this season, she clearly has the potential excel in both events.

The 22-year-old from Shaftesbury Barnet has beaten her personal best both in the hurdles and the flat this year, building on a hugely promising 2025.

‌



She won a pair of medals at the European Indoors in the 4x400m relays before dominant displays at the European U23 Athletics Championships in Bergen saw her come away with two gold medals.

One of those came in the 400m hurdles, where she set a new championship record to finish more than a second clear of the field.

And with Dutch star Femke Broeders-Bol having made the step up to the 800m this season, Newnham will be hoping to take advantage of her absence at the head of the field.

‌



Newnham’s personal best of 53.92, set in Madrid this year, would have been enough for silver in this event two years ago, behind only Broeders-Bol, so she could be right in the mix this time around.

Success Eduan (200m)

Given her first name, Success Eduan had no choice but to flourish once she set her mind to athletics and she has certainly lived up to it so far in her career.

‌



The 21-year-old demonstrated her potential when she won a European U20 medal over 200m at just 17, and last year she claimed the European U23 title in style in Bergen over the same distance.

She also led home a British victory in the 4x100m at the World Relays Championships in 2025 but the moment which made everyone sit up and take notice came in 2026.

In the UK Champs in Birmingham, Eduan beat World Championship silver medallist to take the national title by more than two tenths and cement her place as one of the brightest sprinting prospects in the country.

‌



She is now set to return to the Alexander Stadium for more of the same against the continent’s best.

Kimani Jack (high jump)

The most unlikely name on this list is Kimani Jack, who has emerged from nowhere in 2026.

‌



A history graduate from the University of Birmingham, Jack won a pair of BUCS outdoor high jump titles and competed at the European U23s last year in Bergen.

But it is this year where he has really caught the eye, clearing 2.30m for the first time, with a personal best of 2.31m at the Torrin Lawrence Memorial in Athens, Georgia.

He followed that up by taking second on his Diamond League debut in Monaco, clearing 2.30m, and if he can manage that again in Birmingham, he should be right in the hunt for the podium.

‌



Charlotte Henrich (400m)

At just 19 years of age, Charlotte Henrich has already set two Welsh national records over 400m, beating a mark that had previously stood for 44 years.

Henrich ran 50.58 to finish third in the UK Championships in Birmingham, before lowering that record with a run of 50.45 seconds at the Wanda Diamond League in London.

‌



Those performances have singled Henrich out as a huge talent and while she might need to drop a couple more tenths to get into the battle for the medals, she has already shown a penchant for breaking records this season.

Innes FitzGerald (5000m)

Still only 20 years old, Innes FitzGerald has already got major championship experience under her belt after making her World Championship debut in Tokyo last September.

‌



While she did not progress through the heats there, FitzGerald will be a strong candidate to do so in Birmingham when she races over 5000m.

As a cross-country athlete, FitzGerald already has six European U20s titles, winning individual and team gold in each of the last three years, while in Tampere last summer she won 3000m and 5000m gold at the European U20 Championships by huge distances, breaking Gabriela Szabo’s 32-year-old championship record in the former.

She will not be able to run away from the competition in Birmingham, so tactical nous maybe an advantage for her more seasoned rivals, but in terms of potential, the sky is the limit for FitzGerald.

Sports.title: Enzo Maresca wants Chelsea star to replace Rodri as Barcelona move advances
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca wants Chelsea star to replace Rodri as Barcelona move advances

Barcelona have seen an opening bid for Manchester City midfielder Rodi turned down on Friday - but the La Liga giants are expected to return as they close in on the World Cup winner

View 3 Images Barcelona have launched an opening offer for Man City midfielder Rodri

Enzo Maresca has earmarked Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez as his top option to replace Rodri this summer.

‌



Barcelona have seen an opening offer of £38.5million rejected out of hand by City, who want closer to £60m. However, with just one year remaining on his contract and coming off a serious knee injury, City are open to selling at the right price.

‌



And Maresca, who is going into his first season as Pep Guardiola ’s replacement, sees Fernandez as the perfect replacement for the World Cup Golden Ball winner.

‌



The Italian worked with Fernandez during his time as Chelsea boss and according to the Independent, City are already exploring a possible move for the Argentinian.

Inside Bruno Guimaraes' dream Arsenal transfer six years in making for Mikel Arteta READ MORE :

Fernandez is yet to report for Chelsea this summer after playing a huge role in Argentina’s rollercoaster ride to the World Cup final. The 25-year-old scored crucial goals in the knockout stages, including a screamer in the dramatic comeback against England in the semis.

However, he arguably cost his nation the chance of lifting a fourth world title after he inexplicably picked up two yellow cards in a matter of minutes.

‌



Chelsea paid £106m for the midfielder in 2023 and would want to make a profit on that, if they were to entertain an exit this summer.

Fernandez was sanctioned earlier this year after his desire to leave the London club was made public. Ex-boss Liam Rosenior was also forced to strip him of the vice captaincy before he was sacked for a disastrous run of results.

View 3 Images Chelsea want a reported £120m for Enzo Fernandez (Image: Visionhaus/Getty Images)

‌



New Blues boss Xabi Alonso hasn’t been able to train with the talismanic midfielder during his short tenure, but made it clear he wants him to remain at the club.

Speaking in July, Alonso said: "Yes we have spoken. But as you can imagine what we have spoken remains private,” and then when pressed if he wanted Fernandez to stay, he replied “yes”.

City have already smashed their own transfer record this summer, signing Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for a whopping £116m. But with the exit of Bernardo Silva and the expected one of Rodri, more cover is required before the Premier League campaign begins.

‌



They have also been heavily linked with Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille, who shone at the World Cup with Morocco, but his £86m valuation has led talks to an impasse.

View 3 Images Enzo Maresca worked with Fernandez during his time as Chelsea boss

Speaking after City’s most recent pre-season friendly, Maresca admitted the club still had work to do in order to replace a number of senior players.

‌



“Fortunately this is a squad that doesn’t need to do many things,” he told media at a press conference ahead of Wednesday’s clash with K-League All Stars.

“At the same time, we already know the squad lost some important players with experience with Bernardo, John [Stones], Nathan [Ake]…different players. For sure, there are things we need to do.

He added: “The reason I said there are things to do is because the transfer window is open and when it is open, anything can happen. It is August and then from September, when it’s closed, it is completely different.”

Sports.title: Arsenal star's gesture to Bruno Guimaraes ahead of £75m transfer comes to light
Sports.content:
Arsenal star's gesture to Bruno Guimaraes ahead of £75m transfer comes to light

Arsenal are preparing to confirm the £75m signing of Bruno Guimaraes after the soon-to-be former Newcastle captain completed his medical - and his shirt number seemingly been leaked

View 2 Images Bruno Guimaraes will join Arsenal for £75million (Image: Mark Leech/Offside/Offside via Getty Images)

Bruno Guimaraes is set to wear the No.39 shirt for Arsenal after academy star Louie Copley moved to a new number. Arsenal are preparing to confirm Guimaraes' arrival from Newcastle after the two clubs agreed a fixed fee of £75million to end the transfer saga.

‌



The 28-year-old said his goodbyes at Newcastle's training camp in Spain before completing his medical with Arsenal and signing a four-year contract. His signing still hasn't been announced, although the Gunners have dropped a clear hint on their website.

‌



Copley, who wore the No. 39 shirt in each of Arsenal's first two pre-season friendlies as well as in training sessions, has had his squad number changed to 38. It's a telltale sign that Guimaraes is now a Gunner and has taken his favourite number.

‌



The midfielder has worn 39 throughout his club career, including for former clubs Lyon and Athletico Paranaense. Guimaraes likes to wear the number because his dad's taxi cab in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil was #039.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Inside Bruno Guimaraes' dream Arsenal transfer six years in making for Mikel Arteta READ MORE :

Tottenham respond as Arsenal consider shock transfer for Spurs skipper Cristian Romero READ MORE :

Whether the decision was Copley's is unknown, although he did wear No.38 when captaining Arsenal's under-21 side last season. Unfortunately for Copley, who's just 19 and highly regarded at London Colney, he suffered an injury just minutes after coming on as a half-time substitute during the Gunners' 3-1 loss against Real Betis in a friendly on Wednesday.

‌



Mikel Arteta said post-match: "It doesn't look good, the mechanism is not too positive, the symptoms that he already has either. Let's hope that tomorrow [Thursday] the news is better than we hope."

Guimaraes will become Arsenal's most expensive signing of the summer, with the Gunners having also brought in Christos Tzolis for £34m and Illan Meslier on a free transfer. The Brazilian is expected to partner Declan Rice in midfield once the season gets going.

Who should Arsenal sign next? Have your say in the comments section.

‌



View 2 Images Louie Copley's number has been changed on the Arsenal website

By leaving Newcastle, Guimaraes becomes the third key player to depart St James' Park this summer as well as manager Eddie Howe. New Magpies boss Matthias Jaissle said: "I met him quickly, but the decision was already made. It was a nice conversation.

"He's a fantastic player and a great human being. It's tough but for him now it's the next challenge and we need to deal with it at a later stage. We trust the players who are here already, but we will also see some changes."

Sports.title: Arsenal's 7 Vinicius Jr alternatives ranked as obvious pick comes out on top
Sports.content:
Arsenal's 7 Vinicius Jr alternatives ranked as obvious pick comes out on top

Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius Junior has ended after the winger signed a new deal with Real Madrid, leaving Mikel Arteta to consider his next move

View 7 Images Arsenal will not sign Vinicius Junior (Image: Antonio Villalba/Real Madrid via Getty Images)

After weeks of intense speculation and plenty of hope on the part of the Arsenal faithful, the Vinicius Junior to north London transfer saga has come to an end. And it’s not the outcome the Gunners wanted.

‌



The red half of north London was sent into a frenzy two weeks ago as reports emerged of Arsenal’s concrete interest in the Real Madrid superstar. Given Vinicius’ deal was set to expire and Real were refusing to improve on their latest contract offer, which was below the Brazilian’s expectations, there was a real belief that Arsenal could pull off a stunning coup.

‌



That sentiment gathered even more momentum as the Premier League champions prepared a huge financial package for Vinicius and reportedly even spoke to the player directly. But despite doing everything in their power to bring him to the Emirates Stadium, Vinicius reached an agreement over a new Los Blancos contract on Thursday, less than 24 hours after a crunch meeting with club officials.

‌



FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Vinicius Jr to Arsenal transfer saga reaches conclusion as Real Madrid star strikes agreement READ MORE :

It was always a highly ambitious and difficult deal to pull off due to the Brazilian’s preference to stay in Madrid and the La Liga giants not wanting to lose their talisman, though that won’t ease the bitter disappointment of losing out on a truly world class player.

With that, questions have been raised by fans over what comes next as Mikel Arteta still clearly wants a left winger capable of taking the club to the next level. Here, Mirror Football takes a look at seven alternative options Arsenal could pursue ahead of the upcoming 2026/27 season, with less than a month left of the transfer window.

‌



7 - Iliman Ndiaye

There are suggestions that Arteta is interested in Everton winger Iliman Ndiaye. The 26-year-old has reportedly rejected a contract offer at Everton but is still believed to cost in the region of £75m.

The Senegalese registered six goals and three assists last season, which only adds to the underwhelming feeling surrounding this particular transfer target. Ndiaye may be Premier League-proven and a good player for Everton, but he is far from world class and arguably isn’t better than Arsenal’s current options. He would be a hugely disappointing signing compared to someone of Vinicius’ calibre, especially given he’d cost such a hefty sum.

6 - Marcus Rashford

View 7 Images Rashford's wages are too high (Image: Hannah Peters - FIFA, FIFA via Getty Images)

‌



Marcus Rashford seems to be linked with a move to Arsenal every summer. That’s somewhat understandable given his situation at Manchester United and just how effective the forward can be on his day, as shown by his 10 goal involvements against the Gunners in 17 Premier League appearances.

But the 28-year-old’s form is hit or miss at the best of times and wouldn’t justify the £325,000-a-week salary Arsenal would be expected to offer him if they pursue a permanent deal. It would make him Arsenal’s top earner ahead of Bukayo Saka, ripping apart their carefully planned wage structure. Rashford’s astronomical wages may well be the reason Barcelona shrewdly opted not to exercise the option-to-buy deal they had negotiated with United earlier this summer.

5 - Rafael Leao

View 7 Images Rafael Leao has been offered to several clubs including Arsenal (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Not too long ago, Rafael Leao was one of Europe’s most highly rated young wingers and the general perception was that he wasn’t too far off Vinicius in terms of raw ability. But the Portuguese has endured two underwhelming seasons that have greatly reduced external interest in him. That, along with the fact he is now 27 and already in his physical peak with no upside, has reportedly reduced AC Milan’s asking price to £45m-£50m.

Leao has also reportedly been offered to Arsenal and several other clubs. While tempting, this signing is a risk Arteta should not take. There are big question marks over his suitability to the Premier League, given his lack of urgency when pressing and the higher quality of defenders he would have to face compared to Serie A.

4 - Nico Williams

View 7 Images Nico Williams has a £77m release clause (Image: Ion Alcoba Beitia, Getty Images)

‌



Another name that has long been linked with an Arsenal move is Nico Williams. football.london reports Arteta is a keen admirer of the 24-year-old, who attracted plenty of attention after helping Spain win the Euros in 2024. However, after Arsenal and Barcelona both flirted with the idea of activating his £50m release clause, Williams shut down any speculation of a move by signing a 10-year contract with Athletic Club.

That has seemingly been to his own detriment, with the winger failing to fulfil his world class potential since and scoring just 16 goals in La Liga across his last three seasons. Reports claim his contract includes a release clause worth around £77m (€90), which remains well within Arsenal’s reach.

Although he possesses the kind of flair and dribbling Arteta requires on the left flank, Williams’ poor stats in a noticeably worse league, as well as his recent injuries, suggest he would struggle to have the kind of impact Arsenal want from such an expensive signing.

‌



3 - Stick with current players

View 7 Images Arsenal have already signed Christos Tzolis (Image: Getty )

Of course, another option, given the lack of quality available on the transfer market currently, is to go into the new season without making another left wing signing. That is borderline shocking to think given the position has been a clear weakness for the Gunners for three years.

But they have already signed Christos Tzolis for £34m this summer. While the Greek international isn’t a flashy name and was brought as a direct replacement for Leandro Trossard, he has looked impressive in pre-season and, along with Gabriel Martinelli, means Arteta is well-stocked in terms of depth in that position.

‌



The Spaniard should also look to deploy Eberechi Eze out on the left more frequently, where he most notably looked impressive away at Manchester City last season. With the market looking so barren, relying on these three options would allow Arteta to bolster the centre forward position instead this summer, until a suitable left winger emerges either in January or next year.

2 - Bradley Barcola

View 7 Images Arsenal and Liverpool have both been linked with Barcola (Image: Getty)

If they deem it necessary to sign a left winger this month, Arteta and Andrea Berta should look to hijack Bradley Barcola’s likely move to Liverpool. Arsenal were interested in signing the PSG winger earlier this summer before going all-in on Vinicius.

‌



Yet, even then, Arteta’s preference was to sign Morgan Rogers, who ended up joining Chelsea in a staggering £117m deal. PSG’s eye-watering valuation of Barcola at £128m is thought to be putting off the Gunners.

Additionally, Barcola is said to favour a move to Liverpool, making a potential deal even more difficult. It's been reported that he's already spoken to Andoni Iraola and he's giving his priority to the Reds over other interested clubs. Therefore, Barcola should only be pursued if the Gunners’ decision-makers believe he is available and financially realistic, given there is no doubting his ability.

1 - Kenan Yildiz

View 7 Images Kenan Yildiz would be Arsenal's best option this summer (Image: (Photo by Nicolò Campo/LightRocket via Getty Images))

‌



Aside from Barcola, the only winger with world class potential that Arsenal have even a slight chance of signing is Kenan Yildiz of Juventus. The Gunners enquired about the 21-year-old earlier this year but were told he was not for sale, considering he signed a four-year contract back in February.

football.london reports Juventus also knocked back an enquiry from Arsenal for Yildiz earlier in the current window. The Turkish international is considered untouchable, but a massive transfer fee and an effort by the player to force an exit might tempt a sale.

Any deal would be very difficult to pull off and would require Arsenal to be creative in terms of their finances - just as they were when it came to forming Vinicius’ pay package. However, it would be well worth the hassle, given it could lead them to secure one of the brightest talents in Europe.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
