Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has called for Ukrainian men of conscription age who are not legally working to be deported to Ukraine. The policy, which continues a recent hardening of PiS’s position towards Ukraine and Ukrainians as it competes with the far right for support, was condemned by government figures, who called it “absurd” and “disgusting”. 🇵🇱 Bezpieczeństwo obywateli powinno być priorytetem każdego rządu. Potrzebne są zdecydowane działania wobec osób przebywających w Polsce niezgodnie z prawem. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/m8MctmmPXd — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, PiS, which has recently been hit by falling support in the polls and the defection of a large breakaway group of more moderate MPs, held a policy convention at which it presented ideas it wants to implement if it returns to power after next year’s parliamentary elections. “One of [our] government’s first, most significant decisions will be to deport men, Ukrainians of military age, who are not legally working in Poland,” announced Tobiasz Bocheński, a deputy leader of the party. “They will have the opportunity to fight for their homeland, so that the horrors of this war can quickly end,” he continued. “Because for Central and Eastern Europe to be secure and free, Ukraine must win.” Bocheński denied that the policy was inhumane, noting that, in 2022, when PiS was in government, “Poles, like no other nation in Europe, opened their hearts, their homes and their wallets to women, children, the elderly and disabled people fleeing Putin’s bombs”. Poland was the primary destination for refugees fleeing Ukraine in 2022. Almost one million of them remain in the country, alongside hundreds of thousands of other Ukrainian immigrants, many of whom arrived before 2022. They are by far Poland’s largest foreign national group. In their announcement of the proposed policy, PiS gave no details of how it would work in practice, nor on what legal basis Ukrainians who are legally resident in Poland and have not violated any laws would be deported. News website Interia, which had reported on PiS’s plans shortly before they were officially announced, notes that data from Poland’s labour ministry show that only around 11,000 Ukrainians are registered as unemployed in Poland. The figures are not broken down by gender, but most are believed to be women. However, PiS’s policy would also apply to Ukrainians in the so-called grey economy, where people work informally without registering or paying taxes, reports Interia. Military-age Ukrainian men in other European countries should not receive social benefits, says Poland's foreign minister, @sikorskiradek. "There should be no financial incentives for avoiding the draft" https://t.co/5TcTqyDa6X — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 16, 2024 PiS’s plan was immediately criticised by government figures, with interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka calling it “an absurd idea” and “pure demagoguery”. She noted that over 95% of Ukrainian men of conscription age in Poland are working legally and paying taxes. “Without these people, many key sectors of the Polish economy would simply grind to a halt,” wrote Gałecka. “Stop the incitement.” Deputy interior minister Maciej Duszczyk, meanwhile, told broadcaster TVN that, among the Ukrainian men not working, many are wounded soldiers in Poland for treatment and rehabilitation or fathers caring for disabled children. Deportations are a “purely political, disgusting idea”, he added. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that, “when [PiS] was in power, they couldn’t even deport those who were breaking the law, and now they’re supposedly going to deport everyone without rhyme or reason”. Since taking power, the current government has increased deportations of foreigners who are in Poland illegally or broke the law while in the country. Last year, it carried out over 9,000 deportations, up from 7,200 in 2023, the last year that PiS was in power Absurdalny pomysł @pisorgpl ws. deportacji Ukraińców to czysta demagogia! Ponad 95% mężczyzn w wieku poborowym legalnie pracuje w 🇵🇱 i płaci podatki (dane ZUS).@OficjalnyJK zapowiada deportacje. A jak miałoby to wyglądać w praktyce? Patrole sprawdzające dokumenty na ulicach?… — Karolina Gałecka (@K_Galecka) August 6, 2026 During the conference on Thursday, PiS emphasised its tough approach to migration more broadly, saying that it would “create a new, restrictive system for foreigners” that would track each immigrant in the country. “Every foreigner will have their own individual account,” and if they commit any offences or fail to abide by any administrative obligations, “the information will be immediately entered into the system, and the deportation process will begin”, said Bocheński. “The only good migration is the return of Poles from abroad,” declared the party on social media. 🛡️ Bezpieczne granice to bezpieczna Polska. Skuteczna ochrona granic i walka z nielegalną imigracją to obowiązek każdego odpowiedzialnego państwa. 👉 Udostępnij! 🔥 Ku nowemu rządowi! pic.twitter.com/rRPZpmXi5U — Prawo i Sprawiedliwość (@pisorgpl) August 6, 2026 In fact, it was during PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023 that Poland saw the largest wave of immigration in its history, and one of the largest anywhere in Europe. In every year between 2017 and 2022, Poland was the EU member state that issued the highest number of first residence permits to immigrants from outside the bloc. There are now over two million foreigners registered as living in Poland, making up just 5% of the population. Around three quarters are Ukrainians (1.55 million), with the next largest groups being Belarusians (139,300), Indians (26,100), Georgians (22,200), Russians (19,500), Vietnamese (15,100) and Turks (14,500). The number of foreigners with residence permits in Poland has reached two million, making up just over 5% of the country’s population, new government data show. The largest national group by far are Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians and Indians https://t.co/SI09WtR7hR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 26, 2026 While in government, PiS welcomed Ukrainian migrants and refugees and was a strong supporter of Ukraine in its defence against Russian aggression. However, since going into opposition, it has taken an increasingly tough line. That has reflected a broader shift in Polish society, with a variety of polls showing rising negative sentiment towards Ukraine and Ukrainians. Recent months have also seen a rise in reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland, including a number of high-profile incidents. Meanwhile, two far-right parties that have long taken an anti-Ukrainian stance, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have soared in the polls, placing pressure on PiS to toughen its own position. One Confederation MEP, Stanisław Tyszka, mocked PiS’s latest policy announcement. “PiS wants to heroically deport hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians whom they themselves let into Poland,” he wrote. “Comedy.” The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show. Poland’s power grid operator, PSE, has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid an ongoing heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. However, following a meeting with PSE and other state energy officials, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has assured Poles that, despite “a very difficult period”, the “situation is under control” and power supplies are secure, thanks in part to the growth of renewables in recent years. ❗️PSE ponownie ogłaszają okresy przywołania na rynku mocy❗️ To już 3. raz w tym roku, kiedy operator sięga po to narzędzie. W historii zdarzyło się to tylko 5 razy, wliczywszy 3 przypadki tegoroczne, co pokazuje wyjątkowość roku 2026 dla energetyki. pic.twitter.com/DbCPnpyae4 — Jakub Wiech (@jakubwiech) August 6, 2026 PSE has called on contracted electricity generators to increase output and large consumers to cut use to help balance the grid on Thursday between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m., as temperatures have this week approached 40°C (104°F) in many parts of the country. The same measures were introduced on Tuesday, as the heatwave pushed up electricity consumption, partly due to increased use of air conditioning and refrigeration. Participants in Poland’s capacity market are paid for maintaining standby capacity and fulfilling their obligations when called upon by the operator. According to PSE, the mechanism is “a remedial measure” used when the generation capacity available to the operator falls significantly below the required safety level. Previously, the measures were invoked in June this year, amid another heatwave that saw Poland hit its highest-ever recorded temperature of 40.5°C. But before that, they had only been used twice since being introduced in 2018. Temperatures in Poland have reached the highest level on record, with a figure of 40.3°C (104.5°F) recorded this afternoon, as the heatwave that has hit Europe this week moves eastwards https://t.co/eRhRxiuCGq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 28, 2026 Poland’s weather institute IMGW issued heat warnings on Thursday for 13 of the country’s 16 provinces, with daytime temperatures forecast to reach between 33C and 38C. High temperatures and prolonged drought conditions have also pushed water levels in many rivers to extremely low levels, with the Vistula, Poland’s longest river, only 5 centimetres above the historic low of 4 centimetres it fell to in Warsaw last year. Some other parts of the river have hit all-time record lows, reports Polsat News. One result has been a disruption of cooling supplies to Poland’s power sector. State energy firm Enea this week announced reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants that are cooled by water from the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity (just over 1% of Poland’s total) has gone offline. On Wednesday, Prime Minister Donald Tusk convened a meeting of a government crisis team, including PSE’s deputy president, to discuss the current heatwave and its potential impact on the power sector. However, afterwards he assured that “the situation is under control” and that the fact that Poland now has “a lot of energy from solar panels and wind turbines makes our system relatively secure”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). Poland’s renewable sector has expanded rapidly over the last decade. Last year, it provided just over 29% of the country’s power, with onshore wind supplying 14% of the energy mix and solar 12%. Renewables generated 29.4% of Poland's electricity in 2025, almost exactly the same figure as in 2024, ending a period of strong growth since 2021. Coal (52.2%) remained the dominant source, though its share declined. Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, meanwhile, wrote on social media: “Just as we said, there is and will be no money for grifters.” Tak jak mówiliśmy, dla przekręciarzy pieniędzy nie ma i nie będzie. https://t.co/4Kqexj6NoC — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 5, 2026 The PKW’s decision to cut PiS’s funds was made after it found that government resources – including from the justice ministry, Government Legislation Centre (RCL) and Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) – had been used to support the party’s election campaign. However, PiS has always argued that the decision was a political one, implemented at the behest of the new Tusk government in order to undermine the main opposition party. Radosław Fogiel, a senior PiS lawmaker and former party spokesman, said that the new NSA ruling “does not change the essence of the matter: it unlawfully deprives the main opposition party of the subsidy to which it is entitled. Russian standards.” Chłopie, powstrzymaj emocje! Ekscytacja jak u nastolatka przed pierwszą randką. A czego dotyczy ów "miażdżący wyrok"? Skargi na bezczynność Ministra Finansów. World.title: Polish prosecutors end 10-year treason investigation into Tusk over Smolensk air disaster
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident. Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government. However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place. Uprzednio wygrałem sprawę cywilną z posłem @OficjalnyJK, który w efekcie musiał wpłacić 50,000zł na siły zbrojne broniącej się Ukrainy. Teraz potwierdzenie @PK_GOV_PL: nie było żadnej zdrady dyplomatycznej ani żadnej intencji jej popełnienia. Oczywiście żaden z kłamców… https://t.co/VKZHlF5xkX — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 5, 2026 Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit. “They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.” The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”. Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash. Donald Tusk's government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”, he adds https://t.co/5ae0gHJj3B — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 4, 2022 The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power. Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster. In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run. However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”. In a statement explaining the decision, the National Prosecutor’s Office said that the legal basis chosen for cooperating with Russia on an investigation – Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation – was, in fact, “the most advantageous solution” for Poland. It ensured the participation of Polish representatives in the Russian-led investigation, including access to the wreckage and crash site. Other legal options would have offered no greater benefits and involved significant risks, concluded the Polish prosecutors. They acknowledged that Russia “subsequently failed to fulfil some of its obligations arising from the adopted procedure”, but said this should have no bearing on assessing the decisions that were previously made on setting up the investigation. The defence ministry will notify prosecutors of 41 suspected crimes linked to a commission established by the former PiS government to investigate the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński https://t.co/aEAlmk9lDM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2024 The prosecutors also found that, not only did Polish officials choose the best legal solution, but there was also “no evidence indicating that individuals authorised to act on behalf of Poland, including the prime minister and members of the Council of Ministers, acted with the intent to harm Poland”. Given that the crime of diplomatic treason requires intent, this finding further reinforced the decision to drop the investigation. However, the prosecutors note that their decision can still be appealed. At the time of writing, neither Kaczyński, Macierewicz, nor other senior PiS figures had commented on the prosecutors’ announcement. However, it is likely they will point to the fact that the current national prosecutor was appointed by Tusk’s government after it had removed the previous PiS-era incumbent in a legally questionable move. The Supreme Court has issued a ruling that effectively found that the government unlawfully replaced a senior prosecutor earlier this year However, the justice minister says the ruling has no legal force as it was issued by illegitimately appointed judges https://t.co/9fCE6d18uy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 27, 2024 In 2020, in a separate civil case, a court ordered Jarosław Kaczyński to apologise for accusing Sikorski of “diplomatic treason” in relation to the Smolensk crash. Two years later, after Kaczyński had refused to comply with the ruling and Sikorski published the apology himself, Kaczyński was ordered to pay the costs. In 2024, an investigation by Tusk’s government found that the PiS administration had wasted tens of millions of zloty on a commission, headed by Macierewicz, that was tasked with re-investigating the Smolensk disaster. It notified prosecutors of dozens of suspected crimes relating to the functioning of the commission. Macierewicz, however, accused the government of spreading “lies and disinformation” designed to “protect Putin”. Jarosław Kaczyński has been ordered to pay 700,000 zl (€150,000) to publish an apology to ex-foreign minister @sikorskiradek. Kaczyński has yet to comply with a 2020 order to apologise for accusing Sikorski of "treason" in relation to the Smolensk crash https://t.co/o0XkTWFgDR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2022 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. During a special meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Poland shared its own experience of dealing with “weaponised” migration from Belarus, which prompted the Polish government last year to restrict the right to asylum for people who cross irregularly. 🔵 KOMUNIKAT | Polska przedstawiła swoje stanowisko ws. migracji na nadzwyczajnym posiedzeniu Rady JHA w sprawie ostatnich wydarzeń w Ceucie 🇵🇱🇪🇺 Wiceminister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji @MaciekDuszczyk wziął udział w odbywającym się we wtorek (4 sierpnia br.)… pic.twitter.com/glfyiu5ZW3 — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) August 4, 2026 Last week, tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, most of them by swimming there from neighbouring Morocco. Dozens died while trying to cross. Among those who managed to enter Ceuta, Spain says that the vast majority have been returned to Morocco. The incident prompted expressions of concern from many European leaders, including calls to restrict Spain’s participation in the Schengen free movement zone (despite the fact that anyone leaving Ceuta for the European mainland is subject to identity checks). Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. Poland has tightened asylum laws, border procedures, and has built effective barriers on its border with Belarus, which is the eastern border of the EU. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms). A court has ruled that Poland's recently introduced partial suspension of the right to asylum is justified and lawful. It rejected a complaint by a Sudanese man who had been denied the right to claim asylum after crossing irregularly from Belarus https://t.co/jx3s1AxRgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2025 On Saturday, Tusk and 21 other EU leaders jointly signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent stay in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. It added that during Tuesday’s meeting it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. Despite efforts to discourage and prevent crossings, the figures remained high, with just under 30,000 attempted crossings recorded in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have fallen dramatically this year, with only 235 attempted crossings recorded in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the estimated number of successful crossings has been falling, from 12,000 in 2023, to 5,000 in 2024, 1,700 in 2025, and zero in the first half of this year, according to the Polish interior ministry. World.title: Construction Disrupts Prague Tourists and Businesses During Peak Summer Season
World.content:
Construction projects across Prague’s historic center are proving a pain for tourists and locals alike who say the clumps of dirt, building supplies and equipment block popular sites and make it difficult to move around one of Europe’s most visited cities.



Heading down Národní to the Charles Bridge or going for a beer near the Vltava river now looks more like a vast construction site where tourists need to look out for more than the cobble-stone streets and baroque spires.

“It’s their first time here too, [they’ve] never seen it and now it’s torn up,” said Sherryl, a tourist visiting from the United States with her friends.

A major source of the disruption are upgrades to the public transport system. The central tram route delivering travelers to the heart of the city near the Národní Divadlo stop has been shuttered for weeks.

The disruption has taken a heavy toll on surrounding businesses like Aggeo, an Italian grocery store along the corridor. Its manager, Irena Kumpová, noted a sharp drop in foot traffic from travelers and regular local customers, who stroll by the National Theater on their way to gaze at the artist David Černý’s famous Kafka head.

“I’d rather stay closed… it’s a catastrophe,” remarked Kumpová.

With tourism growing every year in Prague, the widespread construction is making its mark this summer. So far this year, 1.7 million people have visited Prague, marking the strongest start in 15 years, according to Prague City Tourism and the Czech Statistical Office.

Tram services are suspended through the city center, clogging the streets and forcing many to find another way to work or home. For businesses that rely on heavy foot traffic during the busiest months of the year, that means less earnings.

“I have a table outside, but mainly just to signal to people that we’re open, but no one sits there right now,” said Kumpová.

The reconstruction is part of Prague’s broader effort to modernize its transport network, including long-term investments such as the future tram connection to Wenceslas Square and the expansion of Metro Line D as the city seeks to expand public transport.

Not everybody minds the disruption. The loud machines, dusty air, and obstructed sidewalks offer a certain charm for some who view the construction as part of the sightseeing experience.

“Despite the construction, it’s still beautiful,” said Raluca Costachescu, a traveler from Romania.

Written by: Mae Bryant, Bilyana Spasova, Milica Petrušová, Zuzana Kormančíková, Zhanna Bekiryan

World.title: Live Nation and PPF to Run Three Major Prague Venues
World.content:
Live Nation and PPF Group are forming a joint venture that will operate three of Prague’s major event venues — O2 Arena, O2 Universum and Forum Karlín.

The companies plan to invest in the venues and upgrade their facilities, with Live Nation set to hold a 51 percent stake in the new company.

The agreement will bring together one of the world’s largest live entertainment companies and PPF, the investment group that owns O2 Arena and O2 Universum through its subsidiary Bestsport.



PPF has also operated Forum Karlín, which has been owned by Patria Investment Company since last year.

The companies announced the planned partnership in a joint statement. Financial details of the transaction and the amount of the planned investment have not been disclosed. The deal remains subject to the required regulatory approvals.

Under the agreement, the new operator will be responsible for the day-to-day running of all three venues, including event planning and programming. The venues themselves will remain under their existing ownership structures, and their names will not change.

The partners said they intend to invest substantially in the facilities over the coming years. The aim is to improve conditions for audiences and performers while expanding the number of events held in Prague and strengthening the city’s position on the international concert and entertainment circuit.

PPF said the cooperation with Live Nation is also part of its strategy of developing the long-term value of its assets alongside major international companies.

Live Nation Entertainment operates across several areas of the live entertainment industry, including concert promotion, ticketing and sponsorship. Its businesses include Live Nation Concerts, Ticketmaster and Live Nation Sponsorship.

PPF Group is an international investment company with holdings across Europe, North America and Asia. Its portfolio includes telecommunications, media, financial services, real estate, e-commerce, industry and biotechnology.

World.title: Prague to Restore Tram Service Between Holešovice and City Center
World.content:
Residents of Prague 7 will regain a tram connection between Holešovice and the city center from September, with tram line 5 set to operate through the district and continue toward Wenceslas Square.

The change follows months of pressure from Prague 7 officials and local residents, who have called for better tram connections since the cancellation of line 14.

The district had previously requested either the return of line 14 or the introduction of an equivalent service and organized a petition supporting the demand.



The new arrangement will initially be temporary. According to the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) system, two trams will operate on the route at least through December 2026.

Line 5 to replace temporary route

The new service is linked to planned transport changes in Žižkov. Because of a traffic closure there, tram line 34 will be replaced by line 5 in Holešovice.

At Holešovice train station, line 5 will connect with line 6, effectively creating a continuous service between the two routes. Trams will run from the station through the Holešovice area, past the market and across Vltavská Street before continuing toward Wenceslas Square and other parts of central Prague.

For passengers in Holešovice, the move restores a connection that was lost when line 14 was discontinued.

Service could change again next year

The situation between January and June 2027 has not yet been fully settled. According to PID, the final arrangement will depend in part on discussions between the incoming leaderships of Prague 3 and Prague 7.

Maintaining the additional tram service in Holešovice during that period could require limited reductions elsewhere in Prague 3. Another option would be to temporarily return to the existing arrangement using combined tram lines 6 and 34.

PID has warned that permanently combining lines 5 and 6 could also create delays at both ends of the route. Such a change could affect passengers travelling through Prague 2 and Prague 5, even though it would provide the direct connection sought by Prague 7.

World.title: “Ivan, Go Home!” Rally to Take Place Outside Russian Embassy in Prague
World.content:
A Czech-Ukrainian rally will take place outside the Russian Embassy in Prague on August 20 to mark the 58th anniversary of the Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia.

The event, titled “Ivan, Go Home!”, is scheduled to begin at 6 p.m. on Thursday, August 20, at Boris Němcova Square in Prague 6.

The rally comes one day before the anniversary of the night of August 20-21, 1968, when troops from five Warsaw Pact countries entered Czechoslovakia to crush the Prague Spring reform movement.



The invasion brought an end to the country’s attempt to pursue a more liberal form of socialism and was followed by two decades of political repression and Soviet military presence.

The event is being organized jointly by People in Need (Člověk v tísni), Memory of the People (Paměť národa), Million Moments for Democracy (Milion chvilek pro demokracii), and the European Congress of Ukrainians.

Organizers say the rally will connect the historical experience of the Soviet occupation with Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.

Participants will gather to remember those killed or persecuted following the 1968 invasion and the people who lived under the communist regime that followed. The organizers also plan to express support for Ukraine and draw attention to what they describe as the continuing use of imperial violence by Russia.

The choice of the rally’s name refers to one of the best-known slogans associated with the 1968 invasion. “Ivan, go home!” appeared on posters, walls, buildings and military vehicles as Czechoslovaks protested against the foreign troops occupying the country.

The invasion halted those reforms. Soviet troops remained in Czechoslovakia until the end of the communist era, while the subsequent period of “normalization” brought censorship, political purges and restrictions on civil liberties.

World.title: World of Warcraft Film Ibelin to Shoot in Prague
World.content:
Production of Ibelin, a new film based on the life of Norwegian World of Warcraft player Mats Steen, is moving to Prague this summer.

Filming is expected to take place at Barrandov Studios from early August through early October, following the production’s spring shoot in Norway.

The film is not connected to the 2016 Hollywood movie Warcraft. Instead, it tells the real-life story of Steen, who lived with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and built friendships, relationships and a social life inside the online world of World of Warcraft.



The Prague production is reportedly seeking extras for roles including blacksmiths, guards and innkeepers. The casting suggests that parts of the film set in the game’s fictional world could be filmed in the Czech Republic. The producers have not yet officially confirmed which scenes will be shot in Prague.

Charlie Plummer leads the cast

American actor Charlie Plummer will portray Mats Steen. Toni Collette and Stephen Graham will play his parents, while the supporting cast includes Bill Nighy, Isabela Merced, Maisy Stella, John Bradley and Ivanna Sakhno.

The film will be directed by Norwegian filmmaker Morten Tyldum, whose credits include The Imitation Game and the science-fiction film Passengers.

At the center of the story is the difference between Steen’s increasingly restricted physical existence and the freedom he experienced online. His character, known in World of Warcraft as Ibelin, became an important figure to people he met through the game.

One of Norway’s largest film projects

The Prague shoot is part of an international production with a reported budget of CZK 1 billion.

According to the Norwegian Film Institute, the project received 20 million Norwegian kroner in production support.

Ibelin is being produced by Vendôme Pictures, Pathé and Neby-Tyldum as an international co-production. The Norwegian Film Institute describes it as an English-language drama with a planned running time of around two hours.

The film is being developed for theatrical release, with its premiere currently expected in the third quarter of 2027.

World.title: GALLERY: Time Capsule Buried Beneath Prague’s Wenceslas Square Tramline
World.content:
A time capsule containing different items, newspapers and messages documenting life in 2026 has been buried beneath Prague’s reconstructed Wenceslas Square.

The capsule was placed on Wednesday, August 5, near the statue of St. Wenceslas as work continues on the upper section of the square.

The Prague New Town Association, which is involved in activities around the statue and the surrounding area, organised the ceremony.

The date was not originally chosen for its historical significance. Construction work ultimately determined both the day and the location of the burial. But the association later discovered that August 5 also marks the 60th anniversary of the release of the Beatles’ Revolver album.

“We were wondering what made August 5 go down in history. Then we found out that it was 60 years ago that the Beatles released their famous album Revolver. So now we are leaving a message here for future generations,” said Monika Vlková, the association’s executive director.



The box, measuring 60 by 40 by 23.5 centimetres and weighing about eight kilograms, was then taken to a prepared pit beside the statue. Workers had excavated the hole to a depth of around 1.7 metres, where the capsule was placed before the site was covered.

The container had been wrapped in transparent protective film, as had its contents.

The collection includes coins, newspapers published during the first week of August 2026, T-shirts, badges and written messages. It also contains proposals submitted by architects during the competition for the redesign of Wenceslas Square.

The box reportedly also holds a hammer and a beer glass.

The objects are accompanied by a 20-page report describing everyday life in the Czech capital in 2026. The capsule also contains USB drives with digital material documenting the period of the Covid-19 pandemic and its effects on life in central Prague.

The capsule is intended to remain underground for decades. The association estimates that Wenceslas Square could undergo another major reconstruction in roughly 50 years, although nobody can predict when the next intervention will actually take place.

World.title: Czechia Tightens Temporary Protection Rules for Ukrainian Men Aged 23 to 60
World.content:
New rules affecting Ukrainian men seeking temporary protection in the Czech Republic will take effect on August 5, 2026.

Under the changes, men aged 23 to 60 applying for temporary protection will have to demonstrate that they are exempt from military service in Ukraine.

The requirement will apply to new applications and certain other applications for protection, but not to people who already hold valid temporary protection.



The Czech Interior Ministry says the new rules follow an EU Council decision published in the Official Journal of the European Union on August 4. The decision also extends temporary protection for people fleeing Russia’s war in Ukraine until March 31, 2028.

For applicants aged 23 to 60, military registration documents will be checked as part of the application process. Applicants will use Ukraine’s Reserv+ system to demonstrate their military status, with the electronic military registration document showing whether they are exempt from military service.

The rules are different for younger applicants. People aged 18 to 22 will only need to demonstrate that they are registered in the Reserv+ system.

The new requirement concerns people applying for temporary protection for the first time, as well as repeat applications and applications connected with family reunification. It does not apply to people who already have valid temporary protection.

The military-service requirement will also not be introduced as part of the regular extension process. Ukrainians whose temporary protection is already valid will therefore not have to provide this additional documentation when extending their status through March 2028.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the Czech government had pushed for stricter conditions for new applicants. According to the ministry, the change is expected to reduce the number of new arrivals and ease pressure on public services, including health care and social security.

World.title: Filming of American Spy Series to Bring Restrictions to Prague 7
World.content:
Filming for the American series Birdwatcher will take place at the Prague 7 tax office on Kapitána Jaroše Embankment from August 8 to 24, bringing temporary restrictions to the area.

The production will use the tax office building at Kapitána Jaroše Embankment 1000/7, while part of the sidewalk outside the building will be closed to accommodate filming equipment.

The restrictions will not affect the normal operation of the tax office.



Drivers should also expect temporary parking restrictions on nearby Na Ovčinách Street. Vehicles will still be allowed to pass through the street, but parking will be prohibited during the designated filming periods.

The restrictions will not be in force continuously throughout the filming period. They will apply only on specific dates, with Prague 7 publishing a map showing the affected areas and individual dates on its website.

Prague has become a major filming location

Birdwatcher is an American spy fantasy series set during the Cold War. The production is being led by Legendary and Apple TV, with Andy Goddard directing. Wyatt Russell plays the lead role.

The story follows Colonel Lee Shaw as he embarks on a covert mission behind enemy lines to prevent the Soviet Union from unleashing a new Titan capable of devastating the United States and altering the balance of the Cold War.

The series is set in the 20th century against the backdrop of the Cold War, and parts of the production are being filmed in Prague.

Czech production company Stillking Films is handling the local production. The company has previously worked on major international productions filmed in the Czech capital, including The Gray Man.

World.title: Why is it a problem if Péter Magyar decides who can lead Hungary’s public media?
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s intervention in two public media appointments has caused debate over the independence of Hungary’s state broadcaster.

The independence of Hungary’s public media has been one of the country’s most sensitive political issues ever since the democratic transition of 1989–90. Following the change of government in 2026, it appeared almost inevitable that the operation of the Media Service Support and Asset Management Fund (MTVA) and the wider public service media would undergo far-reaching reforms.

One of Péter Magyar’s flagship campaign promises was to bring the era of political propaganda to an end and establish a genuinely independent public broadcaster.

A cleaner public media – but at what cost?

Events over the past few days, however, have opened an entirely new chapter in that debate. The controversy began when MTVA announced the appointment of Gábor Hajdú—who had previously worked for Hír TV and Echo TV—as the new editor-in-chief of M1 News. At the same time, Miklós Borsa, a former presenter of the broadcaster’s flagship news programme, was set to return to the screen.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar clearly had a different view. Remaining true to his increasingly familiar style of direct political communication, he commented on a news article covering the appointments with just 4 words (which were two words in Hungarian):

“I don’t think so…”

The following day, MTVA announced that both appointments had been withdrawn. The speed of the reversal immediately reignited a fundamental constitutional question: should a prime minister—whether formally or informally—be able to influence who occupies senior positions within the country’s public broadcaster?

The criticism once aimed at Fidesz

The episode is particularly striking because one of the strongest criticisms levelled against Fidesz for years was precisely its alleged political control over Hungary’s public media.

Opposition politicians and independent observers frequently argued that anyone who had watched the so-called “state television” during the previous sixteen years could hardly fail to notice its editorial bias.

Yet even Viktor Orbán generally avoided creating the impression that editorial decisions were being made directly from the Prime Minister’s Office. The latest developments appear considerably more explicit: a brief public comment by the sitting prime minister was followed almost immediately by the withdrawal of two high-profile appointments.

Whether this sequence reflects direct political intervention or merely coincidental timing is open to interpretation. Nevertheless, the public perception it creates is difficult to ignore.

Echoes of the Judit Polgár nomination

Many commentators have therefore drawn parallels with another recent controversy: the nomination of Judit Polgár for the presidency. The issue then was not primarily the nominee herself. Hungary’s greatest-ever chess player would likely have been an acceptable choice for many voters.

Rather, critics argued that the government had abandoned its own promise of broad public consultation and instead acted unilaterally, much as previous governments had done when filling the country’s highest constitutional offices.

A similar criticism now emerges in the case of MTVA. For many, the problem is not necessarily that the two withdrawn media executives had previously worked within what critics describe as the former government’s media machinery. Supporters of the current administration argue that figures associated with political propaganda have no place in a renewed public broadcaster.

Instead, the concern centres on the process itself. If the prime minister can effectively overturn appointments through a public social media comment, questions inevitably arise about where institutional autonomy begins, and political authority ends.

A question that goes beyond Péter Magyar

The debate extends far beyond the current prime minister, Péter Magyar. If it becomes accepted practice that a head of government may informally reverse senior appointments with a single public remark, the same precedent would inevitably be available to every future administration, regardless of political affiliation.

That is precisely why democratic institutions are designed to function according to transparent rules rather than the preferences of individual office-holders. Supporters of Péter Magyar naturally offer a different interpretation.

In their view, this was not political interference but a necessary correction. They argue that leaving individuals who had played leading roles in what they regard as the previous government’s propaganda system would have fundamentally undermined the credibility of efforts to rebuild public service broadcasting.

From this perspective, the intervention was intended to restore institutional independence rather than weaken it.

Good decisions also require the right process

That argument, however, addresses only part of the issue. In a constitutional democracy, legitimacy depends not only on whether the final decision is correct but also on whether it is reached through a fair and transparent procedure.

If senior appointments are made through an established professional process only to be withdrawn immediately after a prime minister’s public intervention, many observers will inevitably conclude that political will ultimately overrides institutional decision-making. Ironically, this is exactly the type of governance that Fidesz’s opponents criticised for years.

The independence of public media is not strengthened simply because a different political force now exercises influence over it. It becomes stronger only when no governing party is able to shape its day-to-day operation according to immediate political interests.

If Péter Magyar genuinely intends to open a new chapter for Hungarian public broadcasting, the long-term objective should be to ensure that senior appointments are made through transparent, institutional procedures that remain as independent from political actors as possible.

Such an approach would not only reinforce confidence in the public media today. It would also establish a democratic standard that every future Hungarian government would be expected to follow.

World.title: A taste of summer at Axis Café & Lounge: a lunch well Spent
World.content:
There’s a particular kind of relief that comes from stepping out of Budapest’s midday summer heat and into somewhere cool, calm, and quietly beautiful. That’s exactly what I found on a recent lunch visit to Axis Café & Lounge, tucked inside the Crowne Plaza Budapest, where the kitchen has rolled out a new summer menu built around a simple idea: real nourishment, real flavor, and a bit of a reset for the senses. I went in curious and left genuinely impressed — here’s how the lunch unfolded.

First Sip: ISLA DE PIÑA

I started, as any reasonable person should on a scorching midday, with a cocktail. The ISLA DE PIÑA arrived pale gold and glistening, a blend of rum, passion fruit purée, lime, and pineapple juice. It was tropical without tipping into syrupy — the passion fruit gave it a tart, almost floral edge, while the pineapple juice rounded everything out into something that tasted like vacation in a glass. It was the kind of drink that makes you slow down immediately, loosen your shoulders, and start reading the menu properly instead of skimming it. A strong, breezy opening move for a midday break from the office grind.

A Rich Start: Duck Liver Terrine

Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

Before the smoky courses arrived, I started with the duck liver terrine, and it set the bar high right from the first bite. Silky and rich, it had that melt-away texture that only a well-made terrine can pull off, balanced by a bright, slightly sweet accompaniment that kept it from feeling too heavy — even in the middle of summer. Spread onto a crisp slice of toasted bread, it struck that classic bistro-style balance between indulgence and freshness, and it was clear from this very first course that the kitchen wasn’t cutting any corners, even on a lighter, seasonal menu. A confident, elegant opener.

Photo: Dailynewshungary.com

Smoke and Sunshine: The Baba Ghanoush

Next came the smoky baba ghanoush — roasted tomato and pepper, parsley, olive oil, and warm flatbread on the side. This dish immediately transported me somewhere else: the charred, smoky depth of the eggplant felt like it had come straight off a summer grill, yet here it was, plated elegantly in the middle of the city. It’s built to be shared, and I can see why — it’s the kind of food that invites conversation, second helpings, and a bit of lingering. The vegetables, herbs, and olive oil worked together in that effortless, Mediterranean way where nothing feels heavy, but everything feels satisfying. Scooped up with warm flatbread, it was fresh, and quietly addictive.

The Baba Ghanoush. Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

The Main Event: Creamy Salmon Tagliatelle

If the baba ghanoush was the warm-up act, the creamy salmon tagliatelle was the headliner. Silky ribbons of pasta wrapped in a rich, velvety sauce, studded with sweet green peas and tender spinach — it managed to feel indulgent and light at the same time, which isn’t an easy balance to strike. The freshness of the peas and spinach cut through the creaminess just enough to keep every bite feeling summery rather than heavy. It’s easy to see why this dish is tipped to be a crowd favorite this season — it has that rare quality of being comforting enough for a lazy terrace lunch or dinner, yet polished enough for a proper go out.

Salmon tagliatelle. Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

A Sweet Landing: Salted Caramel Cake

I closed things out with a slice of salted caramel cake, and it turned out to be the perfect final note. Rich, buttery caramel balanced by just the right touch of salt, it managed not to feel like an afterthought — often desserts can feel like an obligatory add-on after a savory meal like this, but this one held its own. Sweet, a little smoky-toned from the caramel, and satisfying without being overwhelming, it was a fitting way to end a meal built around balance.

Salted Caramel Cake at Axis. Photo: Dailynewshungary.com

Worth Going Back For

Even with a satisfyingly full table, I couldn’t help but notice a couple of other dishes on the menu that I’m already planning to order next time. The cauliflower and white bean cream soup, finished with harissa and toasted cashews, sounds like exactly the kind of dish that’s light enough for a hot afternoon but still hearty enough to carry a lunch — the legumes promise a plant-based richness, while the harissa adds a bit of a kick without taking over.

Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete Photo: Axis Café & Lounge/Antonio Fekete

And for anyone after something a touch more elegant, the pan-seared sea bass fillet with sautéed chard, garlic, roasted baby carrots, and salsa verde looks like the more refined choice on the menu — bright, herby, and beautifully balanced, if the description is anything to go by. Both are firmly on my list for a return visit.

If you missed it: Gordon Ramsay chooses Budapest for first Central European restaurant – opening date revealed

The Bigger Picture

What struck me most about the meal wasn’t any single dish — it was the coherence of the whole experience. Chef Csuklich Viktor’s summer menu at Axis clearly isn’t just about seasonal ingredients for the sake of it; it’s built around the feeling of stepping away from the heat and pace of the city and actually recharging, even if just for the length of a meal. Plant-forward dishes sit comfortably alongside more indulgent choices, and the cocktail list — full of citrus, herbs, floral notes, cucumber, mint, and grapefruit — reinforces that same sense of freshness throughout.

Whether you’re grabbing a quick business lunch or settling in for a longer, unhurried midday or evening meal on the terrace, this feels like a menu designed to meet you wherever you are — and to send you back out into the city a little more refreshed than when you arrived.

If you are at Nyugati, don’t forget that Axis Café & Lounge is open daily for breakfast from 8:00–12:00 and for lunch and dinner from 12:00–22:00. The service is superb – something everyone can experience for themselves.

World.title: Budapest Festival Orchestra to give free open-air concert at Heroes’ Square
World.content:
Iván Fischer and the Budapest Festival Orchestra (BFO) will give a free open-air concert at Heroes’ Square on the evening of Sept 12 to open the autumn season, the orchestra said ina statement on Friday.

The concert begins at 6.30pm and will feature Schubert’s Eighth, the Unfinished Symphony, as well as works by Arvo Part and Prokofiev. The BFO Children’s Choir will perform the Part piece in the original Estonian under Fischer’s baton.

The organisers said the concert is primarily aimed at families and the youngest music lovers. The BFO’s new children’s choir will also make its debut at the event.

The concert is free to attend, and no registration is required. The organisers ask the audience to arrive early for better seating, and cardboard chairs will be provided on site, which can be taken home after the concert.

World.title: Treasure hunt: what experts found around the German motorbike recovered from the Danube in Budapest – photos
World.content:
A Bosch W 175 T 1 spark plug and bakelite plug holder, an oil bottle, a grease tube, insulating tape, a cylinder-head spanner, a spark-plug wrench, a small wire brush and a tyre-pressure gauge were among the items recovered from the pannier of a Second World War-era German motorbike, which emerged from the rapidly receding Danube last weekend alongside the remains of a German soldier, the Institute and Museum of Military History said in a Facebook post on Friday.

Human remains found beneath the German motorbike

The glue and patch material from a puncture-repair kit had also survived intact. The institute’s experts additionally found a drive-chain link, several bolt heads, a hammer head and Y-straps when they opened the side box of the DKW NZ 350-1 German motorbike, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

Museum specialists will clean and conserve the artefacts, and restore those suitable for restoration, they added.

One comment beneath the post said the remains and identity tags of a Wehrmacht soldier and a Waffen-SS soldier had been found next to the motorcycle, along with a decoration known as the Kuban Shield. The medal was awarded to soldiers who successfully defended the Kuban bridgehead in Russia and along the shores of the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov during fighting between February and October 1943.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

A passer-by spotted the motorbike

The Institute and Museum of Military History had previously announced on social media that cleaning and urgent conservation work had begun on the Second World War motorcycle discovered at the weekend in the bed of the Danube, where water levels had fallen to a record low.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

This is how it was taken out from the mud of the Danube: Valuable WWII German motorcycle, human remains and explosives pulled from the Danube in Budapest – photos

It recalled that a passer-by had spotted the motorcycle’s front fork protruding from beneath the rocks on the embankment at Batthyány Square the previous weekend. Museum experts identified the machine and excavated it together with its associated items. The rare find was transported to the institution’s hangar on Kerepesi Road in the early hours of Monday, and work to clean and conserve the motorcycle began during the week.

Photo: Facebook/HM Hadtörténeti Intézet és Múzeum

The work was inspected on Wednesday by László Kürtös, the Ministry of Defence’s parliamentary state secretary, and Colonel Roland Maruzs, commander of the Ministry of Defence’s Institute and Museum of Military History, the post said.

World.title: Massive explosion and devastating fire at strategic MOL oil refinery: will fuel prices rise again? – video
World.content:
A fire has broken out at the MOL oil refinery in Bratislava/Pozsony, with witnesses reporting at least one enormous explosion – here is what we know so far.

Explosion and fire at MOL oil refinery in Bratislava/Pozsony

A fire erupted on Friday at the MOL oil refinery complex in Bratislava, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said at the Government Information Centre briefing, citing freshly arrived information. According to the official account, a storage tank caught fire; there were no injuries and the incident is not expected to have any implications for supply security, the Hungarian news agency reported.

The Bratislava-based Új Szó daily reported that the blaze was preceded by damage to one of the tanks storing petroleum products, after which the contents ignited. Anton Molnár, an MOL spokesman, said it involved a double-walled tank that complies with the strictest safety regulations.

Illustration: the MOL plant in Tiszaújváros. Photo: MOL

The company said the fire did not spread to other technological units or storage tanks and did not disrupt refinery operations. No one was injured in the accident.

Fire to be extinguished shortly

By the time reporters arrived, little smoke could be seen at the scene and the flames had practically died down. According to the MOL spokesman, the fire would be completely extinguished within a short time.Local witnesses said there had been an explosion at the refinery, clearly audible across the surrounding area. They described windows in several nearby buildings shaking as thick smoke rose above the oil refinery.

Here is a video of the fire:

Momentálna situácia v bartislavskom závode Slovnaft. Bola počuť explózia okolo 13:40, následne vysoké plamene a momentálne sa hustý čierny dym valí na Petržalku a smerom do Rakúska. pic.twitter.com/PA9afM7sjP — Peter Svitek (@SvitekPeter) August 7, 2026

The Slovnaft refinery, owned by MOL, processes Russian crude oil and has a maximum capacity of 6.1 million tonnes a year, equivalent to 124,000 barrels of crude oil per day when running at full tilt. It is regarded as one of Europe’s most complex refineries and is of key importance to MOL, as well as to fuel supplies in the region, Portfolio wrote.

Illustration. Photo: Anadolu/State Emergency Service of Ukraine

The owners of MOL

MOL is widely considered a Hungarian state-owned company, although it has multiple owners:

Foreign Investors : ~31.2% (mostly international institutional funds)

: (mostly international institutional funds) MOL-New Europe Foundation : 10.49%

: Maecenas Universitatis Corvini Foundation : 10.00%

However, the Hungarian State directly holds only the single “Series B” voting preference share (golden share), which grants veto rights over key strategic decisions.

World.title: Polymarket already knows who Hungary’s next president will be – do you agree?
World.content:
On Polymarket, you can bet on almost anything, and its opposite. Now you can place your money on who will become Hungary’s next president. The website, which has been blocked in Hungary, has already “predicted” victories for Donald Trump and Péter Magyar. If it gets this one right, it could prove a particularly humiliating blow for Fidesz – and for Viktor Orbán personally.

A communications blunder over Judit Polgár

On the night of his election victory, Péter Magyar made it clear which public officials and other leaders appointed or elected by Fidesz – but whom he regarded as puppets – should resign within a matter of weeks. At the top of his list was Tamás Sulyok, then Hungary’s president. All Magyar, the prime minister-in-waiting, expected of him was to ask him to form a government and then resign immediately afterwards.

Sulyok did not resign. The defeated Fidesz made a feeble attempt to stand behind him, invoking alleged Tisza authoritarianism, but the argument attracted little meaningful public support. By then, Sulyok’s name had become inseparable from the Orbán system, and only the most committed Fidesz voters – just 15 to 20 per cent of the population – believed he should remain in office.

The stand-off was resolved when the Tisza parliamentary supermajority passed a constitutional amendment terminating Sulyok’s mandate. The president then signed it.

Péter Magyar announced a broad public consultation on the identity of the next president, invited suggestions and, just a few hours later, named chess legend Judit Polgár. Both Tisza supporters and its opponents turned against him, seeing the process as an Orbán-style snap decision rather than the promised consultation. Polgár ultimately declined the nomination. Magyar apologised, but his popularity appears to have suffered somewhat as a result of the blunder.

Judit Polgár and Arnold Schwarzenegger. Source: Facebook/Polgár Judit hivatalos oldala

Parliament to elect a new president

Under Hungary’s current constitutional arrangements, the president must be elected by Parliament. Hungary is a parliamentary republic: power rests with the prime minister rather than the president. The head of state is largely ceremonial and has no realistic prospect of wielding executive power, although Judit Novák’s downfall demonstrated clearly that a president can still make mistakes – and that the consequences can rebound on the political community that elected them.

The Hungarian Parliament – in which Tisza holds 141 of the 199 seats – will make its decision next Tuesday. It is widely expected, however, to approve whoever the Tisza parliamentary group nominates this Saturday.

Based on the meetings held by Péter Magyar and Bálint Ruff, the minister in charge of the Prime Minister’s Office, there may be four possible candidates. Naturally, however, nothing prevents the prime minister from putting forward another name.

The potential candidates – based on the meetings

Ágnes Forsthoffer, Tisza’s Speaker of the House and acting president, would be the obvious choice. Magyar has already indicated that the current acting president will remain in the post until the constitutional drafting process is complete. That process could take years if the promised public consultation goes ahead.

Magyar and Ruff have met Botond Fülöp, the so-called “Vidéki Prókátor”, who was the first to notice that Katalin Novák had granted a presidential pardon to Endre Kónya, an aide to the director of the children’s home in Bicske, where children had been abused. The ensuing public outrage swept Novák from office.

Fülöp kept his identity secret for a long time, revealing it only after the change of government, on 11 May. Since then, he has spoken out on public affairs several times – and not always in support of the Tisza government, including most recently over the exercise of the presidential pardon power.

András Baka – Former president of the Supreme Court and a respected legal scholar, Baka was removed by Viktor Orbán in 2011 after publicly criticising the newly formed Fidesz government’s policies, its judicial reforms and changes affecting the independence of the courts.

Ignác Romsics – A Széchenyi Prize-winning historian, academic and university professor, Romsics is the author of the textbook on 20th-century Hungarian history used by more university students than any other when studying modern Hungarian history. He, too, has spoken out against the Fidesz government on several occasions. You can read his interview on the subject in a July 2025 Válasz Online podcast.

Who is Polymarket backing?

On an online betting platform where you can wager on almost anything, why should Hungary’s next president be any different? The same was possible in the most recent Hungarian parliamentary election, when Péter Magyar was already leading by a huge margin on Polymarket even though his advantage was not yet so clear in the opinion polls.

Polymarket currently allows users to bet on five prospective presidential candidates who have attracted more than 1 per cent of the wagers.

Botond Fülöp is the frontrunner, with 35 per cent of the bets placed on him. He is followed by Adrienn Laczó, a lawyer and former criminal judge, on 25 per cent, according to Blikk. Ágnes Forsthoffer, retired Lutheran Bishop Tamás Fabiny and Ignác Romsics are currently on 5, 4 and 4 per cent respectively, while Péter Bárándy, a former Socialist justice minister, stands at 3 per cent.

If you missed: Will Fidesz split soon? A survey says the breakaway camp would have a strong chance

Péter Magyar’s cryptic remarks

At today’s press conference, the prime minister said that ten names had been considered for the post. The Tisza leadership had already discussed the matter on Friday and would put forward three names. Anyone who had been following the news in recent days, he suggested, would not be surprised by the shortlist.

He added that the country now needed someone for the role who had never previously held a position in party politics.

Sándor Palace: the official residence of the Hungarian President in the Buda Castle. Photo: Facebook/Dr. Sulyok Tamás

He also indicated that one of the candidates was someone he had mentioned in a Facebook post, while another was someone whom the algorithm had prevented him from posting about, Telex wrote.

Who do you think will be Hungary’s next president?

World.content:
Hungary is due to elect its next president on Tuesday, 11 August, with the ceremonial oath of office already listed on Parliament’s official agenda. World.title: Power and water concerns at Sziget Festival? Founder reveals what’s really going on
World.content:
Sziget Festival founder Károly Gerendai has vowed that there will be no power or water shortages at this year’s event.

Lots of guests expected at this year’s Sziget Festival

Gerendai told MTI on Friday that daily attendance of 60,000-70,000 would be reassuring, and the festival would not need to use its backup diesel generators, which have a larger environmental footprint. Whereas the festival has enough generators to cover 95 percent of its power needs, recent government announcements suggest no additional self-imposed restrictions from the country’s grid will be required, he added.

How the number of festivalgoers changed since the start of the Sziget Festival. The peak was years ago. Photo: MTI

To mitigate water supply issues, organisers have installed sprinkler systems at their own expense and prepared water tanks in case of low pressure in the main system. They have also laid down more walkway panels than in previous years to reduce dust on the main stage area, he noted.

Gerendai said ticket sales have slowed in the past week or two, likely due to the “mood of catastrophe” caused by extreme heat and energy restrictions. However, he said a sell-out crowd was unlikely, and 60,000-70,000 punters a day would be preferable to the permitted 95,000 in the current dry and dusty conditions.

Major international performers coming to Sziget Festival 2026

The official programme runs from 11 to 16 August on Óbuda Island (Hajógyári Island), with headliners including Twenty One Pilots, Florence + The Machine, Bring Me The Horizon, Skrillex, Zara Larsson, and Lewis Capaldi. Two Hungarian acts, Sisi and Carson Coma, will also perform on the main stage.

Other announced performers include Ashnikko, Biffy Clyro, Parcels, Underworld, Wolf Alice, Richie Hawtin, Dom Dolla, Sara Landry and Hungarian rapper Beton.Hofi. Organisers say the complete festival will feature more than 600 music, theatre, circus, dance, workshop and sporting programmes.

If you missed: MÁV railway group preparing with extra services for the Sziget Festival – details

A special Day Zero will also be held on 10 August, reviving a feature familiar from earlier editions of Sziget. Faithless, Morcheeba and Goran Bregović and his Wedding and Funeral Orchestra will return to evoke some of the festival’s most memorable previous decades.

Sziget Festival in Hungarian ownership again

In November 2025, the festival left Superstruct and returned to the hands of its founder, Károly Gerendai, and the existing management team. Gerendai rejoined Sziget after an eight-year absence, while chief executive Tamás Kádár remained in his position.

The new owners have placed renewed emphasis on Sziget’s relationship with Budapest, its cultural diversity and its identity as an independent festival. Sziget City is one of the clearest signs of that strategy: an attempt to ensure that international visitors discover not only the stages of the Island of Freedom, but also the neighbourhoods, clubs and cultural communities that shape Budapest throughout the year.

World.title: Romanian shipyard delivers hull of largest cable-laying ship in Japan
World.content:
The VARD shipyard in Tulcea, eastern Romania, has completed the construction of the hull of “Discovery,” the largest vessel intended for the installation of submarine cables and the first such project delivered by the VARD group for the Japanese market.

The ship, valued at over USD 200 million, will have an important role in the development of infrastructure for offshore wind energy and the transport of electric energy through submarine cables.

The construction of the vessel’s hull was carried out in Romania, at the VARD shipyards in Tulcea and Brăila, and after launching, it was towed to the VARD Langsten shipyard in Norway, where the specialized equipment was installed, and the final tests were carried out before delivery. The vessel was officially handed over to the Japanese company Toyo Construction at the end of June and is currently heading to Japan, where it will be based in the port of Ishikari Bay.

“Discovery” was designed to meet the specific conditions in Japan, where the water depth increases rapidly near the coast. The vessel can operate both in shallow waters and offshore, where future floating wind farms will be installed.

The vessel is approximately 151 meters long, 28 meters wide, and can transport up to 9,000 tons of submarine cables, distributed in two carousels with capacities of 4,000 and 5,000 tons.

On board, the ship has a main crane with a lifting capacity of 400 tons and an auxiliary crane of 100 tons. The vessel is also equipped with a dynamic positioning system, a heliport and equipment for the operation of remotely operated underwater vehicles.

In addition to the installation of submarine cables, “Discovery” can also be used for offshore construction works, including the installation of foundations for wind turbines and anchoring operations for floating turbines.

The vessel is equipped with a hybrid propulsion system, in which diesel engines are used to produce electric energy, while propulsion is provided by electric motors. The system includes batteries and the possibility of shore power supply during stationing, in order to reduce fuel consumption and emissions. Up to 90 crew members and technicians can work on board.

The Japanese government has set the rapid expansion of offshore wind energy capacities as an objective in the coming period, and this vessel will be used for the installation of the submarine electric cables necessary to connect the new farms to the energy grid.

For VARD, the project marks the first delivery to the Japanese market in the segment of specialized vessels for the offshore wind industry. In recent years, the VARD Tulcea shipyard has specialized in the construction of the hulls of some of the most complex vessels intended for the offshore industry, including vessels for the installation of submarine cables and for the development of offshore wind energy projects.

Several of the most advanced vessels of this type currently used worldwide were built in Romania and subsequently equipped at the VARD group’s shipyards in Norway.
