World.title: Alleged torturers to seek bail as 15yo assessed for electronic monitoring
World.content:
A 15-year-old alleged torturer will be assessed for an electronic monitoring device in an attempt to apply for bail, while the court has heard several co-accused also intend to apply for bail, after a 17-year-old with an intellectual disability was found bashed, zip-tied and wrapped in plastic in bushland.

Seven co-accused faced Townsville Magistrates Court charged with a string of offences including torture after the teenager was found in bushland in Pallarenda on July 18.

The police prosecutor told the court several people were gathered at a house when two relatives of the victim made allegations about the victim, which led to the alleged assault.

The prosecutor said the group, which had moments before been socialising, allegedly kicked the victim and whipped him with a "horse whip" leaving him "crawling out onto the road".

Police allege the assault continued, with more alleged perpetrators arriving in a vehicle and allegedly continuing to strike the victim with a bat and a metal implement and stomping on him.

The victim was allegedly dumped in bushland near Pallarenda in Townsville. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

Police allege the victim was then wrapped in industrial clear plastic with his legs zip-tied together, put in the boot of a vehicle before being dumped in bushland.

Police prosecutor Harriet Hearn told the court the victim needed surgery as he had sustained a broken nose, spinal fracture, fractured tibia, friction burns, and lacerations.

Days after prior offending

The court was told the accused 15-year-old allegedly committed the torture offence the day after receiving a warning from the court for other offending.

The victim required surgery after sustaining multiple injuries. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

"This is some of the most serious types of offences we might see in this court … yet alone offences that have been committed by a juvenile," Ms Hearn said.

The 15-year-old's defence lawyer, Sarah Belford, said the case against her client was "circumstantial" and that he was party to the offences, not a participant.

Police allege his fingerprints were found on the industrial plastic wrap.

'Outrageous' allegations

Police charge 11 people after teen bashed, wrapped in plastic and ‘dumped’ Eleven people have been charged after a 17-year-old boy was bashed and dumped wrapped in plastic in bushland in Townsville.

Magistrate Steven Mosch said the 15-year-old had a "limited" but "recent" criminal history and that the "exceptionally serious" new charges were an "escalation".

"The allegations are outrageous," he said.

Magistrate Mosch said it could be 12 months before the matters were finalised before the court, but he needed assurance the 15-year-old would comply with bail conditions, if granted.

The matter was adjourned to August 13 for Youth Justice to carry out a suitability assessment for the use of an electronic monitoring device for the 15-year-old.

Meanwhile, police will check the suitability of the addresses submitted by three co-accused who intend to apply for bail. Their cases were adjourned to August 10.

The cases of another three co-accused were also adjourned until August 10.

World.title: Why broadcasting row has Tour de France Femmes fans 'pissed off'
World.content:
The catchcry of the Tour de France Femmes by its lead sponsor, Zwift, is pretty simple: Watch the Femmes.

By and large, the viewership data shows that people are doing exactly that.

And why wouldn't they?

After a riveting seven days of racing so far, capped by Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney's masterful ascent of the legendary Mont Ventoux, the top three riders in this year's race are separated by just 39 seconds.

Six different riders have claimed stage victories so far, with the overall race lead changing hands three times since the opening stage.

The 2024 champion, Niewiadoma-Phinney, holds a 15-second advantage over Demi Vollering, the woman she beat two years ago by a measly four seconds.

This is a race that has had it all.

The three-way battle between Demi Vollering, Marlen Reusser and Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney has captivated fans this year. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

But fans, as yet, cannot watch the race in its entirety, with just three of the nine stages of this year's race televised from start to finish.

The lack of comprehensive live coverage is a growing pain that the women's edition of the Tour de France is hoping to overcome as the fifth edition of its most recent iteration comes to a close in Nice this weekend.

It is something that women's riders' union, The Cyclists' Alliance (TCA) — whose president is Australian former world and Olympic champion Grace Brown — has criticised throughout the race.

"For the biggest race in women's cycling, partial coverage is no longer enough," TCA wrote in a social media post.

The 'accursed' mountain that stands apart this Tour de France The ascent to hell on the punishing slopes of Mont Ventoux is one of the Tour de France's most formidable and iconic theatres.

"Fans will still miss the attacks, the tactics, and the moments that could define the race."

Broadcaster Orla Chennaoui, who hosts the coverage for TNT Sports in the UK, was less diplomatic.

"I'm getting really annoyed now. I'm getting really, really pissed off," she said on an Instagram reel that she titled: Women's sport done a disservice Editions #4957.

"What the heck? There is so much excitement and interest in the Tour de France Femmes.

"The riders, the race have proven over and over again how dynamic and dramatic this sport is.

"I have never seen my [social media] algorithm so flooded with excitement, with joy, with celebration for this race.

Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney won her first Tour de France Femmes stage on the slopes of Mont Ventoux. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"It's everywhere, on Instagram, podcasts popping up all over the place, YouTube videos, more written articles that I would ever have imagined when I started covering women's cycling 10 years ago.

"And we still, despite this, despite how proven the interest is, we cannot get live TV coverage.

"ASO [Amaury Sport Organisation], what are you doing? Why can we not get to watch all stages live?"

The astonishing story behind the women's Tour The Tour de France Femmes produced one of the closest finishes in cycling stage race history last year. But when the women's Tour was first revived, it was called "ugly".

Chennaoui said there was a "huge will" from broadcasters to show the race in its entirety every day in that post, which she acknowledged she may get in trouble for and be asked to delete.

All 21 stages of the men's Tour de France were broadcast live in their entirety.

On the same day that the third stage of the women's Tour de France Femme was half-shown, stage one of the men's Tour de Pologne World Tour race was shown in full, all five hours, four minutes and 11 seconds of what was a flat, 234.2-kilometre race.

The duration of the Tour de France Femmes broadcast has increased to 27 hours and 40 minutes for this year's race, up five hours and 20 minutes from what was shown live in 2024.

However, TCA noted that France Télévisions data showed a 40 per cent increase in viewership from 18.3 million in 2024 to 25.7 million in 2025.

"The demand is undeniable," TCA said.

"We are asking for the coverage to catch up."

One of the pre-race favourites, Demi Vollering crashed early in the stage. (Getty Images: Alex Broadway)

That post was put up in the hours before stage three took place, a stage won by Norway's Sigrid Haugset with an 88km breakaway attack.

However, the move that saw the Norwegian break away from the peloton was completely missed, as the TV cameras had not started rolling.

Additionally, one of the pre-race favourites, Vollering crashed early in the stage, an incident that was, again, missed by the cameras, and could have huge repercussions for the rest of the race.

"That was disappointing," former world champion on the track and the road Lizzie Deignan told the For The Love Of Cycling podcast.

"There's no substitute for footage. You can't get a feel of the race, of the tension, of the atmosphere."

According to organisers, this year's Tour de France Femmes is being broadcast in 190 countries, including by SBS in Australia.

France Télévisions keeps the supporters of women's cycling in the shade with their coverage. (Getty Images: NurPhoto/Romain Doucelin)

However, SBS and the Tour's other broadcast partners around the world can only show the footage they are provided with.

France Télévisions handles production and distribution of the broadcast on behalf of the Amaury Sport Organisation [ASO].

The ASO is also responsible for the men's Tour de France, as well as other major cycling events, including two of cycling's monument one day races, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Paris-Roubaix.

The organisation was heavily criticised for its coverage of the women's edition of Paris-Roubaix earlier this year, with less than 90 minutes of the three-and-a-half hour race shown.

"Paris-Roubaix this year, regardless of what they are going to say about TV numbers, was a step backwards," Chennaoui said in her Instagram reel.

"They're still doing a disservice to women's racing."

Tour de France Femmes race director Marion Rousse says things are moving in the right direction. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

As for the Tour de France Femmes, Deignan, who won the 2020 edition of La Course by Le Tour de France, a one-day precursor to the current women's multi-stage Tour, said the lack of coverage was a return to the "old days" of following professional cycling.

"It was very hard to follow from home," Deignan said of stage three of this year's Tour.

"It was like being back in the old days, refreshing news feeds, trying to figure out what's going on."

Cycling Weekly spoke to race director Marion Rousse about the criticism, and she said the race was moving towards full broadcast coverage.

"We're giving serious consideration to broadcasting all the stages in full in the future because the women deserve it," Rousse told Cycling Weekly.

"It works well in terms of audience figures.

"We're currently giving it real consideration, which is a step forward. Things are moving in the right direction."

World.title: Tokyo once had 13,000 geisha. Now that number has plummeted
World.content:
Ikuko moved gracefully as she danced for shoppers in a busy Tokyo mall, the geisha's black kimono gently swaying with each precise movement.

Only, the 86-year-old wasn't really there — it was a hologram; a 3D projection of one of Japan's oldest and most famous geisha, displayed in a life-size white box.

"Thank you very much," she said to passers-by, before bowing and changing to a younger version of herself, created with AI.

Ikuko doesn't think AI is "cut out for this dance" just yet — or to replace their legendary hospitality — but with geisha numbers dwindling, she's resigned to embracing new things to save one of Japan's most iconic art forms.

Loading...

Ikuko sorts through dozens of kimono she's acquired in a long career as a geisha. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

There were once 200 geisha in Akasaka, the area of Tokyo where Ikuko practises, but over Ikuko's 60-year career she has watched their number fall to about 20.

"I felt we had to preserve this culture, so I did it for the sake of that very culture," she told Foreign Correspondent. "This is the era we are entering, so I have to go along with it."

After an illustrious career, which includes being the first geisha awarded Japan's prestigious Order of the Rising Sun, Ikuko feels a special responsibility to preserve the tradition, granting Foreign Correspondent rare access into a hidden world.

"I'm already at the end of my life," she said. "My greatest regret is that I hope Tokyo's geisha districts will truly survive for another few decades."

The pinnacle of hospitality

Tokyo's geisha live and work in special districts called hanamachi, or flower towns.

There were once dozens of them in the city, but today only six major hanamachi remain, while the number of geisha across the city has also fallen from about 13,000 in 1940 to around 200.

With their striking white makeup and bold black wigs, geisha is synonymous with Japan, but a lot of people — even many locals — don't really understand what they do.

Geisha operate largely behind closed doors, traditionally catering to an exclusive group of customers.

Young geisha take a selfie before a performance. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

They are artisans who are said to embody omotenashi, the Japanese art of wholehearted, selfless hospitality.

They dedicate their lives to perfecting traditional Japanese arts, which they rehearse by day.

At night, they host banquets in exclusive, high-end restaurants and specialist teahouses, which have traditionally been run on a referral-only basis, where new patrons must have an introduction from an existing client.

At a banquet, they dance, play music on traditional instruments like the shamisen and taiko drum, and ensure conversation flows between guests.

"This is the very pinnacle of hospitality," Ikuko said. "Indeed, perhaps only the most distinguished guests are permitted to enter."

Ikuko as a young woman. (Foreign Correspondent: Natalie Whiting)

There were around 400 geisha in Asakasa when Ikuko started. Now, there are 20. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

In her long career, Ikuko has entertained politicians, business leaders and chairmen.

She's also been confronted with the misconception that geisha are prostitutes.

Once, during a visit to America, she ended up in hospital and had to spend her convalescence educating the nurses, who mistakenly thought she was a sex worker.

Though having sex with clients has never been the job of a geisha, the lines have blurred at times, and Ikuko doesn't shy away from that history.

"In the old days, there were certainly many geisha who sacrificed themselves for their families and their households," she said. "Nobody wants that sort of thing anymore. There are no sellers and no buyers."

Ikuko is one of Japan's most famous geisha. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

The beginning of the end

Ikuko made her debut as a geisha in Tokyo, in 1964, as the city was hosting the Olympics, "a time when the whole of Japan was buzzing with excitement," she recalled.

In the "busy, old days," she said, "if a booking for this banquet was 30 minutes, I'd have to rush straight off to the next one."

Iwashita Hisafumi, who was working in a prominent geisha district at the time, also remembers those days.

He can pinpoint the moment things started going downhill for the geisha.

Iwashita Hisafumi is a writer specialising in geisha culture. (Foreign Correspondent: Sissy Reyes)

It was 1993, and in an effort to clean up politics and protect confidentiality, then-prime minister Hosokawa Morihiro announced politicians and businessmen should stop using the restaurants, called ryotei, for meetings.

"From the very next day, I saw for myself that the customers stopped coming," Mr Iwashita said. "That was when the decline began."

Ryotei restaurants started closing, and many of the city's geisha districts ceased to exist.

Mr Iwashita, who's now a writer and expert on geisha, is concerned Tokyo's remaining ryotei have been too slow to find new customers and income sources to keep the tradition alive.

"Ultimately, it is culture, but culture cannot flourish where money doesn't flow," he said.

Changing to survive

Some are trying to adapt. In a banquet room 15 minutes away, the old rule book has been thrown out.

Asakusa Miyakadori no longer requires a referral or invitation to attend, advertising heavily on social media and taking bookings online.

The experience has been tailored for tourists, with the crowd made up of guests from Mexico, Australia, the United States, Singapore and Germany.

It might not sound like it, but it's a radical approach in what was once such a closed world, but Kawamura Yuta said drastic action was needed, not only for the survival of the restaurant but for his mother Okami Chikage's legacy.

Okami Chikage, who owns Asakusa Miyakadori, and her son Kawamura Yuta. (Foreign Correspondent: Sissy Reyes)

She became an apprentice geisha at just 15 years old and, after more than 35 years practising, took on a new role as the owner of Asakusa Miyakadori.

She once hosted banquets here — now she runs the place.

"If the industry were to fade away and come to an end before my mother dies, I'd feel terribly sad," Mr Kawamura said.

Okami Chikage didn't need too much persuading to start doing things differently.

"I feel we have to take one step, then another, and keep moving forward," she said. "To do that, I think it might sometimes mean stepping slightly outside the tradition rather than sticking to it rigidly."

Tourists pose for a photo with geisha in Tokyo. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

The changes have been met with some backlash, she said, mostly from "among our own".

But she doesn't let it bother her. "I reckon there are always people who will complain," she said.

Three geisha performed for the guests at the banquet, dancing and playing the shamisen, before playing a traditional drinking game called konpira fune fune.

"When you see [geisha] on TV, it's great, but you're not there," said one patron, Arturo Rabade, a Cuban who lives in Miami. "You don't sense the emotion — and that's what I did today."

His wife PoShan Wong Rabade agreed, "I think it's part of the history of Japan that we don't want to lose, right?"

The next generation of geisha

From the outside, the glass-fronted, multi-storey building looks the same as the others nestled alongside it on the thin Tokyo street.

But when the elevator opens on the third floor, it's like stepping back in time.

The geisha of Ikuko's house flourished fans and danced behind a choreographer to traditional Japanese music, practising for an upcoming performance at an outdoor street festival.

"I should be up dancing up there, I should be practising," said Ikuko, who sat on the sidelines due to an injury.

But she wasn't taking it easy, following the moves with her hands in the air in total concentration.

A geisha's training is never complete.

Geisha rehearsing traditional Japanese dance with a dance master. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

They continue to rehearse and take music and dance lessons throughout their career, something the youngest geisha in Ikuko's house, Koume, understands.

"I think it will take me several more decades of study before I can be considered a fully fledged geisha," said Koume, who recently completed her apprenticeship.

She's been living with Ikuko for two years — a common situation for apprentices and young geisha in training — and described learning from her as "a tremendous honour".

It wasn't until a school exchange trip to the regional Australian city of Ballarat, where Koume's host family asked her about geisha, that she started thinking seriously about it as a career option.

" I didn't know much about geisha," she recalled. "I used to think that geisha were people from a bygone era, the sort you see in period dramas. "

When she returned to Japan, she started researching them, and, inspired by their "elegant demeanour" and "beautiful kimono", decided to join the ranks.

Yakoi, Saku and Ryoma are hangyoku (apprentice geisha) in Tokyo. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

Geisha dedicate themselves to learning traditional Japanese instruments. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

Geisha can have children in some areas, and technically they can get married and continue to practise, but many choose to retire to have a family.

It's a life of intense dedication, but there are still young women signing up for it.

"I'd have liked to have been a university student," said 19-year-old Ryoma when asked what, if anything, she's had to give up to follow her geisha dream.

Watch The Geisha of Tokyo on ABC iview Foreign Correspondent gets rare access inside the hidden world of Japan's geisha.

"Same here," her friend and fellow apprentice, Saku, said.

"It's true, isn't it? All my friends finish uni and go out, staying out until late or even staying overnight," Ryoma continued. "During those hours, the evenings, we're already working at banquets, so I used to feel envious."

Ryoma and Saku are among six apprentices, known as hangyoku in Tokyo, currently training in the city's biggest geisha district, Mukojima.

These days, some geisha houses recruit apprentices online or on social media.

Young hopefuls attend meetings with the houses to try to get accepted, and then it can take them anywhere from six months to several years to graduate.

A geisha preparing for a performance in Mukojima, Tokyo. (Foreign Correspondent: Ellie Grounds)

"Behind the curtain, we're constantly being told off, so it's not just a world of pretty girls," Saku said.

But both of the young women believe what they have gained outweighs what they have given up, pointing to the banquet guests they would otherwise never get a chance to meet and to the opportunity to perform on stage.

Ryoma recently made her stage debut at a public performance in the Mukojima district featuring more than 50 geisha.

"I'm truly deeply moved that in just a year I could stand on such a big stage," she said in the backstage area, before playing the taiko drum for the crowd.

"I've always wanted to stand on [the Mukojima stage], so I'm happy."

Bringing a hidden world to light

Ikuko wants to see a similar performance but on a much bigger scale, and is lobbying for all six of Tokyo's major districts to come together for a joint performance.

She believes promotion is key to preserving the tradition, and worries too few Japanese people even know there are still geisha in Tokyo.

"It's certainly true that the present and the past are so different, but the idea is to move forward one step at a time," she said.

But first she needs to persuade the city's politicians.

Geisha Ikuko in front of the Tokyo Tower. (Foreign Correspondent: Sissy Reyes)

She's currently meeting with a member of parliament and wants the Tokyo Metropolitan Government to protect the geisha districts.

If the city government could help secure a venue for a joint performance, she believes the event could "bring the geisha world back to life, just like in the old days."

"It might be nothing more than a pipe dream to think I can charge headlong towards that hope, but I reckon I wouldn't be able to give it a go if I didn't have that feeling," Ikuko said.

In the interim, she and her geisha recently took to the stage at the outdoor festival in her local neighbourhood of Akasaka, where they were greeted with loud cheers.

One woman who was watching in the crowd approached Ikuko afterwards to praise the performance.

"I hope that not only people from overseas, but also the Japanese people themselves, will take another look at these traditions and appreciate just how wonderful they are," she said.

Foreign Correspondent's The Geisha of Tokyo is available to watch now on ABC iview and ABC YouTube.

World.title: London's parched Hyde Park reflects 'unprecedented' drought ravaging UK
World.content:
Britain is known for its grey skies and miserable weather.

But as a devastating drought grips more than half the country, many of its famous parks and pastures have become almost unrecognisable.

London's lush green spaces have been transformed into brown and yellow dust bowls, rivers are running low and more than 2,700 "excess deaths" are thought to have been heat related during sweltering weather in May and June, according to the country's official weather service.

More than 10 million people have had their water use restricted. A hosepipe ban has come into force, meaning hoses cannot be used for watering gardens, cleaning cars, filling pools or cleaning windows.

The crisis is even threatening one of the United Kingdom's most iconic dishes: fish and chips.

Farmer Richard Barr grows potatoes for chippies across the country at his farm in Warwickshire in the West Midlands.

Richard Barr says this is the worst drought he has seen in the UK. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

But he said most of his crops would not make it to the fryer this harvest, after England endured its driest July on record.

"You pick up the potatoes, and they are less than half the size they should be," Mr Barr said.

"You want big, long potatoes to make chips, but you can't make chips out of these, they're just too small."

Mr Barr, who has worked on the farm for 30 years, said he had never seen a summer like this one.

"Our main crops are in dire straits; they are all shrivelled up," he said.

"The prolonged heat is just killing the potatoes; they are dying off, and they are just giving up."

These potatoes are too small to make chips from, Mr Barr says. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

The UK government has declared half of England, and all of Wales, as officially being in drought.

Parts of London recorded no rain last month, and in multiple parts of the country, July was the driest on record.

Many farmers are facing the worst harvest they have seen.

Mr Barr's yields are expected to be less than half of what they should be.

"I've never known crops like this dying off in August; they should be green until October," he said.

" Our green and pleasant lands are just desolate at the moment. "

England's patchwork of green fields has disappeared this summer. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

As heat records tumble in the UK this year, its European neighbours are also struggling.

Firefighters in Spain, France and Portugal have struggled to control dozens of blazes being fuelled by dry pastures and sweltering weather, triggering an ecological and humanitarian crisis.

Even parts of Britain have been burning, and the country's Environment Agency has said the UK is facing an "exceptionally serious situation".

May and June brought record-breaking heatwaves, including a new temperature high of 37 degrees Celsius in London, according to the Met Office — Britain's official weather service.

The effects of those successive heatwaves are visible across the capital.

In Hyde Park, the iconic green lawns have been replaced by barren, brown ground, with picnic-goers now sitting on dirt instead of the usual lush grass.

"I mean it's very, very dry. It's kind of giving desert vibes," one woman who was picnicking in the park told the ABC this week.

"It's usually really nice to come here when it's bright green grass, so it is a shame."

London's Hyde Park is almost unrecognisable amid the drought. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

England has experienced three droughts in the past five years.

"The conditions we're seeing in the UK at the moment are a result of climate change," climate scientist from the University of Oxford Chloe Brimicombe said.

"It's very alarming the amount of extreme weather events we've seen this summer.

"Wildfires are affecting many regions and going into autumn we could see flash flooding, so there are a lot of compounding hazards."

Dr Brimicombe said the UK was experiencing increasing "climate whiplash" that was also having a psychological effect on people.

"In the winter, we had 41 days of consecutive rainfall. It was very grey, very green and that is the sort of climate that may be expected of the UK, so this is the opposite of that and therefore it doesn't look like a pleasant green place to live, it's very brown and very crispy," she said.

"Research is showing that people are now feeling hopeless in the UK about heatwaves, and that's not good because we want them to be able to feel like they can take action and there is something they can do, which there is."

Authorities say the unusually wet winter means drinking water reserves are not threatened by the current drought.

At Charles Goadby's farm in Warwickshire, his cows were struggling to cope with the relentless heat, with milk production down 20 per cent.

Charles Goadby is worried this drought will have flow-on effects in future years. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

"They're no different to you and me — when you're hot, you're not wanting to eat, you're not wanting to work, so it's the same for them, and when they're not eating, they're not producing," he said.

"We've still got the same import costs, so that's hitting us hard in the pockets."

Potato crops in some parts of the country have been struggling to grow in the heat. (ABC News: Daniel Pannett)

Many farmers are already using their winter crops to feed their stock.

Mr Goadby, who has installed a shower for his cows to try to keep them cool, said the heat had also affected their fertility.

"This is going to go on for the next 12 months because the cows are not getting back in calf because of the heat stress," he said.

"It's going to have a real long-term knock-on impact.

" This is unprecedented in the UK. I'm nearly 50 years old and I've never seen anything like this and I hope to God I never see anything like this again. "

Forecasters are warning that much-needed rainfall may not arrive until October, and that the drought conditions could worsen before they improve.

"You're fighting against the weather, climate change, government polices, everything seems to be against us at the moment," Mr Goadby said.

"It's still the best job in the world, but my God it's tough."

World.title: Inner-west Victorian home sells for $817,500 in post-auction negotiations
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Inner-west Victorian home sells for $817,500 in post-auction negotiations Wes Mountain August 8, 2026 — 1:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An updated single-fronted Victorian home in Footscray sold for $817,500 in post-auction negotiations on Saturday, after passing in on a single genuine bid. A short walk from Barkly Street, Footscray station and Footscray Market, 26 Fitzroy Street features a stylishly renovated interior, with new bathroom and kitchen, while maintaining a classic Victorian weatherboard front and paved rear courtyard. The two-bedroom property had a price guide of $800,000 to $825,000, which Loutakis agent and auctioneer Michael Loutakis said had been revised up from $700,000 to $770,000 after considerable interest early in the campaign. World.title: ‘I just kind of toughed through it’: Annie and thousands of others face family violence alone
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaDomestic violence ‘I just kind of toughed through it’: Annie and thousands of others face family violence alone Wendy Tuohy August 8, 2026 — 1:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s only now, about seven years after she fled a violent home, that Annie King, 23, can concentrate on starting to heal. From her mid-teens, she was focused on survival. Memories of family violence from as young as the age of five still re-emerge, “but they are quite blurry”. How it felt to be turned away as an adolescent by people she thought would help her get to safety is far fresher. Annie King was 15 or 16 when she fled a home in which she experienced and witnessed family violence, but was turned away by services. Justin McManus “I was subjected to and witnessed violence,” said King, who was living in regional Victoria. “I initially approached my school counsellor, who didn’t believe me, which was very upsetting. “After that, I had a period of time when I didn’t tell anyone because I thought they wouldn’t believe me.”



She found and called a crisis centre through an online search when aged 15 or 16, but was told an adult needed to approach the service on her behalf. “When you’re aged 14 to 18, you’re in between child protection and adult services, so there’s not much out there to support those young people in a lot of cases where the mum isn’t ready to get support yet,” said King, now the co-chair of Victoria’s Victim Survivors’ Advisory Council. Loading King got out of her violent home by dropping out of school, finding work and living as a farm hand through the pandemic. “I never really got a response from the [family violence] system or support from services, I kind of just toughed through it and did it myself,” she said. Data from Equity Economics, commissioned by Victoria’s peak family violence body Safe and Equal, shows King is among about 3750 Victorians a year experiencing family violence who cannot get help from services, mainly because demand is so high.



In 2024-25, Victoria Police recorded more than 106,000 family violence incidents, a higher number than in any of the previous five years – but the Equity Economics analysis revealed 5000 existing family violence clients could not get the services they needed, “mainly accommodation”. Related Series

Crime Remember their faces: Women killed in Australia Jocelyn Bignold, chief executive of Victoria’s largest women-only family violence and homelessness organisation, McAuley Family Services, said of the findings: “The danger is real. We’ve been telling women, especially in Victoria, for a decade to come forward, and we will help you, and we can’t help everybody. “There’s nothing more dangerous in a family violence context than a woman making a move to leave and then being thwarted and having to go back.” The research, to be published on Saturday, found it takes more than a week for most Victorians – 85 per cent – to be assigned a case manager for help with safety measures such as intervention orders. The average wait for people in the “at risk” category is 12.5 days.



“When demand goes unmet, victim-survivors’ lives are at stake,” says the report, The Cost and Benefits of Fully Meeting Demand for Specialist Family Violence Services in Victoria. Violence against women is again in the spotlight after four killings of girls and women in one week in July, including Vermont mother of two Lavanya Chappa, and 13-year-old Layla Jeffrey, who lived in regional Donald. A third Victorian woman, Brooke Timmins, was also killed last month. Loading Timmins, a 29-year-old mother of two, was found dead in her Clyde North home on July 27 and her partner, Jorden Turney, 32, has been charged with murdering his partner of seven years while their two young sons were at home. Nationally, the latest woman killed died on Thursday night in Queensland. Julia Brunsdon, 23, was pregnant, and her 18 month-old daughter was in the home in outback Charleville, when she died in what police say was an apparent murder-suicide. Her partner, Michael Waltke, 45, was found dead at the property after a siege with police.



Safe and Equal chief executive Dr Joumanah El-Matrah said demand for help from family violence services had increased because of greater awareness that women did not need to remain in unsafe situations, but the delay in finding services could increase their safety risk. Related Article Crime Murderer glares at victim’s family while trying to fight life sentence The research found some women trying to get help gave up after failing to find it on the first attempt and returned to dangerous situations. “I spent quite a few years working with [frontline family violence] services, what I’ve seen happening a lot is women being too afraid to leave because they don’t feel they have options sustainable into the future,” El-Matrah said. That 45 per cent of women and girls seeking assistance for homelessness nominate family violence as the cause was “staggering”, she said. “I don’t think Australians accept that this is OK,” El-Matrah said.



“When people understand the scale of the problem, they’re often shocked. Safe housing can’t be treated as an optional extra, or just too big a problem for us to fix.” Equity Economics estimates that fully meeting current demand for family violence support in Victoria would require the next state government to increase funding from an expected $300 million to $487 million in 2026-27. Dr Joumanah El-Matrah, the new chief executive of Safe and Equal. Justin McManus El-Matrah also warned that comments by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson on July 22 that domestic violence is a “two-way street” and women “shouldn’t put up with it” (so should leave unsafe situations) falsely painted the victim as equally to blame as the abuser. Hanson’s comments, El-Matrah said, were dangerous. “Telling a victim to ‘just leave’ shifts responsibility away from the perpetrator. Leaving is often the most dangerous time for victim-survivors,” she said. “This year alone nine women and girls have been killed by men in Victoria.”



Professor Kate Fitz-Gibbon, a Monash University academic in violence against women, said funding of services for women fleeing violence should match the scale of the harm. Related Article Updated

Tragedy Toddler rescued as two found dead in outback murder-suicide “The community is right to be asking why, after decades of reviews, inquiries and reform agendas, we continue to see women killed in circumstances that are so tragically familiar,” she said. “The answer is that the actions taken have not kept pace with the scale of the crisis we are seeking to address.” A spokesman for the Victorian government said it had invested $4 billion since the state’s 2015 Royal Commission into Family Violence “to strengthen how we prevent and respond to family violence”, and the state had some of the nation’s strongest legal protections for survivors.



Annie King did not finish secondary school, but put herself through a diploma of community services and a graduate certificate in family violence, and now works with children and young people experiencing it. She has also just been able to find free trauma-support services. “Recently, I have reached out to the therapeutic side of services to start working on recovery and long-term healing, and connected with a really incredible counsellor who has helped me so much,” she said. “When those services are available, it makes such a huge difference to how the rest of people’s lives will turn out.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. World.title: ‘Walled in’: Bondi seniors sink developer’s six-storey beachfront tower
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Walled in’: Bondi seniors sink developer’s six-storey beachfront tower David Barwell August 8, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney developer’s attempt to use an affordable housing incentive scheme to build luxury apartments overlooking Bondi Beach has been blocked after residents of a neighbouring seniors’ housing complex labelled the proposal a form of “elder abuse” that would rob them of sunlight and ocean views. Waverley Council’s local planning panel unanimously rejected the $4.9 million proposal to redevelop a seven-metre-wide site at 34 Campbell Parade into a six-storey, mixed-use building containing a ground-floor shop, two luxury dual-level apartments and a single affordable housing unit. A photo of the proposed development site (left) and the Astra building (right). Steven Siewert The ruling halts plans by developer STM123 No. 32 Pty Ltd, directed by property investor Vaughan Blank, and brings to a close a planning dispute that exposed growing tensions over the NSW government’s push to increase housing supply through planning schemes allowing developers to exceed local controls in return for affordable housing. More than 770 objections were lodged against the proposal, with residents arguing it would block windows and ocean views from neighbouring properties, encourage overdevelopment along the beachfront, and that it was a misuse of planning incentives intended to address the housing crisis.



The campaign was led by residents of the heritage-listed Astra building, a former hotel converted into independent seniors’ accommodation sitting directly north of the 34 Campbell Parade site above the Bondi Trattoria restaurant. Planning documents showed the proposed building would have extended along the Astra’s 35.4-metre southern boundary, significantly reducing natural light and blocking ocean views from dozens of studio apartments occupied by elderly residents. Darryl Bourke, one of the residents who would have been impacted by the development. Steven Siewert For 88-year-old Frances Stumbles, who has limited mobility and spends much of her day indoors, the prospect of losing the outlook from her apartment had caused months of anxiety. “I moved into the Astra 13 years ago and through my windows, my only windows, I look out onto the world,” she said.



“I enjoy the natural light and the sea breeze. With this proposal I was terrified at the prospect of looking onto a blank six-storey wall. Quite simply, I would have been walled in.” Another resident, 87-year-old Cleo Lynch, described the proposal as “blatant elder abuse with a gender bias”, noting many of those affected residents were older women who relied on the Astra to continue living independently. “Some residents rarely leave their units because of mobility or health issues, and this development would have condemned them to spend their last years in a bricked-up prison,” she said. “Elderly we might be but stupid we’re not. The justification for the proposal – affordable housing opposite Bondi Beach – is an oxymoron.”



The dispute reignited debate over the state’s Housing State Environmental Planning Policy – a planning scheme that allows developers to receive 30 per cent bonuses in building height limits and floor space if sections of new developments are dedicated to affordable housing for periods typically up to 15 years. At 34 Campbell Parade, where local planning controls limit buildings to 15 metres, the incentive boosted the height limit to 19.5 metres. The proposed building reached 19.3 metres – almost 30 per cent above the standard height limit. An artist’s image of the proposed development at 32 Campbell Parade, which would have blocked south-facing windows at the Astra building (right). Waverley Council Waverley councillor Margaret Merton questioned whether developments containing predominantly luxury apartments were delivering the public benefits intended by the policy. “None of the residents are opposed to more housing but building one affordable unit and two luxury apartments does nothing to address the housing shortage we’re in,” she said.



The developer’s planning consultant Lee Kosnetter rejected suggestions the affordable housing component was merely tokenistic, saying it would account for about 20 per cent of the building’s residential floor space and be rented to essential workers for between $700 and $750 a week in a suburb where comparable rents exceed $2000. “We have a comprehensive list of local key workers – nurses, police officers and teachers – who are scrambling for accommodation in the area,” Kosnetter said. The proposed development site at 32 Campbell Parade. Waverley Council Planning documents submitted to the council argued the building had been carefully designed to minimise impacts on neighbouring properties, complied with accepted view-sharing principles, and would revitalise an underused site dating back to the 1920s. Waverley Council’s planning staff had initially recommended approving the project. While acknowledging the loss of views for Astra residents would be “devastating”, staff concluded those views “cannot reasonably be expected to be maintained upon redevelopment of surrounding sites”.



Related Article Exclusive

City life Revealed: The plan to let Sydney councils ditch controversial housing reforms The four-member planning panel unanimously disagreed, refusing the application after finding “the substantial amenity and view impacts” on the Astra building outweighed the public benefit of a single affordable housing apartment. Astra resident Len Horne welcomed the decision. “The Astra is one of the few affordable housing options in Bondi, and the proposal has caused enormous anxiety, residents asking: ‘If this is built next door to us, what will we do? Where will we go?’” he said. “We understand Sydney needs more housing but this proposal pushed the boundaries of every planning control. It was simply the wrong development for this site.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Melbourne says bye, bye sunshine, hello ‘blustery, rainy’ weather
World.content:
Victoria will be plunged into wild winter weather once more as a series of cold fronts rolls across the state from Saturday night, dusting the top of the Victorian Alps with snow.

While Melburnians were treated to sunny, late-winter conditions and a forecast top of 17 degrees on Saturday, temperatures will fall on Sunday as drizzle and strong winds dominate.

Expect more soggy scenes like this, as rain and chilly conditions will return to Melbourne from late Saturday night, according to the Bureau of Meteorology. Joe Armao

Monday will bring the heaviest showers of the cold snap – with some areas receiving up to 15mm of rain – while much of Victoria welcomes “healthy” double figure rain totals, according to the Bureau of Meteorology’s Helen Reid.

The meteorologist said multiple cold fronts were now working their way across from Western Australia, the first of which is expected to arrive into western Victoria on Saturday, before moving across the rest of the state.

World.title: Property at centre of suspected dog attack was site of earlier tragic death
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Property at centre of suspected dog attack was site of earlier tragic death Julie Power August 8, 2026 — 1:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The property known as the Universal Power House in Sydney’s south where a 23-year-old man was found dead this week after a suspected dog attack was meant to become a global mecca spreading a message of peace, love and truth. The bizarre building – also known as Saturn’s Rings or Mount Universe – and its founder, Polish immigrant Stefan Dzwonnik, has fascinated locals, inspired art installations and videos, and attracted stickybeaks. Multiple dogs were removed from the property near Campbelltown on Friday after a 23-year-old man was found dead. Sitthixay Ditthavong Dzwonnik’s universal principles were designed for humans and animals to live in harmony. Attempts to visit the unusual building on Badgally Road, Eschol Park near Campbelltown, have not always ended with peace and love, but with security and dogs, locals say. For Caroline Adams’ late sister, 16-year-old Melanie Bazley, a visit to the unfinished site in early 1982 ended in tragedy. Melanie died after falling from the top of one of the unfinished building’s “Saturn rings”.



On the Campbelltown/Macarthur community noticeboard a few years ago, Adams addressed false reports that her sister’s death was an “urban myth”. “My sister Melanie Bazley was killed in an accident there in February 1982, after falling 40 metres from the top level.” The Herald’s archives include a photograph and notes confirming Melanie’s death. The property remained unfinished for many years. YouTube A sign on the Eschol Park property. Sitthixay Ditthavong Construction of the building began in the late 1970s, then stalled for some years.



Adams wrote: “What is hard to accept is the fact that, this place, in its unfinished form for years … abandoned, was renowned for kids hanging out, riding bikes, drinking, etc and nothing was done to stop it.” Five dogs were removed from the property on Friday to be euthanised, and a 53-year-old man was treated for a minor hand injury. NSW Police said that extensive investigations were continuing. They said the injuries on the man’s body suggested he had been attacked by dogs before his death. Melanie Bazley, 16, died when she fell off the top of the building known as Saturn’s Rings on February 23, 1982. Her sister said she fell 40 metres from the top level. Reports by this newspaper say she had climbed to the top to look at the lights and the stars. Barry James Gilmour/Fairfax Media Campbelltown City Council’s historian and local cities librarian, Andrew Allen, gets more comments and questions about it than anything else. He said it was one of those things that “just fascinate people”.



Allen wrote on his blog, The History Buff, that one of the more “unusual constructions built in Campbelltown was the Universal Power House or Saturn’s Rings perched high on a hill”. Construction began around 1979 and continued for some years afterwards. “At the time, the building was regarded as one of the most spectacular in NSW with a limitless, panoramic view of the surrounding countryside,” Allen wrote. Related Video Video icon 2:02 Man dead after suspected dog attack in Sydney’s south-west “So what was the purpose of this unique building?” he wrote. “Stefan Dzwonnik had plans for it to be the mecca for a worldwide movement directed towards a better life on Earth. It was intended to become the home of him and his family; the ‘power house’ of his proposed Universal Power World Society.” The home’s design was based on the rings of the planet Saturn and comprised three concentric units. Its top level was the family home, while the rest was for the society.



A reader told Allen that when he went to see the concrete rings he was “chased down the hill by a dog at one point”. “Never went back there,” he said. Another, NeonTube, said an attempt to visit was halted by a few guard dogs and two security guards. Others were curious. “Us kids trekked all the way up there making it to the top to explore the rings, knowing we were trespassing but excited at being there. Within the two years we lived in Eagle Vale I think I must’ve gone up that hill more than a handful of times.” Anyone with information, CCTV, dashcam and/or mobile phone footage in relation to the recent incident is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: ‘The club went too far’: AFL chairman apologises over concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL chief Andrew Dillon has not ruled out calling in an independent party to lead the investigation into Geelong’s use of a secret concussion waiver with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, as commission chairman Craig Drummond removed himself from league deliberations over the scandal. On Saturday, Drummond, who was the Cats’ president when the deal was signed, apologised, conceding the Cats “went too far” in not seeking league approval before allowing a player to sign a waiver that saw the player assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries. AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui Drummond has apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation”. On Friday, Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of a secret concussion deal with the club, which was scrapped this week after the AFL said it did not approve it.



Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and is insisted he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. Dillon would not be drawn on what sanctions and charges the Cats will face until the league receives a response from the club over what the league and Geelong acknowledge to be a procedural failure. Dillon also refused to comment on whether it was tenable for Drummond, the Cats president when the waiver was inserted, to remain as the chairman of the AFL commission, a position he has held since March. Pressure is mounting on the AFL to mete out heavy penalties to the Cats. The league issued Carlton a $75,000 fine for their handling of Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode during a game this year, and also docked former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley $20,000 for taunting Hawthorn’s Jake Ginnivan with an aeroplane gesture in 2024. Dillon did not rule out the league calling in an independent figure to oversee the investigation into the Cats.



“What we’re looking at now is getting the information from Geelong, and then we will see what we’ve got from there, and then make a decision at that stage,” Dillon said on SEN. “I know people want answers really quickly, and we’re working on that, but we want to hear back from Geelong, give them the chance to reply to that, and then we see where that goes.” Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij, pictured in April, has identified himself as the player involved in the agreement. AFL Photos In his statement, Drummond said Kolodjashnij’s circumstances were “very carefully considered by the Geelong board” in 2024. “I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024,” the AFL chairman said.



“This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board. “Jake’s welfare was central to all discussions and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days. “While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play. “Regardless of the player’s agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed.” Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The Cats are not the cultural beacon they once claimed to be Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age



Drummond said the waiver didn’t remove Kolodjashnij’s protections as a player under statutory health and safety laws. “As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA [AFL Players Association]. “I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations. “I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation.” Dillon said the waiver was a breach of the AFL rules and repeatedly used the word “failure” in describing the Cats’ handling of the issue.



The scandal has shone the spotlight on the league’s declaration it places player health and safety as its number one priority. “I don’t think the position’s weakened, but there have been failures and they’ve been owned, and then there will be accountability,” Dillon said. Kolodjashnij, who has a history of concussions, appeared before the AFL’s concussion panel process and is forthright that he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. “There have been players who’ve gone to the panel, and the advice has been clear: you shouldn’t play. And we’ve had players retire on the back of that,” Dillon said. “We’ve had players retire as a result of concussions who haven’t gone to the panel, and they’ve come to that conclusion with their club doctor or with their independent doctor. But again, we’re very thankful for the doctors who give up their time and they serve on that panel. It’s a really important role for the game.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.
