Crime Remember their faces: Women killed in Australia Jocelyn Bignold, chief executive of Victoria’s largest women-only family violence and homelessness organisation, McAuley Family Services, said of the findings: “The danger is real. We’ve been telling women, especially in Victoria, for a decade to come forward, and we will help you, and we can’t help everybody. “There’s nothing more dangerous in a family violence context than a woman making a move to leave and then being thwarted and having to go back.” The research, to be published on Saturday, found it takes more than a week for most Victorians – 85 per cent – to be assigned a case manager for help with safety measures such as intervention orders. The average wait for people in the “at risk” category is 12.5 days.



“When demand goes unmet, victim-survivors’ lives are at stake,” says the report, The Cost and Benefits of Fully Meeting Demand for Specialist Family Violence Services in Victoria. Violence against women is again in the spotlight after four killings of girls and women in one week in July, including Vermont mother of two Lavanya Chappa, and 13-year-old Layla Jeffrey, who lived in regional Donald. A third Victorian woman, Brooke Timmins, was also killed last month. Loading Timmins, a 29-year-old mother of two, was found dead in her Clyde North home on July 27 and her partner, Jorden Turney, 32, has been charged with murdering his partner of seven years while their two young sons were at home. Nationally, the latest woman killed died on Thursday night in Queensland. Julia Brunsdon, 23, was pregnant, and her 18 month-old daughter was in the home in outback Charleville, when she died in what police say was an apparent murder-suicide. Her partner, Michael Waltke, 45, was found dead at the property after a siege with police.



Safe and Equal chief executive Dr Joumanah El-Matrah said demand for help from family violence services had increased because of greater awareness that women did not need to remain in unsafe situations, but the delay in finding services could increase their safety risk. Related Article Crime Murderer glares at victim’s family while trying to fight life sentence The research found some women trying to get help gave up after failing to find it on the first attempt and returned to dangerous situations. “I spent quite a few years working with [frontline family violence] services, what I’ve seen happening a lot is women being too afraid to leave because they don’t feel they have options sustainable into the future,” El-Matrah said. That 45 per cent of women and girls seeking assistance for homelessness nominate family violence as the cause was “staggering”, she said. “I don’t think Australians accept that this is OK,” El-Matrah said.



“When people understand the scale of the problem, they’re often shocked. Safe housing can’t be treated as an optional extra, or just too big a problem for us to fix.” Equity Economics estimates that fully meeting current demand for family violence support in Victoria would require the next state government to increase funding from an expected $300 million to $487 million in 2026-27. Dr Joumanah El-Matrah, the new chief executive of Safe and Equal. Justin McManus El-Matrah also warned that comments by One Nation leader Pauline Hanson on July 22 that domestic violence is a “two-way street” and women “shouldn’t put up with it” (so should leave unsafe situations) falsely painted the victim as equally to blame as the abuser. Hanson’s comments, El-Matrah said, were dangerous. “Telling a victim to ‘just leave’ shifts responsibility away from the perpetrator. Leaving is often the most dangerous time for victim-survivors,” she said. “This year alone nine women and girls have been killed by men in Victoria.”



Professor Kate Fitz-Gibbon, a Monash University academic in violence against women, said funding of services for women fleeing violence should match the scale of the harm. Related Article Updated

Tragedy Toddler rescued as two found dead in outback murder-suicide “The community is right to be asking why, after decades of reviews, inquiries and reform agendas, we continue to see women killed in circumstances that are so tragically familiar,” she said. “The answer is that the actions taken have not kept pace with the scale of the crisis we are seeking to address.” A spokesman for the Victorian government said it had invested $4 billion since the state’s 2015 Royal Commission into Family Violence “to strengthen how we prevent and respond to family violence”, and the state had some of the nation’s strongest legal protections for survivors.



Annie King did not finish secondary school, but put herself through a diploma of community services and a graduate certificate in family violence, and now works with children and young people experiencing it. She has also just been able to find free trauma-support services. “Recently, I have reached out to the therapeutic side of services to start working on recovery and long-term healing, and connected with a really incredible counsellor who has helped me so much,” she said. “When those services are available, it makes such a huge difference to how the rest of people’s lives will turn out.” If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), Lifeline 131 114, or Beyond Blue 1300 224 636. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Walled in’: Bondi seniors sink developer’s six-storey beachfront tower
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life ‘Walled in’: Bondi seniors sink developer’s six-storey beachfront tower David Barwell August 8, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Sydney developer’s attempt to use an affordable housing incentive scheme to build luxury apartments overlooking Bondi Beach has been blocked after residents of a neighbouring seniors’ housing complex labelled the proposal a form of “elder abuse” that would rob them of sunlight and ocean views. Waverley Council’s local planning panel unanimously rejected the $4.9 million proposal to redevelop a seven-metre-wide site at 34 Campbell Parade into a six-storey, mixed-use building containing a ground-floor shop, two luxury dual-level apartments and a single affordable housing unit. A photo of the proposed development site (left) and the Astra building (right). Steven Siewert The ruling halts plans by developer STM123 No. 32 Pty Ltd, directed by property investor Vaughan Blank, and brings to a close a planning dispute that exposed growing tensions over the NSW government’s push to increase housing supply through planning schemes allowing developers to exceed local controls in return for affordable housing. More than 770 objections were lodged against the proposal, with residents arguing it would block windows and ocean views from neighbouring properties, encourage overdevelopment along the beachfront, and that it was a misuse of planning incentives intended to address the housing crisis.



The campaign was led by residents of the heritage-listed Astra building, a former hotel converted into independent seniors’ accommodation sitting directly north of the 34 Campbell Parade site above the Bondi Trattoria restaurant. Planning documents showed the proposed building would have extended along the Astra’s 35.4-metre southern boundary, significantly reducing natural light and blocking ocean views from dozens of studio apartments occupied by elderly residents. Darryl Bourke, one of the residents who would have been impacted by the development. Steven Siewert For 88-year-old Frances Stumbles, who has limited mobility and spends much of her day indoors, the prospect of losing the outlook from her apartment had caused months of anxiety. “I moved into the Astra 13 years ago and through my windows, my only windows, I look out onto the world,” she said.



“I enjoy the natural light and the sea breeze. With this proposal I was terrified at the prospect of looking onto a blank six-storey wall. Quite simply, I would have been walled in.” Another resident, 87-year-old Cleo Lynch, described the proposal as “blatant elder abuse with a gender bias”, noting many of those affected residents were older women who relied on the Astra to continue living independently. “Some residents rarely leave their units because of mobility or health issues, and this development would have condemned them to spend their last years in a bricked-up prison,” she said. “Elderly we might be but stupid we’re not. The justification for the proposal – affordable housing opposite Bondi Beach – is an oxymoron.”



The dispute reignited debate over the state’s Housing State Environmental Planning Policy – a planning scheme that allows developers to receive 30 per cent bonuses in building height limits and floor space if sections of new developments are dedicated to affordable housing for periods typically up to 15 years. At 34 Campbell Parade, where local planning controls limit buildings to 15 metres, the incentive boosted the height limit to 19.5 metres. The proposed building reached 19.3 metres – almost 30 per cent above the standard height limit. An artist’s image of the proposed development at 32 Campbell Parade, which would have blocked south-facing windows at the Astra building (right). Waverley Council Waverley councillor Margaret Merton questioned whether developments containing predominantly luxury apartments were delivering the public benefits intended by the policy. “None of the residents are opposed to more housing but building one affordable unit and two luxury apartments does nothing to address the housing shortage we’re in,” she said.



The developer’s planning consultant Lee Kosnetter rejected suggestions the affordable housing component was merely tokenistic, saying it would account for about 20 per cent of the building’s residential floor space and be rented to essential workers for between $700 and $750 a week in a suburb where comparable rents exceed $2000. “We have a comprehensive list of local key workers – nurses, police officers and teachers – who are scrambling for accommodation in the area,” Kosnetter said. The proposed development site at 32 Campbell Parade. Waverley Council Planning documents submitted to the council argued the building had been carefully designed to minimise impacts on neighbouring properties, complied with accepted view-sharing principles, and would revitalise an underused site dating back to the 1920s. Waverley Council’s planning staff had initially recommended approving the project. While acknowledging the loss of views for Astra residents would be “devastating”, staff concluded those views “cannot reasonably be expected to be maintained upon redevelopment of surrounding sites”.



Related Article Exclusive

City life Revealed: The plan to let Sydney councils ditch controversial housing reforms The four-member planning panel unanimously disagreed, refusing the application after finding “the substantial amenity and view impacts” on the Astra building outweighed the public benefit of a single affordable housing apartment. Astra resident Len Horne welcomed the decision. “The Astra is one of the few affordable housing options in Bondi, and the proposal has caused enormous anxiety, residents asking: ‘If this is built next door to us, what will we do? Where will we go?’” he said. “We understand Sydney needs more housing but this proposal pushed the boundaries of every planning control. It was simply the wrong development for this site.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Melbourne says bye, bye sunshine, hello ‘blustery, rainy’ weather
World.content:
Victoria will be plunged into wild winter weather once more as a series of cold fronts rolls across the state from Saturday night, dusting the top of the Victorian Alps with snow.

While Melburnians were treated to sunny, late-winter conditions and a forecast top of 17 degrees on Saturday, temperatures will fall on Sunday as drizzle and strong winds dominate.

Expect more soggy scenes like this, as rain and chilly conditions will return to Melbourne from late Saturday night, according to the Bureau of Meteorology. Joe Armao

Monday will bring the heaviest showers of the cold snap – with some areas receiving up to 15mm of rain – while much of Victoria welcomes “healthy” double figure rain totals, according to the Bureau of Meteorology’s Helen Reid.

The meteorologist said multiple cold fronts were now working their way across from Western Australia, the first of which is expected to arrive into western Victoria on Saturday, before moving across the rest of the state.

World.title: Passed in, then sold: Local couple pays $1.46m for North Shore apartment
World.content:
A local family with a young child paid $1,463,000 for a three-bedroom apartment in Lane Cove after it passed in at auction on Saturday.

Bidding for the property at 2/15 Longueville Road opened at $1.38 million, increasing in bids of $10,000 to reach $1.45 million when bidding stalled and it passed in. The lead bidder was then invited to increase their offer and, after half an hour of negotiating, the property sold.

The apartment had a guide of $1.4 million and a reserve of $1.5 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide.

Two bidders registered, although Raine & Horne Lower North Shore sales agent Oscar Nicholls was initially expecting only one. The underbidder was an investor who had seen the property once early in the campaign and was attracted to it for its yield potential, Nicholls said.

World.title: Property at centre of suspected dog attack was site of earlier tragic death
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Property at centre of suspected dog attack was site of earlier tragic death Julie Power August 8, 2026 — 1:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The property known as the Universal Power House in Sydney’s south where a 23-year-old man was found dead this week after a suspected dog attack was meant to become a global mecca spreading a message of peace, love and truth. The bizarre building – also known as Saturn’s Rings or Mount Universe – and its founder, Polish immigrant Stefan Dzwonnik, has fascinated locals, inspired art installations and videos, and attracted stickybeaks. Multiple dogs were removed from the property near Campbelltown on Friday after a 23-year-old man was found dead. Sitthixay Ditthavong Dzwonnik’s universal principles were designed for humans and animals to live in harmony. Attempts to visit the unusual building on Badgally Road, Eschol Park near Campbelltown, have not always ended with peace and love, but with security and dogs, locals say. For Caroline Adams’ late sister, 16-year-old Melanie Bazley, a visit to the unfinished site in early 1982 ended in tragedy. Melanie died after falling from the top of one of the unfinished building’s “Saturn rings”.



On the Campbelltown/Macarthur community noticeboard a few years ago, Adams addressed false reports that her sister’s death was an “urban myth”. “My sister Melanie Bazley was killed in an accident there in February 1982, after falling 40 metres from the top level.” The Herald’s archives include a photograph and notes confirming Melanie’s death. The property remained unfinished for many years. YouTube A sign on the Eschol Park property. Sitthixay Ditthavong Construction of the building began in the late 1970s, then stalled for some years.



Adams wrote: “What is hard to accept is the fact that, this place, in its unfinished form for years … abandoned, was renowned for kids hanging out, riding bikes, drinking, etc and nothing was done to stop it.” Five dogs were removed from the property on Friday to be euthanised, and a 53-year-old man was treated for a minor hand injury. NSW Police said that extensive investigations were continuing. They said the injuries on the man’s body suggested he had been attacked by dogs before his death. Melanie Bazley, 16, died when she fell off the top of the building known as Saturn’s Rings on February 23, 1982. Her sister said she fell 40 metres from the top level. Reports by this newspaper say she had climbed to the top to look at the lights and the stars. Barry James Gilmour/Fairfax Media Campbelltown City Council’s historian and local cities librarian, Andrew Allen, gets more comments and questions about it than anything else. He said it was one of those things that “just fascinate people”.



Allen wrote on his blog, The History Buff, that one of the more “unusual constructions built in Campbelltown was the Universal Power House or Saturn’s Rings perched high on a hill”. Construction began around 1979 and continued for some years afterwards. “At the time, the building was regarded as one of the most spectacular in NSW with a limitless, panoramic view of the surrounding countryside,” Allen wrote. Related Video Video icon 2:02 Man dead after suspected dog attack in Sydney’s south-west “So what was the purpose of this unique building?” he wrote. “Stefan Dzwonnik had plans for it to be the mecca for a worldwide movement directed towards a better life on Earth. It was intended to become the home of him and his family; the ‘power house’ of his proposed Universal Power World Society.” The home’s design was based on the rings of the planet Saturn and comprised three concentric units. Its top level was the family home, while the rest was for the society.



A reader told Allen that when he went to see the concrete rings he was “chased down the hill by a dog at one point”. “Never went back there,” he said. Another, NeonTube, said an attempt to visit was halted by a few guard dogs and two security guards. Others were curious. “Us kids trekked all the way up there making it to the top to explore the rings, knowing we were trespassing but excited at being there. Within the two years we lived in Eagle Vale I think I must’ve gone up that hill more than a handful of times.” Anyone with information, CCTV, dashcam and/or mobile phone footage in relation to the recent incident is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000.

World.title: ‘The club went too far’: AFL chairman apologises over concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL chief Andrew Dillon has not ruled out calling in an independent party to lead the investigation into Geelong’s use of a secret concussion waiver with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, as commission chairman Craig Drummond removed himself from league deliberations over the scandal. On Saturday, Drummond, who was the Cats’ president when the deal was signed, apologised, conceding the Cats “went too far” in not seeking league approval before allowing a player to sign a waiver that saw the player assume responsibility for future on-field head injuries. AFL Commission chairman and former Geelong president Craig Drummond. Luis Enrique Ascui Drummond has apologised for “the mistakes made in this very complex situation”. On Friday, Geelong premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij identified himself as the player at the centre of a secret concussion deal with the club, which was scrapped this week after the AFL said it did not approve it.



Kolodjashnij didn’t directly address signing any document pertaining to his playing contract but said he “participated fully” in the AFL’s concussion panel process and is insisted he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. Dillon would not be drawn on what sanctions and charges the Cats will face until the league receives a response from the club over what the league and Geelong acknowledge to be a procedural failure. Dillon also refused to comment on whether it was tenable for Drummond, the Cats president when the waiver was inserted, to remain as the chairman of the AFL commission, a position he has held since March. Pressure is mounting on the AFL to mete out heavy penalties to the Cats. The league issued Carlton a $75,000 fine for their handling of Elijah Hollands’ mental health episode during a game this year, and also docked former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley $20,000 for taunting Hawthorn’s Jake Ginnivan with an aeroplane gesture in 2024. Dillon did not rule out the league calling in an independent figure to oversee the investigation into the Cats.



“What we’re looking at now is getting the information from Geelong, and then we will see what we’ve got from there, and then make a decision at that stage,” Dillon said on SEN. “I know people want answers really quickly, and we’re working on that, but we want to hear back from Geelong, give them the chance to reply to that, and then we see where that goes.” Geelong’s Jake Kolodjashnij, pictured in April, has identified himself as the player involved in the agreement. AFL Photos In his statement, Drummond said Kolodjashnij’s circumstances were “very carefully considered by the Geelong board” in 2024. “I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024,” the AFL chairman said.



“This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board. “Jake’s welfare was central to all discussions and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days. “While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play. “Regardless of the player’s agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed.” Related Article Opinion

AFL 2026 The Cats are not the cultural beacon they once claimed to be Caroline Wilson Football columnist for The Age



Drummond said the waiver didn’t remove Kolodjashnij’s protections as a player under statutory health and safety laws. “As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA [AFL Players Association]. “I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations. “I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation.” Dillon said the waiver was a breach of the AFL rules and repeatedly used the word “failure” in describing the Cats’ handling of the issue.



The scandal has shone the spotlight on the league’s declaration it places player health and safety as its number one priority. “I don’t think the position’s weakened, but there have been failures and they’ve been owned, and then there will be accountability,” Dillon said. Kolodjashnij, who has a history of concussions, appeared before the AFL’s concussion panel process and is forthright that he is fully healthy and fit to play at the highest level. “There have been players who’ve gone to the panel, and the advice has been clear: you shouldn’t play. And we’ve had players retire on the back of that,” Dillon said. “We’ve had players retire as a result of concussions who haven’t gone to the panel, and they’ve come to that conclusion with their club doctor or with their independent doctor. But again, we’re very thankful for the doctors who give up their time and they serve on that panel. It’s a really important role for the game.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: City Rail Link 'First Look' events begin
World.content:
Aucklanders have been getting their first chance to see inside the new City Rail Link, with a busy turnout for the first of a series of public open day events at new railway stations - this one at Maungawhau Station.

City Rail Link (CRL) is the country's largest transport infrastructure project to date, with about three and a half kilometres of tunnels, and set to cost $5.5b. It has been long-awaited and is scheduled to open on 13 September, with promises to speed up and modernise public transport in the sprawling city.

Auckland's first CRL station opens to the public Saturday Morning Download MP3 5m

But before it opens, a series of public 'First Look' weekend events are on offer in August, with the first at the new Maungawhau Station (formerly Mount Eden Station), between Mount Eden and Eden Terrace, on Saturday.

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

Auckland Transport said about 17,000 people had registered for the open day. And that translated to a steady stream of people coming in to have a look, CRL communications manager Joel Rowan said, mid-morning on Saturday.

Food and activities were set up in the surrounding streets, with busking and community performances inside the train station.

"There's a stage set up, we've got the local community really part of this. A local school kapa haka group has actually just been warming up. We've had heaps of interest in today, and everyone just seems to be just really enjoying it," Rowan said.

"I think people are relieved. Last night we had some of the locals and local businesses in here for a little preview of today's event. And they've really been hanging out - not just for today, but for the project to open.

Irene Pang and her grandson Christian Yeung, at the event at Maungawhau Station on Saturday morning. RNZ/ Lucy Xia

"This station [has] been closed since 2020 for the construction. So I know that everyone's really looking forward to I guess getting the benefits when the opening finally does arrive on the 13th of September."

Several people RNZ spoke to said they were excited about the new East-West connection and the reduction in travel times. Others say they were glad they would no longer be held up by delays at the bottleneck at the New Market station.

Catherine Hill currently takes the train at Kingsland, and transits at the Waitematā station to get to her work place in Panmure on the Eastern line - often slowed down by what she calls "the bottleneck" at Newmarket.

Now she only needs to hope on the East-West line.

"The CRL is going to be a gamechanger for me, so I only have to catch one train rather than two," she said.

Maungawhau Station (formerly Mt Eden) before its official opening, August 2026. Lucy Xia / RNZ

And for others like Swanson resident Jonathan Rankin, the difference is one of switching from driving to work to taking the train.

Rankin now has a direct route to his workplace off Karangahape Road, whereas previously, it would've taken him about an hour to take the train to Kingsland then bus into town.

West Auckland resident Harrison Fernandes-Burnard said the CRL could take about 20 minutes off his daily commute.

"The old Mount Eden Station was quite basic, rustic you could say - but yeah it's amazing ... there's now four platforms and it's really spacious." It had changed a lot, and was a good  for the city, he said.

3. AUT student Connor McGrath says the opening of the Te Waihoritiu station will reduce his walking time to university by half. RNZ / Lucy Xia

Irene Pang and her grandson Christian Yeung travelled from Meadowlands in East Auckland for the First Look event. Pang hopes there will be more frequent buses to Panmure Station from where she lives.

Yueng said he was excited about taking the train during school holidays and better connections to western parts of the city.

AUT student Connor McGrath, who currently takes the train to Britomart then walks to campus, said the new station at Te Waihorotiu will cut down his walking time by half.

Disability advocate and wheelchair boxer John Fiu, pictured with his wife and brother, says he's happy with the accessibility of the station. RNZ / Lucy Xia

Disability advocate, wheelchair user and heavyweight boxer John Fiu was there on Saturday to check out accessibility. He was pleased with the lifts and said it was easy to get around at the station: "If it wasn't for the lifts we wouldn't be able to access the train station at all, and from an advocate's point of view it's pretty good. Everything is user friendly."

Fiu has a boxing match coming up in October and said he's excited to use the train to get to his match.

At Maungawhau Station on Saturday Lucy Xia / RNZ

Before the old Mt Eden Station closed, the journey downtown from Maungawhau Station to what is now Waitematā Station (formerly Britomart) took about 20 minutes, travelling through Newmarket, Auckland Transport's Joel Rowan said.

It now takes about 10 minutes, or even less for either of the two new closer central stations: just a couple of minutes to Karanga-a-Hape Station, or about seven minutes to Te Waihorotiu Station near the Sky Tower. While people going to or from the westerns suburbs will find their trips much faster using the CRL, Rowan said.

Many rehearsals and trials of the rail schedule had been carried out ahead of the full CRL opening, with big attendance expected from the first day.

Several people told RNZ they were impressed by the artworks. Water cascaded down the wall, and 53 glass triangles were set into the concrete wall to form a map of volcanoes across Auckland.

Bella Cunnington Waugh and her family - her daughter, her nieces and her brother - visiting the Manawhau station on Saturday's "First Look" event. RNZ / Lucy Xia

Aucklander Bella Cunnington Waugh said she liked a feature wall depicting Maungawhau (Mount Eden).

"It's fabulous. I really like the motifs and the imagery, and from what I understand so far of what it's about - the connections to Maungawhau the mountain, to the maunga. Yeah, it looks beautiful."

Auckland Transport's website said the new Maungawhau Station was visually striking, and "combines world-class transport infrastructure with thoughtful design inspired by the surrounding volcanic landscape and deep cultural connections to nearby maunga."

"Its dramatic architecture, natural materials and spacious platforms create a station experience unlike anything else in Auckland."

Maungawhau Station on Saturday RNZ/ Lucy Xia

Ongoing CRL 'First Look' events are planned for Saturday 15 August at Karanga-a-Hape Station and Saturday 22 August at Te Waihorotiu Station, with a succession of one hour tours available on each day starting from 8am.

Auckland Transport said people planning to attend should apply ahead for tickets, which are free.

World.title: Live: Auckland FC Women's XI v Chelsea Women football exhibition match
World.content:
Follow all the football action as the Auckland FC Women's XI take on Chelsea for their exhibition match at Eden Park.

Kick-off is at 4pm.

Irrespective of the result on the scoreboard, Auckland FC's first foray into women's football could be pivotal in the careers of the women invited to take part.

An Auckland FC Invitational XI side made up of international stars, local club footballers, A-League stalwarts and professionals looking for their next contract have come together in unusual circumstances.

With 10 days of preparation, the squad wearing Auckland FC colours will play eight-time WSL champions Chelsea FC Women at Eden Park.

This will be the first time a Women's Super League club has played in New Zealand.

It is an exhibition match that in many ways should not be happening. The A-League club do not have a women's side and will not for a couple of seasons yet. They will be the 'away' side when they take the field.

World.title: Watch: National Party announces list for 2026 General Election
World.content:
Senior National MPs who might have been nervous about the party's polling have been ranked highly to give them the best shot of returning to Parliament next term.

The party released its full line-up of election candidates on Saturday afternoon, largely preserving the existing hierarchy.

Chris Bishop retained third place on National's list, a fairly safe spot, even if he lost his hold on the marginal Hutt South electorate.

Similarly, Paul Goldsmith, who's unlikely to win Epsom from ACT leader David Seymour, retained his current sixth position in caucus.

Speaker Gerry Brownlee, who's running as a list-only candidate, was boosted to the ninth spot, up from 14th in 2023.

The move stops short of the traditional third ranking sometimes given to Speakers, but makes Brownlee's return likely if National performs near its current polling.

Recent polls put National on about 31 percent, which would secure them about 39 or 40 seats. Political analysts have noted that a strong performance across electorates, however, could leave the party with very few list MPs.

But for Bishop, Goldsmith and Brownlee, the election rankings should provide a degree of protection and comfort.

Chris Bishop retained third place on National's list. RNZ / Mark Papalii

In line with the party's constitution, leader Christopher Luxon and deputy Nicola Willis took the top two positions. Willis is also reliant on her list spot to return.

The list ranked Simeon Brown fourth, Erica Stanford fifth, Louise Upston seventh and Mark Mitchell eighth. All four of them are expected to win their electorates.

Tama Potaka shot to 11th on the list, up from from 24th in 2023. In contrast, former broadcasting minister Melissa Lee dropped from 13th to 30th.

New faces who have been awarded high rankings include Dale Stephens in Christchurch Central (23), Mahesh Muralidhar in Tamaki (24), Katie Milne in West Coast-Tasman (25) and Angee Nicholas in Henderson (26).

Deputy leader Nicola Willis at National's list announcement for the 2026 election. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

The party highlighted all four candidates in its promotional material, noting Milne's history as a former Federated Farmers president and Stephens' executive experience.

Luxon: 'It's a week in politics for me'

Addressing reporters at Wellington Airport, Luxon said National was "ruthlessly focused" on maximising its party vote.

He said Brownlee's ranking reflected that he was considered a great "kaumātua" or elder in the party.

"He's been in Parliament now for 30 years. We really value Gerry. We think very highly of him."

Gerry Brownlee. Angus Dreaver / RNZ

National's list announcement comes at a difficult point for the governing party, with its support having fallen significantly from the 2023 election.

It also follows a difficult period for Luxon who began the week apologising to small businesses in Rotorua.

Luxon did win some reprieve, with the latest Taxpayers' Union Curia poll predicting the coalition's return to power - and showing a significant drop in support for the current opposition parties.

Party leader Christopher Luxon speaks at National's list announcement for the 2026 election. RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

He batted away questions from reporters about his performance over the past week, saying he was "moving forward" and focused on the campaign ahead.

"It's a week in politics for me," he said.

"I have some good weeks and some challenging weeks."

Luxon played down his impromptu campaign promise for an MMP referendum, saying it was his job as party leader to make decisions in the moment.

"I'm asked to form a judgement on things. I want to be as definitive and clear as I possibly can."

National president Sylvia Wood also defended Luxon's decision to make a policy decision on the fly: "I'm 100 percent fine with that."

National Party president Sylvia Wood. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Asked whether the board retained confidence in Luxon, Wood replied: "Absolutely."

World.title: New Zealand places further sanctions against Russia supporters
World.content:
New Zealand has placed another round of sanctions targeting those supporting Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The latest package targets 33 individuals and groups, with a particular focus on cyber actors, and those involved in the forced relocation, abduction and re-education of Ukrainian children.

The sanctions also target people supporting Russia's military-industrial complex, political figures, and North Koreans and Iranians providing support to Moscow.

Foreign Minister Winston Peters said New Zealand remained concerned about the treatment of Ukrainian children.

"Children should never be used as instruments of war," he said. "New Zealand remains deeply concerned by efforts to abduct and re-educate Ukrainian children through co-ercive state-directed programmes."

The package also targets malicious cyber actors and people involved in spreading anti-Ukraine propaganda aimed at legitimising Russia's invasion.

Peters said cyber activity could have real-world consequences, including helping Russia gather intelligence, evade sanctions and disrupt opponents of its war.

"New Zealand stands with our partners in calling out Moscow's use of these actors."

This is New Zealand's 36th round of sanctions against Russia, since the Russia Sanctions Act came into force in March 2022.

World.title: Beloved Nelson cafe forced to close after landlord dispute and roadworks woes
World.content:
A popular Nelson cafe and gallery has announced its closure, after a dispute with the landlord and ongoing roadworks made it untenable to continue.

Red Art Gallery & Café owners Ant and Suzi Stevens say after nine years in business, its closure was forced after the landlord chose not to renew the lease, a devastating blow after months of roadworks on the two adjacent streets had seriously impacted revenue.

The work, part of the $78 million Bridge to Better project, has seen water pipes and other infrastructure along the the length of Bridge Street replaced, causing disruption to a number of businesses since it first began last year.

The couple said the decision to close in September was not the outcome they wanted, especially on the back of a tough few years,

"It's just heartbreaking, I just feel like I'm losing a child to be honest, it's just been my baby for so long," Suzi said.

The business had survived a global pandemic, a recession and roadworks which effectively left them an island, with the cafe and gallery entrance hidden behind fences, trucks and diggers.

Bridge Street and Haven Road either side of the business have been closed for months while the roads are ripped up and pipes replaced, with customers having to walk down narrow, uneven gravel paths between temporary fences to reach the business.

The gallery represented about 60 artists, most of them from Nelson and Tasman, and they had taken on more after the Suter Art Gallery made the decision to stop stocking the work of around 40 local artists, after getting advice from external retail specialists.

Roadworks in Nelson are taking a toll on local businesses. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Since announcing the closure on social media, the couple had received hundreds of comments in support.

The cafe was full on Friday morning when RNZ visited. Within an hour, it had made as much money as it had over the previous two days combined.

"We knew there would be strong support, but not the way it's been with the messages, with the people coming in," Ant said.

"Love and compassion and heart will beat greed any day."

He said the council told the couple they would be the "most impacted business" given their proximity to the roadworks, but there had been "zero talk of compensation or help in any way", except to be asked whether they had two hard years in them until the upgrade was complete.

"It'll be wonderful for someone else, but it won't be us," Ant said.

Council agrees to defer rates if landlords come to the party

Nelson mayor Nick Smith previously said he had met with a number of "very distressed" business owners who were feeling the pressure of the ongoing roadworks.

Staff had gone to "tremendous effort" to try and minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses, he said.

Smith acknowledged the work was "incredibly disruptive" but said it was essential to renew and upgrade infrastructure that, in some places, was over 100 years old.

Once complete, Bridge Street was tipped to be a "people-focused corridor" with utility services capable of supporting inner city development.

At a council meeting on Thursday, elected members agreed to allow affected businesses to defer rates from the current year, with repayments split over the next three years, if landlords agreed to provide the equivalent financial relief to the tenant.

Nelson's mayor says council staff are trying to minimise disruption in the city by promoting businesses. RNZ / Samantha Gee

Nelson Tasman Chamber of Commerce chair Venus Guy said it was disappointing to see the closure of long-standing local businesses.

"Red Gallery has been part of our city centre, and our thoughts are with the owners and everyone affected by this decision."

She said while the Bridge to Better project was an important investment in Nelson's future, the major infrastructure work placed very real pressures on businesses during construction.

"It is essential that we continue working together to minimise disruption, support affected businesses and remind our community that our city centre remains open for business.

Central city businesses feeling the hurt

Longstanding cafe and food store Prego Mediterranean Foods & Comida Cafe shut its doors in June, and the owners said at the time that the [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/625679/road-closures-and-rising-costs-force-closure-of-nelson-businessongoing ongoing roadworks were one of the factors in its closure].

Further down Bridge Street, Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten said he thought more could be done to support businesses affected by the infrastructure works.

At lunchtime on Friday, his restaurant was empty and the noise of roadworks outside made it hard to be heard when speaking.

He had organised a meeting with about 30 Bridge Street business owners that were also struggling around two months ago.

He said the rates deferral scheme made little difference. It gave relief of about $80 per month, but would have to be paid back in the years to come.

Pizzeria Bella owner Yusef Corten sits in front of his restaurant and behind a fence while work is done on Bridge Street. Samantha Gee/RNZ

Corten, who had owned and operated hospitality businesses in Nelson for more than a decade, said he bought Pizzeria Bella a year ago. He started out with nine employees, but was now down to three. Only he and his son were working full-time, with debt that kept rising.

Pizzeria Bella's revenue was down 80 percent since the roadworks began. On Tuesday, Corten made $300 between the lunch and dinner services. His accountant had told him he needed turnover of $2000 a day to survive.

"Every day I am more negative, more negative."

Corten said two businesses had closed and it was possible that more would follow.

World.title: New healthcare-focused school subject could jump start next generation of workers - doctor
World.content:
A new healthcare-focused high school subject could jump start the next generation of medical professionals, a Northland provider says.

The government has announced nine new secondary school subjects to be developed by industry groups.

That included a course on "health services and care", which Ngāti Hine Health Trust clinical advisor Dr Mataroria Lyndon said would be a great opportunity to attract youngsters to the sector.

"I came through as a doctor and did my training but never had the opportunity to be exposed earlier, especially at high school," Dr Lyndon said.

"Part of the learning will be around understanding care situations, communication... And then expose them at an earlier stage to the different types of health roles, whether that be medicine, nursing, community carers, mental health workers."

He said students would have a chance to observe different types of health roles in real world settings, which he hoped would include Ngāti Hine clinics.

"As a subject now going forward it'll help young people see a place for themselves in healthcare and in the community workforce," he said.

"Traditionally we might think of health workers as doctors and nurses, but those at the Ngāti Hine Health Trust for example... There are community carers, there are podiatrists, nutritionists, community health workers, health promotion, it's just a good opportunity to have those pathways into the health workforce much earlier."

He hoped students would feel inspired to enter the health workforce at a time when it was facing severe shortages.

"We're among the largest providers in Northland, so hopefully we can grow our own workforce to have more students in Northland studying earlier," Dr Lyndon said.

World.title: 'Māori data in Māori hands': Experts want Google to adhere to data sovereignty principles
World.content:
Māori tech experts have renewed calls to adhere to Māori data sovereignty principles after a first of its kind partnership with tech giant Google.

In July, Google and Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori (the Māori Language Commission) launched an AI-powered text-to-speech (TTS) model for Google Maps that could correctly pronounce cities and towns with te reo Māori names.

In a statement Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori said all Māori data from the model was placed under the kaitiakitanga of Te Taura Whiri.

"Google has a license to use this data for the purposes of this text-to-speech model. The long-term view remains to establish a consortium of interested groups as long term kaitiakitanga.

"The goal is to ensure Māori academics, researchers and communities who are looking to improve speech or similar technology, would have the ability to access this data, share the benefit and contribute to the evolution of this kaupapa."

University of Waikato computer science professor Te Taka Keegan told RNZ any data generated around reo Māori, tikanga Māori, must stay in Māori hands.

"This was one of the first times where Google has ever produced something where that's been the case. So the IP for the data, not the IP for the actual tool and the technology, the techniques, the algorithms, but the IP for the actual data itself remains with Te Taura Whiri."

Keegan said there were a few Māori organisations that would be suitable to take over guardianship in the long term.

"So what Te Taura Whiri needs to do, and they are aware of this and they should start working on it shortly, what they need to do is they need to find another storage avenue, where the data is held by Māori entities, because Māori entities will protect it, this government won't protect it. Te Taura Whiri is a government organisation."

Waikato University associate professor of Computer Science Te Taka Keegan. RNZ / Libby Kirkby-McLeod

Erena Mikaere (Tūhourangi) is the principal technician at Te Kāhui Raraunga, the operational arm of the Data Iwi Leaders group. She told RNZ in the short term, given that Te Taura Whiri had a duty of care for te reo, they probably came to the right arrangement.

Te Kāhui Raraunga released a Māori data governance model in 2023, aimed at a government audience to understand how to govern data in a way that adheres to a Māori worldview and that adheres to Māori data sovereignty principles, she said.

"We're talking about our reo data for now, which is some of our most precious data, absolutely. The Crown have so much of our data and our job is to advocate for that data to be available for iwi. Put iwi Māori data in iwi Māori hands, that is what we advocate for.

"So we have the tools, we have the resources, and we have the time to support and advise government agencies about how they could do that better. And we do think they need to do that better."

In May, Te Kāhui Raraunga launched its own decentralised data storage network, Te Pā Tūwatawata, and Mikaere said it would be open to having a conversation with Te Taura Whiri about the possibility of storing the Google Maps data set within it.

"Because we know it is the only large scale accessible, safe, sovereign storage solution available in Aotearoa owned by Māori. And we can support a governance model that in fact allows access to that data by the right people, the people who have affinity, who have connection and kinship to that data."

Since the launch of the platform Mikaere said it had been approached by a number private companies who saw that by adhering to the Māori data governance model, they were establishing ethical data governance models for their businesses and for their customers.

World.title: Am I too old to be more aggressive? Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

A stupid question but is 46 too old to change to aggressive for my KiwiSaver?

This isn't personalised advice but in general, I wouldn't think so. It depends on a lot of factors like your personal risk tolerance and your investing timeframe.

Aggressive funds are among the most volatile options in KiwiSaver, and have even more exposure to growth assets than growth funds. They invest in things like equities that can fluctuate in value a lot, and you need to have time to ride out any downturns which could see your fund losing up to about 30 percent in a year. But over the long term, taking more risk tends to pay off. Morningstar data shows aggressive funds have returned an average 10.3 percent a year over the past 10 years, the best of the KiwiSaver bunch.

People are usually told they shouldn't be in an aggressive fund if they don't have 10 to 15 years to stick with it.

That said, even if you were a bit older than you are now, it could work. You don't have to pull all your money out at 65, and you may want to keep some exposure to growth assets at that point to help your investment grow.

I would talk to an adviser.

I've just read your response to a question on whether an individual should put their money into a managed fund or KiwiSaver. Your comment was that it's ultimately up to them but in your response you state that "Once you reach 65, a KiwiSaver fund is much the same as any other managed fund, because there are no restrictions on access to your money".

I've recently been told by a financial adviser that this isn't correct and that if you leave your money in a KiwiSaver fund beyond the age of 65 and the government then change the eligibility age for superannuation, this money is then locked into the KiwiSaver fund until you reach that age. Is this correct?

Technically, yes. But in practice I don't think this is something you need to worry about.

At the moment, access to KiwiSaver is tied to the age of eligibility for NZ Super, which is 65.

So if the age were to be increased, at the moment the law would mean the age of access to KiwiSaver would increase, too.

There are already discussions happening, though, about whether that's appropriate. I would expect access to KiwiSaver to be addressed alongside any plans to increase the NZ Super age.

I know some people think having access to KiwiSaver earlier than NZ Super could be a way to help people who want to stop working earlier, if the pension age rises.

I would also note that even if the age was pushed up without any change to the KiwiSaver rules, it would not be something that would affect you as a recently retired person. These sorts of changes are usually signalled well in advance to take effect over a period of time, usually for future generations.

I'm a real layman in regard to financial matters, and am completely lost - perhaps you could illuminate me a little. Now retired, I contributed to a retirement fund (not KiwiSaver) and recently asked them whether PIE (like in my KiwiSaver) was automatically paid across to IRD.

Their reply as I understood it stated that they pay a base fund 28 percent to IRD - but that PIE does not apply in the instance of retirement funds. I was informed that if I withdraw funds/close my account, then I need to inform this via my IR3 and I will be taxed accordingly at my 17.5 percent rate. My quandary is, does IRD make me pay tax on the entire retirement fund amount, or just on the "growth" aspect which has occurred across the years of investing contributions into that fund, the Teachers Retirement Savings Scheme.

Also, am I better off to perhaps withdraw my retirement scheme funds and have them invested together with my other funds which I have in KiwiSaver?

Very quickly, when you're invested in KiwiSaver you're usually paying tax on the income that your investments make, not the growth in the value of the investments themselves. (There are some complexities around this for foreign investments.)

You don't pay tax on withdrawal, except where there could be a "square up" to do on the tax you would normally pay in the year. You aren't going to be charged tax on the total withdrawal amount, or the growth you've had on your investments while you've been investing, or anything like that.

As for the PIE rate, Dean Anderson at Kernel says it's possible that the fund you're in has a fixed PIE rate of 28 percent. In that case, it could be beneficial for you to move to a multi-rate PIE that could allow you you pay tax at a lower rate.

He says it could be that you can now find a fund that's a better fit for your goals, or you might want to consolidate your money into your other investments. "For someone who's now retired, if you're on a lower tax rate then looking for a multi-rate pie is probably a good option because then they tax is automatically at the correct PIR and does not involve any tax filing.

"One of the benefits at the moment of the New Zealand regime is the fact that for an investor in retirement, why PIRs are really good is there is no capital gains tax, there's no other complexity to worry about. You can get into the right risk profile and then say, 'hey I want to sell down $100 or $1000 or I want to take out some holiday money or create a regular income' and there's nothing they have to think about from a tax perspective, it's all going to get handled."

World.title: AFL chair apologises for his part in Cats concussion contract saga
World.content:
AFL Commission chairman Craig Drummond has apologised for his part in Geelong's controversial concussion contract with defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

Drummond was Geelong president two years ago when premiership defender Kolodjashnij signed a contract in which he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

It is understood Kolodjashnij's agent was not aware of the contract, and neither the AFL Players Association (AFLPA) or AFL were informed at the time.

It is also understood that while Kolodjashnij passed an independent medical test, he was still considered at risk of future complications from head injuries.

Jake's twin brother, Kade, was forced to retire from the game in 2020 due to ongoing concussion problems.

"I was president of the Geelong Football Club in 2024," Drummond said.

"This was an extremely complex and sensitive matter, and obligations to both the player and the club were very carefully considered by the Geelong board.

"Jake's welfare was central to all discussions, and I have been thinking of him particularly over the past few days.

Cats face 'please explain' Geelong is finally issued a 'please explain' over its controversial concussion contract with premiership defender Jake Kolodjashnij.

"While the player was medically cleared to play, the club engaged in lengthy discussions including with him, his family, doctors and insurers about his future and the potential risks of returning to play.

"Regardless of the player's agreement, the club went too far in adding a waiver into an informed consent document and it will be removed."

Drummond said it was an error to keep the process quiet, and clarified that he would not be involved in AFL discussions about the matter.

"As the club has also acknowledged, there was also a process failure in relation to lodgement of the agreement with the AFL and the AFLPA," Drummond said.

"I have not and will not be involved in any deliberation in relation to this matter and its assessment under the AFL rules and regulations.

"I apologise for the mistakes made in this very complex situation."

Speaking to ABC Sport ahead of the Saturday games, AFL boss Andrew Dillon reiterated that it was a complex situation.

"This is an issue that is really complex and in this one in particular it's complex and unique," Dillon said.

"But concussion and the effects that has on players or participants in contact sports ... is an issue that's confronting contact sports worldwide.

"What we have here is a player that has suffered multiple concussions, went before an AFL concussion panel, ultimately over a period of months was cleared as fit to play.

"Through that period, over a number of months, Jake's worked with the club doctors, independent medical experts, the club, and the club board and management to make sure that he understood their were risks to continue playing, not withstanding that you've been cleared medically fit to play.

"That was the intent behind what was going on."

Dillon said the please explain was around why the concussion agreement sat alongside his playing contract.

"We've gone to Geelong under the rules and asked them why it wasn't lodged with us," Dillon said.

"So we're waiting to hear back from Geelong on that."

The Cats are expected to be fined over the contract saga after initially being cleared of wrongdoing.

World.title: Surprise parents' visit inspires new leader in Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney launched a decisive attack up Mont Ventoux to win the seventh stage of the Tour de France Femmes and take the overall lead from Marlen Reusser.

The 2024 champion was in tears as she put on the yellow jersey and now leads 2023 champion Demi Vollering by 15 seconds and Reusser by 39 with two stages left.

"I'm just so tired and so blown away with what just happened," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"When I started climbing I looked to the right and I saw my parents standing on the roadside. They came today by surprise. I saw my father yelling for me and I thought I had to make him proud."

Reusser and Vollering could not follow Niewiadoma-Phinney when she broke away about 9km from the top of Ventoux, one of the most iconic climbs in cycling with its barren, lunar aspect.

It was a first Tour stage win for Niewiadoma-Phinney, who won the 2024 edition without claiming a stage. Gritting her teeth in the final few hundred metres, the Polish rider dug deep and with the sun gleaming behind her, raised her arms after crossing the line.

She then almost lost balance through fatigue and had to be helped off her bike. Moments later, she was all smiles as she sat on the road and poured cooling water over her head.

"I never chase victories for the sake of winning, I target them because I like this beautiful feeling I have right now," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"I came here (before) to Mont Ventoux with my friends and my husband, and we rode up the climb three times.

"The feeling of reaching the top of this mountain was amazing. From that moment, I just wanted to experience that feeling again. The pure joy of riding, as if I was a kid."

Vollering dropped Reusser in the closing stages of the 15.7km ascent of Ventoux, which has featured several time on the men's Tour. In one of the darkest days in Tour history, British rider Tom Simpson died after collapsing during a tortuous ascent in 1967.

World time trial champion Reusser battled gamely but lost valuable time in the title fight. The Swiss rider finished the stage fourth as Vollering and two-time Giro d'Italia winner Elisa Longo Borghini of Italy both placed ahead of her.

There were three smaller climbs heading to Ventoux, which was ranked as a Hors Catégorie ascent — the hardest category — and had a gradient of nearly 9 per cent.

Vollering moved ahead first, and Reusser and Niewiadoma-Phinney joined her as others lagged behind. Niewiadoma-Phinney then attacked and, although Vollering stood up in her saddle to chase her the new race leader was riding a brilliant tempo and proved too strong.

"My idea was that I had to make it to Chalet Reynard on my own," Niewiadoma-Phinney said.

"Because from then on the headwind would be quite strong and the chasers would try to stay on each other's wheel for as long as possible."

The eighth stage is a flat 172km route for sprinters finishing in Nice, where the race ends after another mountain stage on Sunday night.

Stage nine features four sharp climbs of Col d'Èze, nestled in the hills overlooking the Principality of Monaco.

Two years ago, Niewiadoma-Phinney beat Vollering on the final stage to win the race by just four seconds.

World.title: AFL issues Cats a 'please explain' over defender's concussion contract
World.content:
Geelong has been handed a belated 'please explain' notice from the AFL after initially avoiding sanction over its controversial secret deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, a player with a history of concussions.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who on Friday evening identified himself as the player in question, whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

The bombshell concussion case emerged on Thursday and pressure mounted on the league and Geelong after the AFL didn't hand down any punishment that night.

On Friday afternoon, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had signed off on the deal and confirmed the 'please explain' notice.

Geelong's Steve Hocking said the club would provide information to the AFL about Kolodjashnij's contract. (AAP Image: Erik Anderson)

"I take responsibility for the fact that we didn't lodge it with the AFL and the (AFL)PA," Hocking told reporters in Geelong.

"… I have received a letter of 'please explain' from the AFL in relation to this matter, so we'll deal with that over the coming days."

Hocking said not registering the deal was a "misstep" and was uncertain what consequences Geelong would face.

"We've got a 'please explain' letter, and at the appropriate time we'll work through that with the AFL," he said.

"We'll have to respond to that, and then it'll be up to the AFL, and whatever that is, we'll accept."

Later on Friday, Kolodjashnij issued a statement through Geelong, confirming he was the previously unnamed player.

"While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally," Kolodjashnij said.

"I participated fully in the AFL's independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since.

"What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private.

"… I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season."

The 2022 premiership defender, 30, has played 209 games.

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, retired prematurely in 2020 due to concussion.

On Thursday night, calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL had insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

Geelong also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

Grief-stricken mother of star footballer reveals AFL executive phone call West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown says AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother says the phone call was "too little, too late".

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board when the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the AFL statement.

Drummond did not front the media and issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Many AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and former number one draft pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham 'Polly' Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multimillion-dollar concussion class action against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.
